# AI Research Lab

A reusable workspace for academic literature research. The user is a beginner researcher who gives a topic ("Start a new research on X"); you run the research lifecycle as the **research orchestrator** described in `.claude/agents/research-orchestrator.md` (delegation table and state ownership live there).

## Rules (full version: `docs/research-standards.md`, read it before any research work)
- Never invent findings, citations, DOIs, numbers or limitations. Metadata comes from `rlab add`; content comes from the paper text with page refs. Unknown → say "not reported" / "not found".
- Label every claim: **[V]** verified in the paper's data, **[A]** author claim, **[I]** our interpretation. Cite `[@key, p. N]`.
- Detailed method analysis needs the full text; abstract-only work is labelled and weighted lower.
- Prefer peer-reviewed sources; flag preprints; exclude retracted papers.
- Legal open access only. Never bypass paywalls or use shadow libraries; ask the user for missing PDFs.
- Never overwrite or delete `paper.pdf`, `fulltext.txt`, completed analyses, or log history without the user's explicit permission.
- A research gap is claimed only after a recorded novelty check.

## Tools
- `rlab` = `python3 scripts/rlab.py` (run from this directory; `-h` lists commands). Use it for every deterministic step: project creation, search, adding papers (resolves + verifies metadata, rejects duplicates), PDF fetch/attach + text extraction, validation, BibTeX, citation checks, indexing, logging. Never hand-edit `metadata.json`, `registry.json`, `literature-matrix.*`, `references.bib` or `research/INDEX.md`.
- After changing project content, run `rlab index <id>`; log decisions with `rlab log <id> <phase> "<msg>"`.
- Skills (`.claude/skills/`): start-research, discover-papers, analyze-paper, compare-methods, find-gaps, write-literature-review, research-report, resume-research.
- External services in use: OpenAlex, Crossref, arXiv, PubMed, doi.org, Europe PMC (no keys needed). Semantic Scholar is rate-limited without a key: use it via WebFetch only as a fallback. Unpaywall runs only if `RLAB_CONTACT_EMAIL` is set.

## Layout
- `research/registry.json` — all projects (via `rlab`); `research/INDEX.md` — human overview.
- `research/<id>/` — one project: `RESEARCH.md`, `RESEARCH-QUESTIONS.md`, `STATUS.md`, `research-log.md`, `literature-matrix.md/.csv`, `evidence-matrix.md`, `gap-report.md`, `references.bib`, `search/`, `papers/<key>/{metadata.json,paper.pdf,fulltext.txt,analysis.md,paper.bib}`, `reports/`.
- `templates/` — project and analysis templates. `docs/` — standards. `tests/` — `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests`.

## Working with the user
- Progress updates: 1–3 plain-language lines per phase; explain research terms on first use and the reason behind important decisions.
- Handle routine work yourself. Ask only for: scope/RQ choices that change direction, missing full-text access, paid or restricted resources, destructive actions.
- State lives in files, not in conversation memory: keep `STATUS.md` (Next actions, Blocked / needs user) current so any session can resume.

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Already in this codebase?** A helper, util, type, or pattern that already lives here → reuse it. Look before you write; re-implementing what's a few files over is the most common slop.
3. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
6. **Can it be one line?** One line.
7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project — but it runs *after* you
understand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it
touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

**Bug fix = root cause, not symptom.** A report names a symptom. Before you
edit, grep every caller of the function you're about to touch. The lazy fix IS
the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a
guard in every caller — and patching only the path the ticket names leaves
every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins — but only once you understand the problem. The smallest change in the wrong place isn't lazy, it's a second bug.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications that cut a real corner with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic) with a `ponytail:` comment naming the ceiling and upgrade path (`# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`).

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.

# Research standards

The rules every skill and agent in this workspace follows. One source of truth: change rules here, not in individual skills.

## 1. Evidence labels
Every substantive statement about a paper or the literature carries one label:

| Label | Short | Meaning | Requirement |
|---|---|---|---|
| VERIFIED | [V] | Checked against the paper's own data, tables, figures or results text. | Page ref `(key, p. N)` |
| AUTHOR-CLAIM | [A] | The authors state it; we cannot independently check it (e.g. claims of novelty, interpretations, conclusions beyond the data). | Page ref |
| INTERPRETATION | [I] | Our own reasoning, synthesis or critique. | Say what it is based on |

Page refs use the `=== [PDF page N] ===` markers in `fulltext.txt` (PDF page index, not printed page number). When a quote is used, it is copied verbatim from `fulltext.txt`.

Citation syntax:
- Inside a paper's own `analysis.md`: `(p. N)`.
- Everywhere else (evidence matrix, reports, reviews): pandoc style `[@key, p. N]` or `[@key1; @key2]`. Keys are the folder names under `papers/`. This works with `references.bib` and pandoc.
- `rlab cite-check <project> <file...>` must pass before any written document is handed to the user.

## 2. Never invent
- Every DOI, title, author, year and venue comes from `metadata.json` (resolved by `rlab add` from Crossref/OpenAlex/arXiv/PubMed). Never type a DOI from memory.
- Every finding, number, limitation and quote comes from the paper text. If the paper does not report something, write "not reported".
- Every citation in written output uses an existing paper key in the project. A claim with no source is either removed or labelled [I].
- If something cannot be found or verified, say so plainly. An honest "unknown" beats a plausible guess.

## 3. Source quality tiers
Prefer higher tiers; state the tier when it matters to the argument.

1. Peer-reviewed journal articles and full papers at reputable conferences (`venue_kind: published`); systematic reviews and meta-analyses at the top for evidence synthesis.
2. Peer-reviewed workshop papers, book chapters from academic publishers.
3. Preprints (`venue_kind: preprint`, e.g. arXiv): usable, always flagged "not peer-reviewed". If a published version exists, use it instead.
4. Theses, technical reports, grey literature: background only, flagged.
5. Blogs, news, Wikipedia, vendor material: never cited as evidence. May guide searching.

`venue_kind: published` means the work appeared in a journal or proceedings; it is not proof of rigorous review. Watch for predatory venues (unknown publisher, implausibly fast review, no indexing) and flag them.
Retracted papers (`RETRACTED` flag from `rlab`) are excluded from evidence; mention only as retracted.

## 4. Reading depth
- Detailed methodology, dataset, setup, metrics, findings and limitations require the full text (`evidence_basis: full-text`).
- Abstract-only analysis (`evidence_basis: abstract-only`) may fill objective and headline claims labelled [A] only. All method sections say "full text not available". Abstract-only papers carry less weight in synthesis and gap claims; say so.
- Read the whole paper: methods, results, tables, limitations, appendix if relevant. Note skipped parts in "Analyst notes".

## 5. Critical appraisal checklist
For every empirical paper check and record:
- Sample size and how it was chosen; power or uncertainty reporting.
- Baselines and whether they are fair and current.
- Evaluation design: train/test separation, leakage, cross-validation, held-out data, blinding, control groups.
- Statistical testing: tests, effect sizes, confidence intervals, multiple comparisons.
- Reproducibility: data, code, hyper-parameters, protocol available?
- Conflicts of interest and funding where relevant.
- Whether conclusions go beyond the data (mark those [A] and note it).

Evidence strength: **strong** = adequate N, sound design, replicated or consistent across studies; **moderate** = sound design but single study or limited N; **weak** = small/unclear N, design flaws, abstract-only, or preprint without replication.

## 6. Contradictions
When papers disagree: record both sides in the evidence matrix "Contradictions" section with page refs, then compare data, population, method, metric and time. Offer an explanation only as [I]. Never silently pick a side.

## 7. Research gaps and novelty
A gap is reported only when:
1. It is supported by evidence from analysed papers (explicit future-work statements, consistent limitations, contradictions, untested populations/conditions, missing method comparisons).
2. A dedicated novelty check was run: at least 3 targeted searches (`rlab search`) across at least 2 sources, recent years included, plus a web search for very recent work. Queries, date and closest hits are recorded in the gap entry.
3. Confidence is stated. "No paper found" is phrased as "we found no paper that ... (searches on DATE)", never "this has never been studied".

## 8. Copyright and access
- Download only legal open-access copies: OpenAlex/Unpaywall OA locations, arXiv, Europe PMC, publisher OA pages. `rlab fetch` enforces this and refuses shadow libraries.
- Never bypass paywalls, logins, CAPTCHAs, or rate limits. Never use Sci-Hub, LibGen, Anna's Archive or similar.
- When no OA copy exists: tell the user and ask them to obtain it through their library, then `rlab attach`. Otherwise analyse abstract-only and label it.
- Quotes stay short and attributed. PDFs stay inside the project folder and are not redistributed.

## 9. Preservation
- Original PDFs (`paper.pdf`), extracted text (`fulltext.txt`) and completed analyses (`status: complete`) are never overwritten or deleted without the user's explicit permission. A hook asks the user first (once `setup/claude-settings.json` is installed).
- Analysis status flow: `draft` (in progress) -> `ready` (analyst self-check passed) -> `complete` (critical review passed). Fix review findings while the analysis is `ready`.
- Revisions to a completed analysis go in a new section `## Revision YYYY-MM-DD` with what changed and why, after the user agrees.
- `research-log.md` is append-only.

## 10. Talking to the user (a beginner researcher)
- Progress updates: short, what was done, what was found, what is next.
- Explain research terms on first use in one plain sentence (e.g. "a *systematic review* is a study that collects and evaluates all studies on a question").
- Explain important decisions and their reason: scope cuts, exclusions, weak evidence, gaps.
- Ask only for: scope or research-question choices that change the direction, missing full-text access, paid or restricted resources, and anything destructive.

    13	
    14	# PackMonitor: Towards Zero Package Hallucinations via Decoding-Time Monitoring
    15	
    16	- Authors: Liu, Xiting; Liu, Yuetong; Zhang, Yitong; Li, Jia; Hu, Shi-Min
    17	- Year / venue: 2026, Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering (published)
    18	- DOI: 10.1145/3832118 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1145/3832118
    19	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
    20	
    21	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
    22	
    23	Source tier: peer-reviewed (PACMSE, ISSTA 2026 issue, article ISSTA027) (p. 1). The text used is arXiv v2, whose first page carries the ACM DOI and publication data (p. 1).
    24	
    25	## 1. Research objective
    26	- [A] Eliminate package hallucinations in LLM dependency recommendations, not merely reduce them. The argument: package-name validity can be decided against a finite, enumerable authoritative package list, so hallucinated names can be made unreachable during decoding (p. 1, p. 2).
    27	- [A] Achieve this without training, as a plug-in, with low latency and no loss of model utility (p. 1, p. 3).
    28	
    29	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
    30	- [V] RQ1: How effective is PackMonitor at eliminating package hallucinations compared with baselines? (p. 10)
    31	- [V] RQ2: How much efficiency overhead does it add? (p. 10)
    32	- [V] RQ3: Does it degrade general code-generation capability? (p. 10)
    33	- [V] RQ4: How much does DFA caching improve inference efficiency and scalability? (p. 10)
    34	
    35	## 3. Methodology
    36	- Research design: [V] A technique proposal tested by controlled comparison against training-free baselines (RAG, Self-Refinement, RAG+SR) on HFuzzer and against SFT on Package4U. It also includes an ablation (with vs without cache) and a scaling test of DFA construction and loading time (p. 10, p. 12–17).
    37	- Approach / model / intervention:
    38	  - [V] A *Context-Aware Parser*, modelled on a context-free grammar, tracks whether the output is natural language, an ordinary code line, or the package names of an installation command. It recognises code blocks by delimiters such as ```bash and switches intervention on only after `pip install` (grammar `INSTALL_CMD_LINE → pip install PACKAGE_NAMES \n`) (p. 8).
    39	  - [V] A *Package-Name Intervenor* compiles the authoritative list into a deterministic finite automaton (DFA, a state machine that accepts exactly the listed names). A token trie is built from the tokenizer vocabulary. At each step, every token that cannot extend the current prefix towards some allowlisted name gets logit −∞. A terminator is allowed only once the prefix is a complete allowlisted name (p. 6, p. 8–9).
    40	  - [V] A *DFA-Caching Mechanism* builds the DFA once offline, stores it as a checkpoint and loads it at inference time (p. 10).
    41	  - [V] **Required access:** the method masks the model's logits at every decoding step, so it needs next-token logits from a locally decoded model plus that model's tokenizer vocabulary (p. 9). No training and no weight changes (p. 3).
    42	  - [I] It therefore cannot be added to a closed chat API (ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot) that does not expose per-step logits or accept an arbitrary token-level constraint. The paper does not discuss black-box APIs.
    43	- Baselines or comparison conditions:
    44	  - [V] Vanilla; RAG (retrieved valid package names injected into the prompt); Self-Refinement (SR); RAG+SR; and SFT, using the fine-tuned checkpoints released by Spracklen et al. (p. 11, p. 13–14).
    45	  - [V] SR and RAG "follow prior work [41]" (p. 11). The RAG retriever, corpus and k are not reported.
    46	  - [I] No baseline is a simple post-generation registry lookup that blocks invalid names.
    47	
    48	## 4. Dataset and sample
    49	- Data source(s):
    50	  - [V] HFuzzer (Zhao et al., ASE 2025) is the primary evaluation framework. It is a fuzzer in which a tester model (DeepSeek-V3, temperature 0) iteratively writes test cases for the target model (temperature 0.7) (p. 10–12).
    51	  - [V] Package4U, the ~40,000-task dataset of Spracklen et al. (about half Python), is used "in a subset of our experiments", namely the SFT comparison (p. 11, p. 14).
    52	  - [V] HumanEval is used for utility (p. 16).
    53	  - [V] Authoritative list: the PyPI index, 706,618 names "at the time of our experiments", obtained via PyPI's official API (p. 12, p. 19). The snapshot date is not reported.
    54	- Sample size (N) and unit:
    55	  - [V] Five open-weight models: DeepSeek-Coder-Instruct-6.7B, CodeLlama-7b-Instruct, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (p. 11).
    56	  - [V] One HFuzzer round of 1,000 iterations per model × configuration (p. 12).
    57	  - [V] Units are recommended packages (P_total from 231 to 2,288 per run) and responses (Table 2, p. 13).
    58	  - The Package4U subset size is not reported.
    59	- Sampling / selection method: [V] Models follow HFuzzer's selection "to ensure a fair comparison" (p. 11). HFuzzer generates prompts adaptively (p. 10). [I] So each configuration sees a different, self-generated prompt stream.
    60	- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Code is at https://github.com/THU-Agent/PackMonitor (p. 20). Settings are in the supplementary material (p. 19). Release of HFuzzer transcripts: not reported.
    61	
    62	## 5. Experimental setup
    63	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
    64	  - [V] Tester temperature 0 and target temperature 0.7 on HFuzzer; temperature 0 for HumanEval (p. 12, p. 16).
    65	  - [V] **Hallucination decision:** a recommended package counts as hallucinated if it is not a valid PyPI name. The metrics come from Spracklen et al. and HFuzzer (p. 12). [I] Whether HFuzzer's oracle is the same 706,618-name list is not stated. If it is, the 0% result holds by construction.
    66	  - **Stdlib handling:** not reported. [I] This matters little here, because only `pip install` arguments are constrained and scored.
    67	  - **Name normalisation** (case, `-`/`_`): not reported.
    68	  - Handling of version pins, flags (`-U`, `-r`), `python -m pip` and `conda`/`npm`: not reported for the experiments. Other ecosystems are discussed only "in principle" (p. 19).
    69	  - [V] **Hardware:** a server with 8× NVIDIA A100 80 GB, 2× AMD EPYC 7543 (64 cores) and 1 TB RAM, running Ubuntu 22.04 (p. 12). GPUs used per run, inference framework and DFA memory footprint: not reported.
    70	  - [V] **Overhead, with cache:** time per response rises ×1.07–×1.28, i.e. +0.06 s to +0.58 s (Table 4, p. 14). The text says "around 0.2s in the worst case" (p. 15), but CodeLlama goes from 2.4296 s to 3.0130 s (+0.58 s) (p. 14).
    71	  - [V] **Overhead, without cache:** ×2.81–×6.24 (Table 6, p. 17).
    72	  - [V] **DFA build vs load:** building takes 0.021 s (7k names), 4.407 s (700k) and 21.121 s (3,000k); loading takes 0.002–0.247 s (Table 7, p. 17).
    73	- Code availability: [V] Public GitHub repository (p. 20).
    74	
    75	## 6. Evaluation metrics
    76	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
    77	  - [V] PHR is hallucinated packages divided by recommended packages. RHR is the share of responses with at least one hallucinated package. P_hall-unique counts distinct hallucinated names, as a measure of diversity. All three are adopted from prior work (p. 12).
    78	  - [V] P_total checks that the method does not work by suppressing recommendations (p. 13).
    79	  - [V] Mean generation time measures overhead (p. 15). HumanEval Pass@1 measures utility (p. 16).
    80	  - [I] There is no metric of whether the forced package is correct or relevant for the task (cf. Package Utility in djire2026evaluating).
    81	- Statistical testing: [V] None. Single runs. Only Fig. 3 shows a standard deviation of latency (p. 15).
    82	
    83	## 7. Key findings
    84	1. [V] PHR and RHR are 0% on all five models on HFuzzer. For example, DeepSeek-Coder goes from 8.39% / 11.60% (vanilla) to 0% / 0% (Table 2, p. 13). The best baseline is RAG+SR on CodeLlama at 1.30% PHR (p. 13).
    85	2. [V] RAG can increase hallucination. Qwen2.5-Coder PHR goes from 3.25% to 3.33%, and Llama-3 RHR from 6.40% to 7.10% (p. 12–13). SR never reaches zero; DeepSeek-Coder ends at 7.55% PHR (p. 13).
    86	3. [V] On Package4U, SFT lowers PHR from 16.14% to 2.66% (DeepSeek-Coder) and from 26.28% to 10.27% (CodeLlama); PackMonitor gives 0% (Table 3, p. 14). The SFT checkpoints could not run through HFuzzer because their instruction-following was degraded (p. 14).
    87	4. [V] Overhead with cache is ×1.07–×1.28, against RAG up to ×1.70, SR up to ×1.94 and RAG+SR up to ×2.65 (Table 4, p. 14–15).
    88	5. [V] HumanEval Pass@1 is unchanged on all five models (e.g. 72.6% vs 72.6%). The SFT drops of −26.9 and −14.0 pp are quoted from [41], not re-measured (Table 5, p. 16).
    89	6. [V] P_total is described as "comparable", e.g. DeepSeek-Coder 1,847 vs 1,648. But CodeLlama goes from 1,004 to 1,514 (p. 13).
    90	
    91	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
    92	- [A] The guarantee is conditional on the correctness and completeness of the list. A stale snapshot or omissions undermine it, so the list must be refreshed periodically (p. 18–19).
    93	- [A] Timing results may vary with deployment hardware. Effectiveness does not (p. 19).
    94	- [A] Scope is chat-based PyPI recommendations after `pip install` only. It does not cover `requirements.txt`, Dockerfiles, CI configurations or coding-agent workflows (p. 19).
    95	- [A] It targets name validity, not executability, API compatibility or version compatibility (p. 19).
    96	- [A] Generalisability across models is argued from five LLMs plus adversarial HFuzzer prompts (p. 19).
    97	
    98	## 9. Limitations we identified
    99	- [I] **0% is largely by construction.** If PHR is scored against the enforced list, the informative results are only overhead, P_total and utility.
   100	- [I] **"Valid" ≠ safe.** Any name on PyPI passes, including hallucinated names already squatted by attackers, typosquats and malware that has not yet been removed. This is the core slopsquatting case (RQ2). Custom allowlists are mentioned (p. 6, p. 19) but not evaluated.
   101	- [I] **Forced substitutions are unmeasured.** When the model would emit a non-existent name, the mask forces it onto some existing name sharing a prefix. That name may be wrong, or itself a squatted look-alike. There is no relevance metric.
   102	- [I] **Prompt streams differ.** Adaptive fuzzing gives each configuration different prompts: CodeLlama P_total differs by 51%, and RAG+SR yields only 231 packages (p. 13). There is one round per configuration and no variance.
   103	- [I] **The HumanEval test cannot reveal harm.** HumanEval contains almost no `pip install`, and decoding is greedy (p. 16), so the intervenor never fires.
   104	- [I] **Narrow trigger surface.** `import` lines, requirements files, version pins and flags are not covered, so an agent writing `requirements.txt` bypasses the monitor.
   105	- [I] **Some baseline numbers appear borrowed.** The Package4U vanilla figures (16.14%, 26.28%) equal those quoted from [41] (p. 4). It is unclear whether they were re-measured.
   106	- [I] **No CPU measurement.** Overhead was measured on A100s only; the CPU cost of the trie/DFA intersection is unknown.
   107	
   108	## 10. Threats to validity
   109	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Adaptive prompt streams differ per configuration. The tester reacts to target outputs.
   110	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [V] Five open 7–8B models, PyPI only, chat setting only (p. 11, p. 19). No API models, agents or npm.
   111	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] PHR is measured against the enforcement list itself. "Valid" means listed, not safe or correct.
   112	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [V] One round per configuration, no tests or confidence intervals (p. 12–13).
   113	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Code, hardware and temperatures are given (p. 12, p. 20). Missing: snapshot date, normalisation, RAG configuration, Package4U subset.
   114	
   115	## 11. Future research directions
   116	- Stated by authors [A]:
   117	  - Extend to `conda`/`npm` and to private allowlists (p. 19).
   118	  - Cover requirements files, Dockerfiles, CI and agents (p. 19).
   119	  - Address executability and version compatibility (p. 19–20).
   120	  - Refresh the list periodically (p. 19).
   121	- Suggested by us [I]:
   122	  - Test a vetted allowlist (minimum package age or downloads).
   123	  - Measure the relevance of forced substitutions.
   124	  - Use a fixed prompt set across configurations.
   125	  - Compare with a plain registry filter.
   126	  - Measure CPU-only overhead.
   127	
   128	## 12. Relevance to our research
   129	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ3, RQ4, RQ5.
   130	- How it informs our work [I]:
   131	  - **Laptop feasibility:** possible in principle for small local open-weight models. It needs logits but no GPU, and loading the cached DFA takes ≤0.25 s (p. 17). However, it is untested on CPU and not usable with closed APIs.
   132	  - **What it leaves open:**
   133	    - Names that already exist on the registry because an attacker registered them.
   134	    - Correctness of forced substitutions.
   135	    - Surfaces other than `pip install`.
   136	    - npm and other ecosystems.
   137	    - Black-box models.
   138	  - **The cheap competitor:** a client-side registry or allowlist check gives the same "no non-existent name is installed" property without logit access. It is the natural low-compute comparison and was not tested.
   139	
   140	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
   141	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
   142	|---|---|---|---|---|
   143	| RQ3 | Decoding-time DFA logit masking against a PyPI list (706,618 names) yields 0% PHR/RHR on 5 open 7–8B models on HFuzzer, vs residual 1.30–7.55% PHR for RAG/SR/RAG+SR | p. 12–13 | V | moderate |
   144	| RQ3 | RAG can raise hallucination (Qwen2.5-Coder PHR 3.25%→3.33%; Llama-3 RHR 6.40%→7.10%) | p. 12–13 | V | weak |
   145	| RQ3 | Overhead with cached DFA ×1.07–×1.28 per response (A100 server); ×2.81–×6.24 without cache | p. 14, p. 17 | V | moderate |
   146	| RQ3 | HumanEval Pass@1 unchanged with PackMonitor on all 5 models (temperature 0) | p. 16 | V | weak |
   147	| RQ3 | Requires per-step logits and tokenizer of a locally decoded model; training-free | p. 3, p. 9 | V | strong |
   148	| RQ3 | SFT checkpoints still leave 2.66% / 10.27% PHR on Package4U | p. 14 | V | moderate |
   149	| RQ4 | Guarantee conditional on correctness/completeness of the authoritative list; list must be refreshed | p. 18–19 | A | moderate |
   150	| RQ2 | Any registry-present name passes the mask, so already-squatted names are not blocked (vetted allowlists not evaluated) | p. 6, p. 19 | I | moderate |
   151	| RQ5 | Not evaluated: requirements.txt, Dockerfiles, CI configs, coding-agent workflows, non-PyPI ecosystems | p. 19 | A | strong |
   152	
   153	## 14. Key quotes
   154	> "this guarantee is conditional on the correctness and completeness of the given authoritative package list" (p. 18)
   155	
   156	> "do not yet cover broader dependency specifications such as requirements.txt, Dockerfiles, CI configurations, or end-to-end coding-agent workflows" (p. 19)
   157	
   158	> "This list comprises 706,618 valid package names at the time of our experiments" (p. 12)
   159	
   160	## Analyst notes
   161	- Reading coverage: all 23 PDF pages (pp. 20–23 are references). Tables 2–7 extracted cleanly. Fig. 3 is known only from the text.
   162	- Uncertainties:
   163	  - Whether HFuzzer's oracle is the same list.
   164	  - Whether the Package4U numbers were re-measured.
   165	  - The Package4U subset size.
   166	  - The worst-case overhead: the text says ~0.2 s, but Table 4 gives +0.58 s (p. 14–15).
   167	- Funding: Chinese MoE, Tsinghua–Tencent lab, Tsinghua–Keystone centre, Beijing NSF (p. 20). No conflict of interest apparent.

under evaluation. We select DeepSeek-V3 [11] as the tester model, as its strong reasoning and
coding capabilities support effective and diverse code-relevant test case generation.
  ❷ Package4U [41]. In addition to HFuzzer, we also evaluate our approach on a dataset released by
Spracklen et al. [41]. Following the title of the original paper, we refer to this dataset as Package4U.
Package4U contains approximately 40,000 coding tasks generated by LLMs or collected from Stack
Overflow, with around half involving Python programming. Each task consists of a natural language
problem description and code-related context. We use this dataset in a subset of our experiments.
Detailed experimental settings and results are reported in the corresponding sections.

4.2   Models
We evaluate our approach on a set of representative LLMs, as summarized in Table 1. Since PackMon-
itor is model-agnostic and can be applied to different LLMs without modifying their parameters,
we follow the model selection of prior work, i.e., HFuzzer [55], to ensure a fair comparison. The
selected models cover different training objectives, including code-oriented and general-purpose
LLMs, as well as different release periods.
 • DeepSeek-Coder-Instruct-6.7B [17] is released by DeepSeek. It is an instruction-tuned, code-
   oriented LLM designed for programming tasks. In the following, we refer to this model as
   DeepSeek-Coder.
 • CodeLlama-7b-Instruct-hf [40] is released by Meta. It is an instruction-tuned code model in the
   Code Llama family, widely adopted as a strong open-weight baseline for code generation. In the
   following, we refer to this model as CodeLlama.
 • Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct [20] is released by the Qwen team (Alibaba). It is an instruction-
   tuned code model from the Qwen2.5 series, optimized for coding and tool-use style interactions.
   In the following, we refer to this model as Qwen2.5-Coder.
 • Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct [34] is released by Meta. It is a general-purpose instruction-tuned
   LLM that provides a strong non-code-specialized baseline for evaluating robustness beyond
   code-centric training. In the following, we refer to this model as Meta-Llama-3.
 • Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [35] is released by Meta as an updated general-purpose instruction-
   tuned LLM. Compared with Llama-3-8B-Instruct, it improves overall instruction-following and
   capability. In the following, we refer to this model as Meta-Llama-3.1.

4.3   Baselines
Following prior work on mitigating package hallucinations [41], we include three representative
baselines in our evaluation: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), Self-Refinement (SR),
and Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT). Their details are introduced in Section 2.2. we additionally
include a stronger baseline, RAG+SR, which combines Retrieval-Augmented Generation with
post-hoc Self-Refinement: we first apply RAG to inject retrieved package information into the
prompt, and then run SR to verify and refine the model’s generated installation commands.

4.4    Evaluation Metrics
To evaluate the effectiveness of PackMonitor and the compared baselines, we adopt three metrics
proposed by prior work [41, 55] that quantify hallucinated packages in model outputs, as described
below:
    • Package Hallucination Rate (PHR). This metric is defined as the ratio of hallucinated
      packages to the total number of recommended packages.
    • Response Hallucination Rate (RHR). This metric measures the percentage of model re-
      sponses that contain at least one hallucinated package.
    • Number of Unique Hallucinated Packages (𝑃ℎ𝑎𝑙𝑙 −𝑢𝑛𝑖𝑞𝑢𝑒 ). This metric is analogous to a
      commonly used indicator in prior work [54], i.e., the number of unique bugs, and reflects the
      diversity of hallucinated packages generated by the model.

4.5    Implementation Details
For all experiments, we use the PyPI [39] index as the authoritative package list for DFA construction.
This list comprises 706,618 valid package names at the time of our experiments, serving as the
source for monitoring package-name generation.
  For each target model listed in Table 1, we execute one full round of HFuzzer testing (with
each round consisting of 1,000 iterations) with PackMonitor and all baselines. To ensure the
determinism of experimental results, the temperature parameter of the tester model is fixed at 0,
while that of the target model is set to 0.7 to strike a balance between generation creativity and
output stability [7].
  All experiments are conducted on a server equipped with eight NVIDIA A100 GPUs with 80 GB
memory each, two AMD EPYC 7543 CPUs with 32 cores per socket (64 physical cores in total), 1
TB system memory, running Ubuntu 22.04 LTS.

5     Experimental Results
5.1    RQ1: How Effective is PackMonitor in Eliminating Package Hallucinations?
In this RQ, we compare PackMonitor with representative training-free and training-based ap-
proaches for mitigating package hallucinations.
5.1.1 Comparison with training-free methods.
   Settings. We evaluate PackMonitor and the training-free baselines introduced in Section 4.3
on the five LLMs described in Section 4.2, using HFuzzer. We report the main metrics—PHR, RHR,
and 𝑃hall-unique —as defined in Section 4.4. In addition, we include two auxiliary statistics: 𝑃total , the
total number of packages recommended in each HFuzzer round, and 𝑃hall , the total number of
hallucinated packages in each HFuzzer round.
   Results. The results of different approaches are reported in Table 2.
   PackMonitor consistently outperforms all training-free baselines across every model,
reducing all hallucination-related metrics to absolute zero. As shown in Table 2, PackMonitor
eliminates package hallucinations on all five LLMs: for example, on DeepSeek-Coder, the vanilla
setting exhibits a PHR/RHR of 8.39%/11.60%, while PackMonitor achieves 0% PHR/RHR. Similar
results hold for Meta-Llama-3.1 and Qwen2.5-Coder, where PackMonitor consistently drives all
hallucination metrics to zero. These results indicate that PackMonitor provides a strict guarantee
of eliminating package hallucinations and generalizes across model families. In contrast, existing
mitigation methods exhibit limited and sometimes unstable effectiveness. RAG can even increase
hallucination rates in several settings—for instance, on Qwen2.5-Coder, PHR increases from 3.25%
(vanilla) to 3.33% (RAG), and on Meta-Llama-3, RHR increases from 6.40% to 7.10%—which we

Since PackMonitor operates by pruning all generation paths that would lead to hallucinated
package names, a natural concern is that it may substantially reduce the number of package
recommendations produced by the model. To examine this, we report 𝑃 total , the total number of
recommended packages in each fuzzing round. We find that across all models, the 𝑃 total achieved
by PackMonitor is comparable to that of the vanilla model. This indicates that PackMonitor
does not eliminate hallucinations by suppressing package recommendations; instead, it removes
hallucinated packages while preserving the model’s tendency to recommend valid packages.

these SFT models exhibit noticeably degraded instruction-following behavior and often fail to
consistently comply with the strict output format required by HFuzzer, making them incompatible
with the HFuzzer evaluation pipeline. Therefore, following Spracklen et al. [41], we evaluate
training-based methods on the Package4U benchmark and report the corresponding package
hallucination rates.
   Results. The results are shown in Table 3.
   Despite requiring no additional training or parameter updates, PackMonitor offers a
fundamentally stronger guarantee of package-hallucination elimination than training-
based approaches. As shown in Table 3, while SFT substantially reduces hallucination rates, it
does not eliminate them: non-zero hallucination rates of 2.66% on DeepSeek-Coder and 10.27%
on CodeLlama remain, which still pose non-negligible security risks. In contrast, PackMonitor
consistently reduces the package hallucination rate to zero across all experimental configurations.
These results demonstrate that, even compared with training-based methods that require costly
fine-tuning pipelines, PackMonitor not only avoids training overhead but also provides a more
robust and deterministic solution for hallucination elimination.

   mitigation approaches can only reduce package hallucinations and cannot eradicate them.



5.2   RQ2: What is the Efficiency Overhead Introduced by PackMonitor?
Although PackMonitor eliminates package hallucinations, it must remain lightweight to be prac-
tical in real deployments. Therefore, we quantify the overhead introduced by PackMonitor and
compare it against existing approaches.

   Settings. We measure efficiency on HFuzzer. For each HFuzzer round, we evaluate the five
models introduced in Section 4.2 with PackMonitor and all the training-free baselines introduced
in Section 4.3, and report the average generation time (in seconds).
   Results. The results are summarized in Table 4 and visualized in Figure 3.
   The average overhead is small. Table 4 shows that integrating PackMonitor introduces only
a modest and consistent slowdown across all five models, with a normalized inference-time ratio
between ×1.07 and ×1.28. In absolute terms, the added latency is limited: +0.0577s on Qwen2.5-

and standard deviation aggregated across models. Compared with SR and RAG+SR, PackMonitor
exhibits noticeably smaller variance, indicating that its overhead is more predictable and does not
suffer from occasional latency spikes. This stability is expected because PackMonitor performs only
lightweight per-step operations (DFA state transitions and logits masking) during decoding, whereas

iterations (and RAG also adds retrieval-related variability).

5.3   RQ3: Does PackMonitor Degrade the General Code Generation Capability of LLMs?
It is crucial to verify that our proposed PackMonitor does not compromise the model’s general
code generation capabilities. To this end, we evaluate whether PackMonitor affects functional
correctness on a standard code generation benchmark.
  Settings. Following the HumanEval [10] protocol adopted by Spracklen et al. [41], we evaluate
the same models before and after integrating PackMonitor, and report Pass@1 as the metric for
functional correctness. For stability, we set the decoding temperature to 0 for all runs in this RQ.
  Results. The results are shown in Table 5.
  Across all evaluated models, HumanEval performance remains unchanged after incor-
porating PackMonitor. As shown in Table 5, the Pass@1 scores remain unchanged with and
without PackMonitor, indicating that our approach does not degrade general code generation
capability. We attribute this to the fact that PackMonitor only intervenes when the model is
generating package names following installation commands. As a result, PackMonitor eliminates
hallucinated packages without interfering with ordinary code generation, thereby preserving the
original utility.
  The utility preservation of PackMonitor contrasts sharply with SFT. Prior work reports
that although SFT can significantly reduce package hallucinations, it may noticeably hurt general
code generation performance. On HumanEval, the Pass@1 scores of DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B and
CodeLlama-7B drop by 26.9% and 14.0%, respectively [41]. This degradation is expected because
SFT changes model weights and may inadvertently harm general code generation performance.

   Answer to RQ3. On HumanEval, integrating PackMonitor does not change Pass@1 across all
   evaluated models, indicating that PackMonitor preserves general code generation capability.

                                        As Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into software development workflows, their
                                        trustworthiness has become a critical concern. In dependency recommendation scenarios, the reliability of
                                        LLMs is undermined by widespread package hallucinations, where models often recommend hallucinated
                                        packages. Recent studies have proposed a range of approaches to mitigate this issue. Nevertheless, existing
                                        approaches typically merely reduce hallucination rates rather than eliminate them, leaving persistent software
                                        security risks.
                                           In this work, we argue that package hallucinations are theoretically preventable based on the key insight
                                        that package validity is decidable through finite and enumerable authoritative package lists. Building on this,
                                        we propose PackMonitor, the first approach capable of fundamentally eliminating package hallucinations
                                        by continuously monitoring the model’s decoding process and intervening when necessary. To implement
                                        this in practice, PackMonitor addresses three key challenges: ❶ determining when to trigger intervention
                                        via a Context-Aware Parser that continuously monitors model outputs and selectively activates intervening
                                        only during installation command generation; ❷ resolving how to intervene by employing a Package-Name
                                        Intervenor that strictly limits the decoding space to an authoritative package list; and ❸ ensuring monitoring
                                        efficiency through a DFA-Caching Mechanism that enables scalability to millions of packages with negligible
                                        overhead. Extensive experiments on five widely used LLMs demonstrate that PackMonitor is a training-

This disparity clearly demonstrates the necessity of DFA-caching mechanism, which converts the
substantial compilation cost into a one-time offline overhead.
   Without the DFA-caching mechanism, PackMonitor would be required to reconstruct the DFA
online for every inference request. At a future scale where the package list reaches 3,000k entries,
this would incur a construction cost of up to 21.121s per inference—an overhead that is clearly
unacceptable for latency-sensitive LLM inference workloads. By introducing DFA-caching, we shift
the expensive DFA construction entirely to an offline phase, leaving only a lightweight loading
operation at runtime. Empirically, even at the 3,000k scale, DFA loading takes only 0.247s, achieving
an approximately 85× speedup compared to construction time costs. This “build once, reuse many”
strategy effectively decouples inference latency from package list scale, enabling PackMonitor to
support million-scale, continuously evolving ecosystems such as PyPI without incurring perceptible
overhead during online inference.

    Answer to RQ4. Overall, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of the DFA caching
    mechanism in substantially reducing inference latency. Moreover, the consistently low DFA
    loading cost across large package lists confirms that PackMonitor scales to real-world,
    evolving software ecosystems.

6     Discussion
In this section, we discuss several key aspects of PackMonitor beyond the quantitative results. We
first analyze why PackMonitor is able to achieve zero package hallucination under our evaluated
settings, and clarify the scope of this guarantee. We then examine its generalizability across package
ecosystems, highlighting how the framework can be extended beyond the PyPI setting to support
diverse installation commands and customizable package lists. Finally, we systematically analyze
potential threats to the validity of our study.



6.1    Understanding Why Zero Package Hallucination Is Achievable
A central result of our evaluation is that PackMonitor consistently reduces package hallucination
rates to zero across all tested models and settings. This outcome may appear unusually strong,
especially given that prior work has shown hallucinations to be pervasive and difficult to eliminate.
We discuss the key reasons why this guarantee is achievable in our setting.
   First, package-name generation fundamentally differs from many other hallucination-prone
generation tasks. Unlike open-ended natural language, valid package names form a finite and
enumerable list. This property enables PackMonitor to derive an exact validity specification and
to structurally exclude invalid package names from the generation space, rather than attempting to
correct hallucinations after they occur.
   Second, PackMonitor enforces validity directly at the decoding level, rather than relying on
prompt engineering, self-verification, or model retraining. By applying logits-level masking based
on an automaton constructed from an authoritative package list, PackMonitor guarantees that
every generated package-name prefix remains consistent with at least one valid package entry. As a
result, hallucinated packages are not merely discouraged but rendered unreachable by construction.
   It is important to emphasize that this guarantee is conditional on the correctness and completeness
of the given authoritative package list. Under these assumptions, PackMonitor ensures that any
generated package name is valid according to the repository at generation time.

PackMonitor: Towards Zero Package Hallucinations via Decoding-Time Monitoring                           ISSTA027:19


6.2   Generalization Across Package Ecosystems
Our approach is not limited to the PyPI setting (i.e., monitoring package names only after pip
install). Owing to its context-aware parser design, PackMonitor can be readily adapted, in prin-
ciple, to different software ecosystems by applying ecosystem-specific package lists to installation
commands such as conda install and npm install. In addition, the set of legitimate packages is
not fixed and can be manually imported and customized to accommodate specific environments
or private dependency scenarios. This endows PackMonitor with robust generalizability and
practical deployment flexibility across various package ecosystems.

6.3   Threats to Validity
We now discuss potential threats to the validity of our study and how we mitigate them:
   ❶ Generalizability Across Models. One potential threat concerns whether our findings gener-
alize beyond the specific models. To reduce this threat, we conducted experiments on five widely
used LLMs with diverse architectures, training data, and instruction-tuning strategies. In addi-
tion, we evaluated PackMonitor using HFuzzer, which generates a broad and adversarial set of
dependency-related prompts. These choices increase confidence that our results are not artifacts of
a particular model or prompt distribution.
   ❷ Dependence on Authoritative Package Lists. PackMonitor relies on an externally main-
tained authoritative package list as the ground truth for package-name intervenor. Any errors or
omissions in this list (e.g., misrecorded entries or missing packages) could undermine the correct-
ness of PackMonitor. In our experiments, we obtained the package list via PyPI’s official API.
However, package ecosystems evolve continuously: new packages are published and existing ones
may be deprecated over time. To maintain long-term effectiveness, a practical deployment can
incorporate a periodic update mechanism to refresh the authoritative list snapshot and synchronize
it with the latest ecosystem state, thereby preserving the hallucination-prevention guarantee.
   ❸ Impact of Deployment Environments. For LLMs, generation speed is a critical metric. In our
experiments, we evaluated a range of speed-related indicators (e.g., model generation latency, DFA
construction time). These metrics typically fall within the millisecond-to-second range, making
them potentially sensitive to variations in deployment environments (e.g., differences in GPU
or CPU specifications). However, this threat is mitigated by the fact that our core effectiveness
(e.g., hallucination-prevention) is independent of such environmental factors. To further support
reproducibility across environments, we have made detailed experimental settings available in the
Supplementary Materials, and our code repository is publicly accessible. These efforts allow our
experiments to be replicated across different devices without compromising the validity of core
conclusions.
   ❹ Scope of Evaluated Contexts and Downstream Executability. Our current implementa-
tion and evaluation focus on chat-based PyPI dependency recommendations after pip install
commands. Therefore, our findings should be interpreted within this monitored setting, and do not
yet cover broader dependency specifications such as requirements.txt, Dockerfiles, CI configu-
rations, or end-to-end coding-agent workflows. In addition, PackMonitor targets package-name
validity rather than full program executability, since a valid package may still be API-incompatible,
version-sensitive, or environment-dependent. We leave these broader evaluations to future work.
   Overall, PackMonitor demonstrates that package hallucinations—often regarded as a challenging
failure mode of LLMs—can be prevented under well-defined monitoring mechanism. By shifting
from post-hoc mitigation to design-level prevention, our approach provides strong package-name
validity guarantees guarantees while preserving generation quality and efficiency. At the same
time, we acknowledge that these guarantees do not cover all dependency specification contexts or

et al. propose monitor-guided decoding, which uses static analysis over repository context to
guide Code LM decoding and avoid invalid continuations, such as unavailable or inconsistent
API usages [1]. These studies show that decoding-time constraints can effectively improve code
generation reliability by leveraging deterministic information from programming languages and

   Our work is inspired by this line of research, but focuses on package hallucination, where the
validity of generated package names can be checked against a finite and enumerable package

2.4   Motivation
The constrained decoding perspective provides a natural way to revisit package hallucinations.
Package installation in software development exhibits a key characteristic that distinguishes it from
many open-ended factuality problems: package-name validity is decidable under a given software
ecosystem. For a given package ecosystem, such as PyPI [39], npm [37], or Maven [4], a finite and
enumerable list of valid package names can be obtained as ground truth, either from an official
registry snapshot or a curated allowlist. Thus, for any candidate package name, its membership in
this list is unambiguous: it either belongs to the set or not.
   This decidability property allows package hallucination to be formulated as a constrained
decoding problem. Consider the hallucinated package example in Figure 1: when prompted to install
Protocol Buffers, an LLM may suggest “google-protobuf” due to spurious statistical correlations
learned from its training data. While “google.protobuf” is a legitimate Python import path, it is
not a valid package name in the predefined authoritative package list. With access to such an
allowlist, PackMonitor intervenes in real time as the LLM generates a package name token by token.
Conceptually, PackMonitor intervenes as follows: for each candidate next token, PackMonitor
checks whether appending the token would keep the current partial string consistent with at
least one allowlisted package name (i.e., whether the updated prefix remains a valid prefix for any
legitimate package name in the allowlist). If a token would lead the generation process to a state
where no allowlisted package name can be matched by any subsequent continuation, selecting the
token would inevitably result in an invalid package name; PackMonitor thus masks the token by
setting its corresponding logit value to −∞. Meanwhile, a termination token (e.g., whitespace or
newline) is allowed only if the current prefix already constitutes a complete, allowlisted package
name. In this manner, PackMonitor prunes all token choices that would inevitably result in a
hallucinated package, while preserving all valid package name completions.
   However, making this idea practical requires addressing two challenges that are specific to
package hallucination. First, package-name constraints should not be applied globally. LLM re-
sponses often contain natural language explanations, code snippets, comments, and ordinary shell
commands. Enforcing package-name constraints over the entire output would unnecessarily restrict
the model and may degrade its general generation capability. Therefore, PackMonitor introduces
a context-aware parser that continuously monitors the output but activates strict constrained
decoding only when package names are being generated in installation commands. Second, package
ecosystems are large and continuously evolving, making naive constraint construction inefficient.
To address this issue, PackMonitor compiles the authoritative package list into a DFA and in-
troduces a caching mechanism to reuse the constructed automaton during inference. In this way,
PackMonitor adapts the general idea of constrained decoding to the package hallucination problem
by formalizing package-name validity as a finite constraint space, applying constraints only in the
appropriate generation context, and making the approach efficient enough for large-scale package
registries.

4     Experimental Setup
This section describes our experimental setup, including the benchmarks, baseline methods, evalu-
ation metrics, selected models, and implementation details. Under this setup, we conduct a series
of experiments to answer the following Research Questions (RQs):
    • RQ1: How effective is PackMonitor in eliminating package hallucinations?
      This RQ evaluates whether PackMonitor can eliminate package hallucinations across different
      models and compares its performance against existing baselines.
    • RQ2: What is the efficiency overhead introduced by PackMonitor?
      This RQ measures the efficiency impact of PackMonitor by comparing the average generation
      speed (or latency) before and after integrating PackMonitor.
    • RQ3: Does PackMonitor degrade the general code generation capability of LLMs?
      This RQ examines whether PackMonitor affects the general code generation capability of
      LLMs.
    • RQ4: How much does DFA-caching mechanism improve inference efficiency and
      scalability?
      This RQ is studied via an ablation analysis comparing cached versus non-cached settings, and
      further characterizing how inference latency scales with increasing package-list sizes.

4.1    Benchmarks
To evaluate package hallucinations in LLMs, we adopt two benchmarks in our experiments: the
HFuzzer framework [55] and an open-source coding dataset released by Spracklen et al. [41].
   ❶ HFuzzer [55]. We adopt HFuzzer as our primary evaluation framework. HFuzzer is a fuzzing
framework designed to systematically probe failure modes of LLMs through iterative test case
generation. Compared to conventional fixed test cases, HFuzzer can continuously explore diverse
generation patterns and effectively induce previously unseen hallucinated packages. In the experi-
ments, HFuzzer involves two cooperating models: a tester model for test case generation, and a
target model responsible for code generation and package recommendation, serving as the model

    13	
    14	# Evaluating Inference-Time Defenses against Package Hallucination in LLM-Generated Code
    15	
    16	- Authors: Djire, Alberick Euraste; Olatunji, Iyiola E.; Tessa, Melissa; Barr, Earl T.; Klein, Jacques; Bissyandé, Tegawendé F.
    17	- Year / venue: 2026, Proceedings of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (published)
    18	- DOI: 10.1145/3832783.3837555 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1145/3832783.3837555
    19	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
    20	
    21	Labels: **[V]** verified · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
    22	
    23	Source tier: peer-reviewed (ASE 2026) (p. 1). The text used is arXiv v1, which carries the ACM DOI (p. 1).
    24	
    25	## 1. Research objective
    26	- [A] Four contributions (p. 1–2):
    27	  - Correct registry-based measurement, which misclassifies standard-library modules as hallucinations.
    28	  - Evaluate seven inference-time defences.
    29	  - Introduce a Package Utility (PU) metric.
    30	  - Stress-test the defences with adversarial prompts.
    31	- [A] The focus is small open models, because they hallucinate more and run on resource-constrained hardware (p. 2, p. 4).
    32	
    33	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
    34	- [V] RQ1: How does baseline PHR vary across model families and languages once stdlib imports are accounted for?
    35	- [V] RQ2: How effective is guided decoding compared with RAG and Self-Refine?
    36	- [V] RQ3: What is the trade-off between mitigation and utility?
    37	- [V] RQ4: How robust are the defences to prompts seeded with fabricated names? (p. 3)
    38	
    39	## 3. Methodology
    40	- Research design: [V] Factorial comparison: 8 models × 4 languages (Python, JavaScript, Ruby, Rust) × vanilla + 7 strategies. Each runs on the full D_eval with 3 independent runs (p. 3, p. 5).
    41	- Approach / model / intervention (with **required access**):
    42	  - [V] **Greedy:** T=0 (p. 5). [I] Works with an API.
    43	  - [V] **Contrastive Decoding (CD):** α=0.5, "amateur/expert layer pairing (model-specific)" (Table 1, p. 5). The text describes subtracting a smaller amateur model's log-probabilities (p. 4). [I] It needs logits from two models (or layers); the description is inconsistent.
    44	  - [V] **DoLa:** contrasts the final layer with early layers {4, 8, 12, 16}; repetition penalty 1.2 (p. 5). [I] White-box: needs intermediate hidden states.
    45	  - [V] **ALCD:** DoLa plus an entropy ≥1 activation policy (p. 5). [I] White-box.
    46	  - [V] **Nudging:** the surrogate is the largest model in the family; top-probability threshold 0.4 (p. 5). [I] Needs token probabilities plus a second model.
    47	  - [V] **Self-Refine:** up to 5 iterations of self-critique (p. 4–5). [I] Black-box. Whether the critique sees registry data is not reported.
    48	  - [V] **RAG:** retrieval k=5 over a per-language registry corpus, following Spracklen et al.'s top-k setup (p. 4–5). Retriever and embedder: not reported. [I] Black-box model plus an external index.
    49	  - [A] CD and Nudging run two models at once, so model sizes were capped to fit one GPU (p. 4).
    50	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] Vanilla decoding with T=1.0, top-k 50, top-p 1.0 (p. 4–5). One fixed configuration per strategy, based on Shi et al. (p. 4).
    51	
    52	## 4. Dataset and sample
    53	- Data source(s):
    54	  - [V] Step 1: the top 1,000 most popular packages per registry via the Libraries.io API, as (name, description) pairs (p. 3).
    55	  - [V] Step 2: full registry name lists "as of March 4, 2026", plus standard-library module lists. The ground truth P_ℓ is registry ∪ stdlib (p. 3).
    56	  - [V] Step 3: GPT-4o-mini writes one coding instruction per pair. The system prompt asks for a bracketed package list (p. 3).
    57	- Sample size (N) and unit:
    58	  - [V] D_eval has 4,000 instructions, 1,000 per language (p. 3).
    59	  - [V] Eight models: gemma-1b/4b, deepseek-coder-1.3b/6.7b, qwen2.5-1.5b/3b, mistral-7b-Instruct-v0.3, llama-3.1-8b (p. 3).
    60	  - [V] Generated packages per configuration range from 1,470 to 32,337 (Table 3, p. 6).
    61	- Sampling / selection method:
    62	  - [V] Adversarial set: 1,000 non-existent names each for Python and JavaScript, produced by Meta-Llama, Alibaba and OpenAI GPT models, verified absent from npm/PyPI by direct lookup. The same names are reused as seeds for Ruby and Rust and placed into "install and use" templates, giving 4,000 prompts (p. 9).
    63	  - [V] Code-generation extension: the same instructions, asking for runnable code; imports are validated against the same snapshots (p. 6).
    64	- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Code, datasets and instructions on Zenodo record 21786704 (p. 11).
    65	
    66	## 5. Experimental setup
    67	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
    68	  - [V] **Hallucination decision:** a name is "classified as hallucinated if and only if it is absent from P_ℓ" (p. 4).
    69	  - Not reported:
    70	    - Name normalisation.
    71	    - Output-parser details.
    72	    - How code-generation imports are mapped to distribution names (e.g. `cv2` → `opencv-python`).
    73	  - [V] **Stdlib:** manifests were collected for "the two applicable languages" (Python, Ruby) (p. 5), although Step 2 says every snapshot is augmented (p. 3). [I] Treatment of JavaScript and Rust built-ins is unclear.
    74	  - [V] **Hardware:** "within the memory budget of a single GPU" (p. 4). GPU type, inference library and runtimes: not reported.
    75	  - **Overhead/latency of the strategies:** not reported.
    76	  - [V] **Code quality:** Semgrep syntax-error rate and code-smell count (p. 7).
    77	  - [V] Mean ± SD over 3 runs; per-run values are in the artifact (p. 5).
    78	- Code availability: [V] Zenodo (p. 11).
    79	
    80	## 6. Evaluation metrics
    81	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
    82	  - [V] Micro-PHR pools all generated names. Macro-PHR averages per prompt, and a prompt with no output counts as 0 (p. 4). [I] Macro-PHR therefore rewards silence.
    83	  - [V] PU is the F1 of precision and recall against R_i: the seed package plus the k−1 packages with most similar descriptions (text-embedding-3-small, cosine), k ∈ {1, 2, 5, 10}, plus a reference set derived from generated code. PU is 0 for empty outputs (p. 4, p. 7). [A] PU "remains a semantic proxy" (p. 4).
    84	  - [V] Syntax-error rate and mean smell count (p. 7–8).
    85	- Statistical testing: [V] Mean ± SD over 3 runs. No significance tests or confidence intervals. Counts like "19 of 32" are not corrected for multiple comparisons (p. 5–10).
    86	
    87	## 7. Key findings
    88	1. [V] **Stdlib correction:** pooled Python vanilla PHR is 24.7% with stdlib vs 32.3% without (+7.6 pp). The maximum is +9.4 pp (Self-Refine); Ruby ranges +1.6 to +2.5 pp (Table 2, p. 5). [V] Table 3's Python counts sum to N_gen 79,965 and N_hall 19,776, which gives 24.7% (p. 6).
    89	2. [V] **Baseline:** corrected vanilla micro-PHR ranges from 16.1% (Mistral-7b) to 47.9% (Qwen-1.5b) overall, peaks at 63.1% (Qwen-1.5b, Rust) and is lowest at 7.6% (Mistral, JavaScript). Larger in-family models cut PHR by 18.3–20.3 pp (p. 5–6).
    90	3. [V] **Defences:**
    91	   - RAG has the lowest PHR in 19 of 32 configurations and lowers the cross-model average from 29.7% to 18.1%. But it raises JavaScript PHR for 7 of 8 models, by 12.7 pp on average (p. 6).
    92	   - Greedy matches Self-Refine at 25.6% average PHR (p. 6).
    93	   - DoLa is the worst guided method at 38.0% overall, and 83.5–91.2% on DeepSeek-1.3b (p. 6).
    94	   - CD is never lowest, and ALCD mostly underperforms vanilla (p. 6–7).
    95	4. [V] **Utility:** Greedy gives the best trade-off, with the highest PU under all five reference sets. PU recall falls from 23.4 (Top-1) to 2.7 (Top-10). DeepSeek models have near-zero PU (p. 7–8).
    96	5. [V] **Code quality:** vanilla and greedy decoding keep near-perfect syntax, while guided strategies add syntax errors, e.g. a 29% rate for DeepSeek-6.7b on Rust under Nudging (p. 7). In code generation, Self-Refine increases both valid and hallucinated references (p. 6).
    97	6. [V] **Adversarial prompts:**
    98	   - Vanilla PHR spans 46.6–92.5%; Mistral-7b rises by 47.8 pp on average. Ruby is the most vulnerable and Rust the most resistant language for every model (p. 9).
    99	   - RAG or Self-Refine gives the lowest PHR in 29 of 32 settings, RAG alone in 16. The lowest value is 11.4% (Gemma-4b, Python, RAG) (p. 10).
   100	   - DoLa is worse than Greedy in 24 of 32 (p. 10).
   101	
   102	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
   103	- [A] Prompts are synthetic (GPT-4o-mini), with no human validation or comparison to real developer queries (p. 10).
   104	- [A] Only 8 small open models and 4 ecosystems. Results may not generalise to larger models, other languages or private registries (p. 10).
   105	- [A] One fixed hyperparameter configuration per strategy, so rankings are not upper bounds (p. 10).
   106	
   107	## 9. Limitations we identified
   108	- [I] **Internal inconsistencies:**
   109	  - The abstract says RAG "reduces PHR in 18 of 32" settings; the results say it has the "lowest PHR in 19 of 32" (p. 1 vs p. 6–7).
   110	  - The abstract says PHR rises "up to 45 pp"; the conclusion says "up to 58.1 pp" (p. 1 vs p. 11). Mistral's +47.8 pp average (p. 9) already exceeds 45.
   111	  - The conclusion says CD "reduced hallucination in 19 of 32" settings and that Nudging is the best trade-off. The results say CD is never lowest and Greedy is the best trade-off (p. 11 vs p. 6–8).
   112	  - Table 1 describes CD as a layer pairing; the text describes two models (p. 4–5).
   113	  - Stdlib augmentation is said to apply to every snapshot vs only "two applicable languages" (p. 3 vs p. 5).
   114	- [I] **Suspicious table values:** Table 4 shows Greedy identical to Vanilla in all 4 languages for deepseek-6.7b and llama-8b (p. 7), although Vanilla is sampled at T=1.0 over 3 runs. This looks like a copy error.
   115	- [I] **Popularity-seeded prompts:** prompts are built from the 1,000 most popular packages, so the right answer is usually a well-known name. RAG retrieves descriptions from the same registry and may simply retrieve the seed package, which flatters RAG and may understate hallucination on niche tasks.
   116	- [I] **No release-date cutoff:** the ground truth is the current snapshot (2026-03-04). Names registered after model training, including squatted hallucinations, count as valid.
   117	- [I] **No cost data:** no latency or memory figures, although the defences are presented as practical. CD and Nudging double the model count.
   118	- [I] **Missing defences:** neither PackMonitor-style constrained decoding nor a plain registry filter is evaluated.
   119	- [I] **Adversarial seeds:** seeds for Ruby and Rust were only checked as absent from npm/PyPI (p. 9). Scoring is still snapshot-based, so this affects prompt design, not scoring.
   120	
   121	## 10. Threats to validity
   122	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Synthetic prompts; possible retrieval of the seed package by RAG; inconsistent reporting.
   123	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [V] Small open 1–8B models only (p. 10). No API models or agents.
   124	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [V] PU is a semantic proxy based on embedding similarity (p. 4). [I] Macro-PHR counts empty outputs as 0.
   125	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [V] 3 runs with SD reported; no tests (p. 5).
   126	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Zenodo artifact and Table 1 hyperparameters (p. 5, p. 11). Hardware and parser are unspecified.
   127	
   128	## 11. Future research directions
   129	- Stated by authors [A]:
   130	  - Make per-language stdlib exclusion a baseline requirement (p. 11).
   131	  - Test indirect prompt injection and multi-turn manipulation (p. 11).
   132	  - Combine guided decoding with lightweight registry verification at inference time (p. 11).
   133	- Suggested by us [I]:
   134	  - Report latency on CPU.
   135	  - Add a registry-filter baseline and constrained decoding.
   136	  - Use release-date-aware ground truth.
   137	  - Use real developer prompts.
   138	  - Test agentic install flows.
   139	
   140	## 12. Relevance to our research
   141	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5.
   142	- How it informs our work [I]:
   143	  - **Laptop feasibility:** Greedy (T=0), Self-Refine and RAG need no internal access and were tested on 1–8B models. The 1–4B models are plausible on a laptop CPU, but the paper gives no runtimes. DoLa, ALCD, CD and Nudging need white-box access and sometimes two models.
   144	  - **Methodology lesson for our measurement:** use a dated snapshot plus a stdlib manifest, and report micro and macro PHR.
   145	  - **What it leaves open:**
   146	    - Overhead and cost.
   147	    - Registry-verification defences.
   148	    - Constrained decoding.
   149	    - Agents and indirect injection.
   150	    - Larger or closed models.
   151	
   152	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
   153	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
   154	|---|---|---|---|---|
   155	| RQ4 | Treating stdlib modules as hallucinations inflates Python PHR by +7.6 pp (vanilla) up to +9.4 pp; Ruby ≤ +2.5 pp | p. 5 | V | moderate |
   156	| RQ4 | Hallucination = name absent from registry snapshot (2026-03-04) ∪ stdlib manifest | p. 3–4 | V | strong |
   157	| RQ1 | Corrected vanilla micro-PHR 16.1% (Mistral-7b) to 47.9% (Qwen-1.5b); up to 63.1% (Qwen-1.5b Rust); larger in-family models −18 to −20 pp | p. 5–6 | V | moderate |
   158	| RQ3 | RAG lowest PHR in 19/32 settings, average 29.7%→18.1%, but raises JavaScript PHR by 12.7 pp on 7/8 models | p. 6 | V | moderate |
   159	| RQ3 | Greedy decoding (T=0, black-box) gives best average mitigation–utility trade-off (PHR 29.7%→25.6%, highest PU) | p. 6, p. 8 | V | moderate |
   160	| RQ3 | Guided decoding (DoLa/ALCD/CD/Nudging) needs internal access and often fails; DoLa worst (38.0% avg) and adds syntax errors | p. 5–7 | V | moderate |
   161	| RQ1 | Adversarial prompts seeded with fake names raise vanilla PHR to 46.6–92.5%; Ruby most vulnerable for all 8 models | p. 9 | V | moderate |
   162	| RQ3 | Under adversarial prompts RAG or Self-Refine is best in 29/32 settings; decoding-only defences unreliable | p. 10 | V | moderate |
   163	| RQ5 | Latency/overhead of defences not reported; registry verification + guided decoding left as future work | p. 4, p. 11 | A | moderate |
   164	
   165	## 14. Key quotes
   166	> "A recommended name is classified as hallucinated if and only if it is absent from Pℓ" (p. 4)
   167	
   168	> "we collected the complete list of package names available in each registry as of March 4, 2026" (p. 3)
   169	
   170	> "inference within the memory budget of a single GPU" (p. 4)
   171	
   172	## Analyst notes
   173	- Reading coverage: all 13 PDF pages. The Figure 3 heatmaps (PU) and Figure 2 are partly garbled in extraction, so I used the text's summary values only.
   174	- Uncertainties: Table 4 Greedy=Vanilla rows; stdlib handling for JavaScript and Rust; abstract–body–conclusion inconsistencies (§9).
   175	- Funding: Luxembourg MFA (D4D/LuxWAyS), ERC NATURAL (p. 11).
