     9	main_finding: Localized LoRA editing cuts Package-HR on high-risk prompts by 79.9% (edit) and 65.4% (unseen) relative, keeping Valid-Rate and HumanEval within ±2%.
    10	relevance: medium
    11	analysed: 2026-11-12
    12	---
    13	
    14	# Mitigating Package Hallucinations in Large Language Models via Model Editing
    15	
    16	- Authors: Liu, Shuhan; Zhao, Yukai; Hu, Xing; Liu, Kui; Yang, Xiaohu; Xia, Xin
    17	- Year / venue: 2026, arXiv (preprint)
    18	- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2607.02052 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02052
    19	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
    20	
    21	Labels: **[V]** verified · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
    22	
    23	Source tier: preprint (arXiv v1, July 2026), **not peer-reviewed** (p. 1). Three of the authors (Zhao, Hu, Xia) also wrote HFuzzer (zhao2025hfuzzer).
    24	
    25	## 1. Research objective
    26	- [A] Propose BOUND, a lightweight localized model-editing framework. It treats package hallucination as a "package-validity boundary" problem: the model's ability to tell valid from hallucinated names in a given task context. The goal is to suppress hallucinated names while keeping valid ones (p. 1–2).
    27	
    28	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
    29	- [V] RQ1: How effective is BOUND compared with package-hallucination mitigation and model-editing methods?
    30	- [V] RQ2: Does it generalise to other package-related tasks?
    31	- [V] RQ3: Ablation of its components (p. 6).
    32	
    33	## 3. Methodology
    34	- Research design: [V] Technique proposal with controlled comparison on 4 edit folds of 50 prompts each, plus ablation, cost and HumanEval checks (p. 5–9).
    35	- Approach / model / intervention:
    36	  - [V] **Localization:** one forward pass per high-risk prompt. A boundary risk score is computed at the first answer token as LSE(logits of hallucinated-name tokens) − λa·LSE(logits of valid-name tokens), then back-propagated through the frozen model. Saliency is mean |∇W R ⊙ W| per projection matrix (q, k, v, o, gate, up, down) over all layers. The top 5 modules are selected (p. 3–4, p. 6).
    37	  - [V] **Editing:** LoRA with r=8, α=16, dropout 0.05, lr 2×10⁻⁴, 3 epochs, batch 1 (p. 6).
    38	  - [V] **Loss:** valid-package NLL + unlikelihood on hallucinated names + locality KL, weighted 1.0 / 0.15 / 0.03 (p. 4–6).
    39	  - [V] **Required access:** full white-box access (weights, logits and gradients), plus a GPU training run per model. PyPI metadata is needed to label valid and hallucinated names when building edit cases (p. 3–5). [I] At inference only the LoRA adapter is needed, with no registry access.
    40	- Baselines or comparison conditions:
    41	  - [V] Full-FT (Spracklen et al.) and Self-Refinement (up to 5 rounds; the model's packages are checked for validity, and invalid ones go into an avoidance list).
    42	  - [V] ROME, MEMIT and DINM, adapted with defaults. All trainable baselines use the same edit cases (p. 5–6).
    43	  - [I] Self-Refinement here gets registry-oracle feedback.
    44	
    45	## 4. Dataset and sample
    46	- Data source(s): [V] The "recent Python subset" of the LLM-generated prompt dataset of Spracklen et al., built from descriptions of popular Python packages (p. 5).
    47	- Sample size (N) and unit (Table I, p. 5):
    48	
    49	| Model | High-risk prompts | Edit prompts | Unseen evaluation |
    50	|---|---|---|---|
    51	| DeepSeekCoder | 741 | 4×50 | 541 |
    52	| Qwen3 | 609 | 4×50 | 409 |
    53	| Llama-3.1 | 1,134 | 4×50 | 934 |
    54	
    55	  - [V] Transfer and ablation use 100 random prompts from the unseen set (p. 7–8).
    56	- Sampling / selection method: [V] Each prompt is queried 5 times and kept as "high-risk" if Sample-HR > 0.5 (p. 5). The size of the pool before filtering is not reported.
    57	- Data availability (public? link?): not reported.
    58	
    59	## 5. Experimental setup
    60	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
    61	  - [V] Models: deepseek-coder-6.7b-instruct, Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. PyTorch + HuggingFace Transformers, bf16 (p. 6).
    62	  - [V] Generation: 5 samples per prompt, T=0.7, top_p 0.9. Maximum 128 tokens for recommendation and `pip install` tasks, 2,048 for code generation (p. 6).
    63	  - [V] **Hallucination decision:** a package is valid only if it exists on PyPI *and* has at least one release before the model's knowledge cutoff; otherwise it is hallucinated (p. 5).
    64	  - Not reported: the PyPI query date (the reference lists "accessed: 2026-06-14", p. 11), per-model cutoff dates, stdlib handling and normalisation.
    65	  - [V] Extraction uses regular expressions, with one-shot prompting to fix the output format (p. 9).
    66	  - [V] Code generation: imports are extracted, and the **unedited base model** maps them to PyPI names (p. 7).
    67	  - [V] **Hardware:** Ubuntu 22.04, 2× Xeon Platinum 8358P (64 cores), 1 TB RAM, 8× A100-SXM4 80 GB (p. 6). GPUs per run: not reported.
    68	  - [V] **Cost (Table V, averaged across models, p. 9):**
    69	
    70	| Method | Localization | Edit | Test time per case | Artifact |
    71	|---|---|---|---|---|
    72	| BOUND | 23.81 s | 83.09 s | 11.30 s | 731.03 KB |
    73	| Full-FT | – | 124.16 s | 15.31 s | 14.27 GB |
    74	| Self-Refinement | – | – | 25.12 s | – |
    75	
    76	  - What a "case" is: not defined.
    77	- Code availability: not reported.
    78	
    79	## 6. Evaluation metrics
    80	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
    81	  - [V] Sample-HR is the share of answers with at least one hallucinated name. Package-HR is the share of hallucinated names among extracted names. Valid-Rate is the share of answers with at least one valid name, which says nothing about semantic correctness (p. 6).
    82	  - [V] Changes are reported as **relative** percentages (p. 6).
    83	  - [V] HumanEval pass@1 and pass@10 (p. 9).
    84	- Statistical testing: [V] None. Averages over 4 folds × 5 samples; no variance (p. 6, p. 9).
    85	
    86	## 7. Key findings
    87	1. [V] **Edit prompts (average):** Sample-HR 0.8500 → 0.2050 (−75.9%), Package-HR 0.4463 → 0.0897 (−79.9%), Valid-Rate 0.8013 → 0.8527 (p. 6).
    88	2. [V] **Unseen prompts:** Sample-HR 0.8573 → 0.3113 (−63.7%), Package-HR 0.4421 → 0.1529 (−65.4%), against −37.8% for Full-FT (p. 6–7). [V] Residual Package-HR on unseen prompts is 0.0927–0.1955 (Table II, p. 7).
    89	3. [V] **Collapse in baselines:** ROME and DINM lower hallucination by collapsing output. Llama ROME has Valid-Rate 0.0110 (p. 7). In the `pip install` task, ROME and Full-FT on Llama reach 0 HR together with 0 Valid-Rate (p. 8).
    90	4. [V] **Transfer:** Package-HR −12.8% in code generation and −34.0% in `pip install` recommendation (p. 7–8).
    91	5. [V] **HumanEval:** changes stay within ±2%, e.g. DeepSeekCoder pass@1 68.96% → 67.58% (Table VI, p. 9).
    92	6. [V] **Ablation:** without hallucinated-name unlikelihood, Package-HR rises from 0.1508 to 0.5646. Without valid-package NLL, Valid-Rate falls from 0.8248 to 0.1512 (p. 9).
    93	
    94	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
    95	- [A] Regex extraction may miss packages; randomness is handled by 5 samples and 4 folds; localization may be noisy (p. 9).
    96	- [A] Only three open models; commercial models were excluded for reproducibility (p. 10).
    97	- [A] PyPI only (p. 10).
    98	- [A] Three tasks only, not configuration files, build scripts or repository workflows (p. 10).
    99	
   100	## 9. Limitations we identified
   101	- [I] **Extreme subset only.** Prompts were kept only if Sample-HR > 0.5, so base rates are ~0.85. Relative reductions on this subset do not translate to population-level rates.
   102	- [I] **Small, same-distribution edit sets.** Each fold has 50 prompts. The "unseen" set comes from the same model-specific filtered pool, so it is not out-of-distribution.
   103	- [I] **Residual risk remains.** About 9–20% of names stay hallucinated on unseen high-risk prompts, which are still squattable.
   104	- [I] **LLM inside the measurement.** In code generation, imports are mapped to PyPI names by an LLM. Stdlib handling is unspecified, so `import os` may be mis-scored.
   105	- [I] **Questionable utility baseline.** Qwen3-8B HumanEval pass@1 of 23.29% (p. 9) is unexpectedly low for that model, and the setup is not explained. This weakens the utility check for Qwen3.
   106	- [I] **Uneven baseline.** Self-Refinement uses registry feedback and is evaluated only on Edit50 (p. 7).
   107	- [I] **Good cutoff design, missing detail.** The release-date cutoff for validity is a sound choice: it excludes post-cutoff registrations, including squatted names. But the cutoff dates are not reported.
   108	- [I] No code or data release is stated, and no variance is reported.
   109	
   110	## 10. Threats to validity
   111	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] High-risk selection; same-pool unseen set; an LLM-based mapping step.
   112	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [V] 3 open 6.7–8B models, PyPI only (p. 10).
   113	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [V] Valid-Rate does not measure task correctness (p. 6). [I] Relative-percentage reporting magnifies effects at high base rates.
   114	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [V] No variance or tests (p. 6–9).
   115	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Hyperparameters and hardware are given (p. 6). Code, data, snapshot date and cutoffs are not.
   116	
   117	## 11. Future research directions
   118	- Stated by authors [A]: more ecosystems and languages (e.g. Java); configuration files, build scripts and repository-level workflows (p. 10–11).
   119	- Suggested by us [I]:
   120	  - Evaluate on representative, not only high-risk, prompts.
   121	  - Combine with a registry check.
   122	  - Test the adapter in quantized CPU inference.
   123	  - Test robustness over time as the registry changes.
   124	
   125	## 12. Relevance to our research
   126	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ3, RQ4.
   127	- How it informs our work [I]:
   128	  - **Laptop feasibility:** not feasible on a laptop without a GPU. Editing needs gradients through 7–8B models in bf16; the authors used A100s. The 731 KB adapter could in principle be loaded by a local runtime for inference, but this was not tested. Not applicable to closed APIs.
   129	  - **Methodology lesson:** the release-date cutoff in the validity rule is worth reusing.
   130	  - **What it leaves open:**
   131	    - Non-zero residual hallucination.
   132	    - npm and other ecosystems.
   133	    - Agents and requirements files.
   134	    - Behaviour on ordinary prompts.
   135	    - Names registered by attackers after editing.
   136	
   137	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
   138	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
   139	|---|---|---|---|---|
   140	| RQ3 | Localized LoRA editing (5 modules, 731 KB adapter) lowers Package-HR 0.4463→0.0897 on edit prompts and 0.4421→0.1529 on unseen high-risk prompts (3 models) | p. 6–7 | V | weak |
   141	| RQ3 | Residual Package-HR after editing stays 0.09–0.20 on unseen high-risk prompts | p. 7 | V | moderate |
   142	| RQ3 | ROME/DINM/Full-FT can reach ~0 HR only by collapsing package output (Valid-Rate ≈ 0) | p. 7–8 | V | moderate |
   143	| RQ3 | Transfer: −12.8% Package-HR in code generation, −34.0% in pip-install recommendation (relative) | p. 7–8 | V | weak |
   144	| RQ3 | HumanEval pass@1 changes within ±2% after editing | p. 9 | V | weak |
   145	| RQ3 | Requires white-box weights, gradients, LoRA training on GPU (8×A100 server) and registry labels; editing ~83 s + localization ~24 s per model | p. 3–6, p. 9 | V | moderate |
   146	| RQ4 | Validity = exists on PyPI with ≥1 release before the model's knowledge cutoff | p. 5 | V | strong |
   147	
   148	## 14. Key quotes
   149	> "A package is valid only if it exists on PyPI and has at least one release before the model's knowledge cutoff." (p. 5)
   150	
   151	> "BOUND is lightweight in practice, requiring only 731 KB of LoRA parameters on average" (p. 2)
   152	
   153	## Analyst notes
   154	- Reading coverage: all 12 PDF pages. The two-column extraction was readable and Tables I–VI were extracted cleanly.
   155	- Uncertainties:
   156	  - PyPI query date and per-model cutoffs.
   157	  - Stdlib handling.
   158	  - Size of the pool before high-risk filtering.
   159	  - Definition of "test time per case".
   160	  - Qwen3 HumanEval setup.
   161	- Funding: not reported.

1	---
     2	key: spracklen2026llm
     3	status: ready
     4	evidence_basis: full-text
     5	design: Technique proposal + controlled experiment (adaptive unlearning vs gradient ascent, NPO, PMC) with loss, inner-epoch and mutation ablations
     6	dataset: 20 hallucination-eliciting Python prompts from the Spracklen et al. benchmark (training) + 40 ChatGPT-paraphrased variants (test); static PyPI snapshot; EvalPlus
     7	sample_size: 2 DeepSeek-Coder models (7B dense, 16B MoE); 20 training prompts; 40 test prompts; samples/identifiers per prompt not reported; single runs
     8	metrics: Hallucination rate over Mode 1 (required) + Mode 2 (useful) package queries; KL divergence from base on code, instruction and package prompts; EvalPlus pass@1 (HumanEval(+), MBPP(+))
     9	main_finding: Full-parameter adaptive unlearning cut package hallucination 21.23%→2.56% (7B) and 27.75%→6.13% (16B) on paraphrased held-out prompts; coding average +1.6 / −4.2 pp.
    10	relevance: medium
    11	analysed: 2026-11-12
    12	---
    13	
    14	# LLM Ghostbusters: Surgical Package Hallucination Suppression via Adaptive Unlearning
    15	
    16	- Authors: Spracklen, Joseph; Aghazadeh, Pedram; Koushanfar, Farinaz; Jadliwala, Murtuza
    17	- Year / venue: 2026, arXiv (preprint)
    18	- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2605.01047 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.01047
    19	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
    20	
    21	Labels: **[V]** verified · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
    22	
    23	Source tier: preprint (arXiv v2, cs.CR, Sep 2026), **not peer-reviewed** (p. 1). It refers to the USENIX Open Science policy (p. 17). Authors overlap with spracklen2024we (Spracklen, Jadliwala). The paper discloses use of an AI writing and coding aid (p. 13).
    24	
    25	## 1. Research objective
    26	- [A] A post-deployment framework, Adaptive Unlearning (AU), that "surgically" suppresses package hallucinations while preserving general utility. It uses only model-generated data and no human annotation (p. 1–2).
    27	- [A] Target properties: precision, generalisation, data efficiency and scalability (p. 2).
    28	
    29	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
    30	- [V] No formal RQs. The implicit claims are:
    31	  - AU beats gradient ascent (GA), NPO and PMC on the joint hallucination–utility–drift trade-off.
    32	  - The hybrid loss, inner epochs and prompt mutation are each necessary (p. 3, p. 9–12).
    33	
    34	## 3. Methodology
    35	- Research design: [V] Technique proposal with controlled comparison against unlearning baselines, plus ablations (p. 8–12).
    36	- Approach / model / intervention:
    37	  - [V] **Closed loop:** sample completions; detect hallucinations with a registry oracle; build a per-token mask with three values (p. 5–7):
    38	    - 0 = context tokens, anchored by a scaled CE term.
    39	    - 1 = valid package names, reinforced with CE.
    40	    - 2 = hallucinated names, suppressed with NPO against a frozen base model.
    41	  - [V] **Nested epochs:** outer epochs resample completions; inner epochs train on the cached samples (p. 5–7).
    42	  - [V] **Prompt mutation:** a prompt is "exhausted" when N samples contain no hallucination or after 5 outer epochs. The model then rewrites the original seed prompt (p. 5–7).
    43	  - [V] **Required access:** **full-parameter fine-tuning** of the weights, explicitly not LoRA (p. 8, p. 19). NPO needs logits and a frozen reference copy (p. 5). The registry oracle is needed during training only, not at inference (p. 12).
    44	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] Base, Gradient Ascent, NPO, PMC. Ablations: CE-only, NPO-only, inner-epoch sweep, mutation-count sweep (p. 8). All methods share the same generation, parsing and detection pipeline (p. 8).
    45	
    46	## 4. Dataset and sample
    47	- Data source(s):
    48	  - [V] 20 code-generation prompts from the Spracklen et al. benchmark. Each was chosen so the base model's completion contains at least one valid and one hallucinated package, with diverse topics. They were deliberately hallucination-heavy, hence the high base rates (p. 8). The prompts are listed in Appendix F (p. 19–20).
    49	  - [V] Utility is measured on EvalPlus (HumanEval, HumanEval+, MBPP, MBPP+) (p. 9).
    50	- Sample size (N) and unit:
    51	  - [V] The test set is 40 prompts: 2 ChatGPT-generated variants of each training prompt, held out from training (p. 8).
    52	  - Not reported: samples per test prompt, total identifiers (N_total), and the size and source of the KL prompt sets.
    53	- Sampling / selection method: [V] Prompts were selected for being hallucination-eliciting (p. 8).
    54	- Data availability (public? link?): [V] An anonymous repository with code, prompts, harnesses and configs (p. 2, p. 13, p. 17).
    55	
    56	## 5. Experimental setup
    57	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
    58	  - [V] Models: DeepSeek-Coder-7b-instruct-v1.5 (dense) and DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite-Instruct (MoE, 16B total, ~2.4B active) (p. 8).
    59	  - [V] Configuration: batch 8, max length 1,024, 6 mutations per prompt, 5 cached samples per outer epoch. Loss weights (1.00, 1.25, 1.00) were chosen from a small grid (p. 8, p. 18). Learning rates and epoch counts per run are in Table 3 (p. 19).
    60	  - [V] **Hallucination decision:** parse `pip install` lines; ask the model (Mode 1) which packages are required to run the code and (Mode 2) which would be useful; parse and de-duplicate; resolve against a static PyPI snapshot collected before all experiments. An unresolved name is a hallucination (p. 8, p. 20–21).
    61	  - Not reported: snapshot date, stdlib handling, name normalisation.
    62	  - [A] Packages distributed outside PyPI may be mislabelled (p. 12).
    63	  - [V] **Hardware:** AMD MI210 and MI300 GPUs (p. 8); Appendix D says "MI200 / MI300" (p. 18). Runs were capped at 24 h wall-clock (7B) and 12 h (16B). The reported 16B AU result comes from a restart at checkpoint 60 for another 12 h (p. 18–19). Number of GPUs: not reported.
    64	  - [A] **Inference overhead:** none, since the change lives in the weights (p. 12).
    65	- Code availability: [V] Anonymous repository, to be made permanent on acceptance (p. 13).
    66	
    67	## 6. Evaluation metrics
    68	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
    69	  - [V] HR = N_halluc / N_total over all identifiers from both modes (p. 9).
    70	  - [V] KL divergence from the base model on code, instruction-following and package prompts, to bound collateral change (p. 9).
    71	  - [V] EvalPlus pass@1 (p. 9).
    72	- Statistical testing: [V] None. Single reported runs and no variance. The loss-weight choice mentions "repeated runs" (p. 18).
    73	
    74	## 7. Key findings
    75	1. [V] **DeepSeek-7B:** HR 21.23% → 2.56% (−88% relative), against GA 7.2%, NPO 14.17% and PMC 11.84% (Table 1, p. 10).
    76	2. [V] **DeepSeek-16B:** HR 27.75% → 6.13% (−78%); GA reaches 13.75% (p. 10, p. 13).
    77	3. [V] **Utility:** EvalPlus average goes from 66.98 to 68.57 on 7B and from 77.4 to 73.17 on 16B (HumanEval 81.1 → 73.2). PMC drops the 7B average to 51.65 (p. 9–10).
    78	4. [V] **Drift on 7B:** AU's KL is 0.0796 on code, 0.9905 on instruction-following and 1.4211 on package prompts. These are the highest code and instruction KL values of any method on 7B (Table 1, p. 10).
    79	5. [V] **Ablations (7B):** CE-only reaches 12.06% and NPO-only 12.42%. With 1 inner epoch HR stays at 13.8%; the minimum is 4.0% at 14 inner epochs. Without mutation HR is 10.7%, falling to 3.9% at 6 mutations and rebounding to 6.3% at 10 (p. 11–12).
    80	
    81	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
    82	- [A] **Oracle dependence:** AU applies only to domains with deterministic ground truth. The oracle checks existence, not correct use, and mislabels non-PyPI packages (p. 12).
    83	- [A] AU complements rather than replaces inference-time verification. Filtering at inference time needs registry access and adds latency per query (p. 12).
    84	- [A] **Oracle poisoning:** names pre-registered by an attacker move from the forget set to the retain set, so AU "reinforces what it was deployed to suppress". The snapshot must be audited (p. 12).
    85	- [A] **Token-disjointness assumption:** the case where a hallucinated name collides with a real identifier is not measured (p. 6, p. 12).
    86	- [A] Two DeepSeek models and Python only. Frontier-scale full fine-tuning exceeded the compute budget. npm, vcpkg and Conan are future work (p. 12).
    87	- [A] The explanation for the 16B MoE result is an untested hypothesis (p. 9).
    88	
    89	## 9. Limitations we identified
    90	- [I] **Near-in-distribution test.** The 40 test prompts are paraphrases of the 20 training seeds, and AU trains on model paraphrases of those same seeds. Generalisation to new tasks is untested. N_total is unreported, so 2.56% may rest on few identifiers.
    91	- [I] **Checkpoint selection.** Table 3 reports "the checkpoint that yielded best results" with no stated validation set (p. 19). If it was chosen on test HR, results are optimistic.
    92	- [I] **Internal inconsistencies:**
    93	  - Fig. 4 shows 25.0% → 4.8% (81%), while Table 1 shows 21.23% → 2.56% (88%) (p. 10).
    94	  - No-mutation HR is 10.7% in the text (p. 12) but 12.7% on p. 7 and in Fig. 7 (p. 13).
    95	  - Appendix G says per-mode rates are reported "in our main results", but Table 1 gives only the total (p. 20).
    96	  - MI210 vs MI200 (p. 8 vs p. 18).
    97	- [I] **"Surgical" is overstated.** On 7B, AU has the largest code and instruction KL (p. 10). On 16B the coding average falls 4.2 pp. The +6.7 pp HumanEval gain on 7B after unlearning is surprising for a single run.
    98	- [I] **Stdlib not handled.** Mode 1 ("required packages") answers can include `os`, `json` and similar. If those count as hallucinations, the base rate is inflated (cf. +7.6–9.4 pp in djire2026evaluating) and training would suppress legitimate names.
    99	- [I] **No release-date cutoff.** Names registered after model release count as valid, which is the poisoning issue the authors raise.
   100	- [I] **Heavy compute.** Full-parameter runs of up to 24 h on data-centre GPUs, repeated per model. This is "lightweight" only relative to retraining.
   101	
   102	## 10. Threats to validity
   103	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Paraphrase leakage between training and test; checkpoint selection; hallucination-heavy prompt selection.
   104	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [V] 2 DeepSeek models, Python only (p. 12).
   105	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [V] The oracle checks existence only (p. 12). [I] Stdlib treatment is unknown, and Mode 2 ("useful") inflates the opportunities to hallucinate.
   106	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [V] Single runs, no variance (p. 10–11).
   107	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Artifacts and per-run configurations are given (p. 17–19). Snapshot date, sample counts and GPU counts are missing.
   108	
   109	## 11. Future research directions
   110	- Stated by authors [A]:
   111	  - Cross-language generalisation (npm, vcpkg, Conan) and other model families (p. 12–13).
   112	  - Semantic-correctness oracles (p. 13).
   113	  - Applying AU to general-purpose LLMs (p. 13).
   114	  - Overlapping or soft-assigned spans (p. 12).
   115	- Suggested by us [I]:
   116	  - Use a larger, non-paraphrase held-out set and report N.
   117	  - Make the oracle stdlib-aware and time-cutoff-aware.
   118	  - Try a LoRA variant to cut cost.
   119	  - Test robustness to poisoned registries.
   120	
   121	## 12. Relevance to our research
   122	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ3 (defence effectiveness and cost), RQ4 (oracle design), RQ2 (oracle poisoning by squatted names).
   123	- How it informs our work [I]:
   124	  - **Laptop feasibility:** not feasible on a laptop. It needs full-parameter fine-tuning of 7B/16B models on MI210/MI300-class GPUs for 12–24 h. Not usable by end users of closed APIs, though the authors pitch it to vendors (p. 13).
   125	  - **What it leaves open:**
   126	    - Lightweight, client-side defences.
   127	    - Other ecosystems.
   128	    - Agents.
   129	    - How to keep a training-based defence correct once hallucinated names have been registered by attackers. The authors' own poisoning analysis argues for pairing it with a vetted registry check.
   130	
   131	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
   132	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
   133	|---|---|---|---|---|
   134	| RQ3 | Adaptive unlearning (full-parameter FT) lowers package HR 21.23%→2.56% (DeepSeek-7B) and 27.75%→6.13% (DeepSeek-16B) on 40 paraphrased held-out prompts | p. 10 | V | weak |
   135	| RQ3 | Outperforms gradient ascent (7.2%/13.75%), NPO and PMC on the same pipeline | p. 10 | V | weak |
   136	| RQ3 | Coding utility (EvalPlus avg) +1.6 pp on 7B, −4.2 pp on 16B; PMC loses 15 pp on 7B | p. 9–10 | V | weak |
   137	| RQ3 | Requires full-parameter fine-tuning on AMD MI210/MI300 GPUs with 12–24 h runs; no inference-time cost | p. 8, p. 12, p. 19 | V | moderate |
   138	| RQ2 | If attackers pre-register hallucinated names, the registry oracle labels them valid and unlearning reinforces them (oracle poisoning) | p. 12 | A | moderate |
   139	| RQ4 | Hallucination detected by asking the model for required (Mode 1) and useful (Mode 2) packages and resolving names against a static PyPI snapshot | p. 8, p. 20–21 | V | strong |
   140	| RQ3 | Both reinforcement (CE) and suppression (NPO) terms are needed; either alone leaves HR ≈12% on 7B | p. 11 | V | weak |
   141	
   142	## 14. Key quotes
   143	> "AU reinforces what it was deployed to suppress" (p. 12)
   144	
   145	> "This 40 prompt test set is completely held-out of training and enables generalized testing on unseen prompts." (p. 8)
   146	
   147	> "The PyPI ground-truth list is constructed from a static snapshot of the registry collected prior to all experiments" (p. 20)
   148	
   149	## Analyst notes
   150	- Reading coverage: all 21 PDF pages, including the appendices (prompts, hyperparameters, PMC formulation, detection pipeline). Figures 4–7 are known only through their text annotations.
   151	- Uncertainties:
   152	  - Samples and identifiers behind each HR.
   153	  - Checkpoint-selection criterion.
   154	  - Snapshot date.
   155	  - Stdlib handling.
   156	  - Figure 4 vs Table 1 discrepancy.
   157	- Funding: not reported.
   158	- Quote note: the first and third quotes span line breaks or hyphenation in `fulltext.txt`.

    18	# Names Can Hurt: Spotting Slopsquatting Risks Caused by Package Name Hallucinations in Local Coding LLMs
    19	
    20	- Authors: Raj, Akash; Sahu, Sargam
    21	- Year / venue: 2026, arXiv (Cornell University) (preprint)
    22	- DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22087562 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23897
    23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
    24	
    25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
    26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
    27	
    28	**Source tier:** arXiv preprint, v1, August 2026 (p. 1); not peer-reviewed. Authors are an M.Tech student and a B.Tech intern; much of the work was done during an internship (p. 1, 15). The metadata DOI is a Zenodo DOI, and `metadata.json` verification is "single-source (openalex)".
    29	
    30	## 1. Research objective
    31	- [A] Build and evaluate a client-side guard that stops a coding LLM's hallucinated Python package names from turning into slopsquatting installs. The guard targets "small, open-weight, locally runnable LLMs in the 7B to 70B range" (p. 2).
    32	- [A] The authors say local models matter because developers outside large companies run them, because they "tend to hallucinate more often than frontier systems", and because local deployment rules out asking a hosted model to verify the output (p. 2). No evidence is given for the second point.
    33	
    34	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
    35	- No formal RQs or hypotheses. The paper lists five contributions instead (p. 2): (1) a two-layer detector (PyPI existence check plus a per-LLM Random Forest); (2) an import-name reconciler; (3) a LangGraph retry/fallback agent; (4) an evaluation on 300 prompts; (5) a user acceptance study.
    36	- Implicit questions answered in §6: how often the pipeline gives up; how much retries and fallback recover; how give-up varies by prompt tier; how many flagged names already exist on PyPI; whether per-LLM classifiers transfer across models; whether a hand-written rule matches the Random Forest (pp. 6–12).
    37	
    38	## 3. Methodology
    39	- Research design: [V] System-building paper with a single-configuration evaluation (one primary/fallback model pair), offline classifier analysis and a convenience-sample survey (pp. 6–12). There is no control condition without the detector, apart from earlier buggy system versions (p. 7).
    40	- Approach / model / intervention:
    41	  - [V] **Extractor.** AST parsing of Python code blocks, keeping only the top-level module name. A regex fallback runs only inside code fences and ignores keywords and shell tokens. `pip install` lines are read only inside code fences (pp. 3, 5).
    42	  - [V] **Layer 1, deterministic check.** A PyPI JSON API lookup per name. A 404 means the name is fake. A 200 sends the package metadata to the classifier (p. 5).
    43	  - [V] **Layer 2, Random Forest.** 400 trees, 10 features (p. 5):
    44	    - 8 name features: length, number of parts, digits, a letter repeated three times, hype words (`super`, `pro`, `ai`, `magic`), generic words (`helper`, `tools`), a `py-`/`python-` prefix, and Levenshtein distance to a list of the top 15,000 PyPI names.
    45	    - 2 metadata features: maintainer count and whether a GitHub URL is present.
    46	  - [V] **Import-name reconciler.** A 24-entry YAML table (e.g. `cv2` → `opencv-python`, `PIL` → `Pillow`). It is consulted only after a PyPI 404. A mapped name is accepted only if the install name passes both layers. The authors' security argument: an attacker-registered `cv2` returns 200, so the reconciler never runs and the classifier must catch it (pp. 5–6).
    47	  - [V] **Agent.** A LangGraph state machine with six nodes. Retry budget is 1 per model ("up to 2 attempts"), with rising temperature (0.7 → 1.0 → 1.2). After the budget is spent, the task goes to a fallback model with its own matched classifier. Every attempt is logged to JSONL (pp. 3, 6).
    48	- Baselines or comparison conditions:
    49	  - [V] Earlier system versions v0/v1 (broken regex, no reconciler) are used as an ablation (p. 7).
    50	  - [V] Three hand-written rules are compared with the Random Forest on the same package-disjoint split (p. 12).
    51	  - [V] LLM self-verification is described as a "baseline" in related work but is **not run** (p. 3).
    52	  - [V] There is no comparison with any published detector or with Spracklen et al.'s method; the reference list has only three entries (p. 15).
    53	
    54	## 4. Dataset and sample
    55	- Data source(s):
    56	  - [V] 300 single-line Python coding prompts, written by hand (p. 6).
    57	  - [V] Classifier data: "Sargam's dataset" (`raw_master_dataset.csv`) of package names generated by seven LLMs (pp. 9, 14). How it was generated (prompts, hosting, dates) is not reported.
    58	- Sample size (N) and unit:
    59	  - [V] Prompts: 300, roughly 140 routine tasks (data engineering, security/DevOps, standard workflows), 55 obscure-dependency tasks and 105 adversarial prompts, in 18 tiers of 5–30 prompts each (pp. 6–8).
    60	  - [V] Runs and verdicts: 385 runs (300 primary + 85 fallback) gave 823 package verdicts (p. 8).
    61	  - [V] Classifier data: 464 unique package names across 7 LLMs; 210 occur in at least two models and 42 in all seven. Each model has 68–108 hallucinated rows, which leaves 2–12 positive examples per test slice (pp. 9–10).
    62	  - [V] Survey: n = 24 CS undergraduates (p. 11).
    63	- Sampling / selection method:
    64	  - [V] Prompts were authored by the researchers. Adversarial prompts name packages or use "tricky wording" such as asking for "the newest and most capable library for X" (p. 6).
    65	  - [V] Survey participants were "Sargam's CS undergraduate peers" / "the intern's friends" (pp. 2, 11).
    66	  - The tier construction criteria and the classifier labelling procedure (who or what decided "hallucinated" in the training data) are not reported.
    67	- Data availability: [A] Code, mapping table, the 300 prompts, seven classifiers, the 385-record run log and the leakage-safe matrix are released at a GitHub repository (p. 15). We did not check the repository.
    68	
    69	## 5. Experimental setup
    70	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
    71	  - [V] **Models.** Classifiers were trained for `gpt-5`, `gpt-oss-120b`, `llama-3.1-8b`, `llama-3.3-70b`, `llama-4-scout`, `qwen3-27b` and `qwen3-32b`. The agent evaluation uses two **Groq-hosted** models chosen to fit "our free-tier budget": primary `llama-3.1-8b`, fallback `llama-3.3-70b` (p. 2). Exact model versions/checkpoints and quantization are not reported.
    72	  - [V] **Classifier.** Random Forest, 400 trees; scikit-learn 1.8 in v2 (pp. 5, 7). Other hyper-parameters are not reported. The decision threshold on P(fake) is not reported.
    73	  - [V] **Split.** The original split was a per-model 75/25 row split with `random_state=42`. It was replaced by a package-disjoint 75/25 split over the 464 unique names (p. 9).
    74	  - [V] **Uncertainty.** Bootstrap 95% CIs with 1,000 resamples for F1 (p. 10).
    75	  - **Hardware: not reported.** All generation ran through Groq's hosted API, and the classifier analysis was "computed offline" (pp. 2, 6). [I] So, despite the title, no model was run on local hardware. "Local" describes the model class (open-weight, 7–70B), not the deployment. The classifier training set also includes `gpt-5`, which is not a local model.
    76	  - [V] **Run budget.** One fallback run was lost to a mid-batch Groq rate-limit event (p. 7). A cross-family fallback was not run because it "would have required 5 times the Groq token budget beyond the free tier" (p. 11).
    77	  - [V] **Survey.** Standalone Streamlit tool, seven dimensions on a 1–5 Likert scale (p. 11).
    78	- Code availability: [A] GitHub repository stated (p. 15); twelve extractor regression tests are said to pass (p. 15).
    79	
    80	## 6. Evaluation metrics
    81	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
    82	  - [V] **Primary give-up rate:** share of prompts where the primary model exhausts its retry budget (p. 6).
    83	  - [V] **Fallback rescue rate:** share of give-ups that the fallback recovers (p. 6).
    84	  - [V] **End-to-end clean rate:** share of prompts that finish with no hallucinated recommendation (p. 6).
    85	  - [V] **Per-tier and per-name breakdowns** (p. 6).
    86	  - [V] **Classifier F1** in a 7×7 train-LLM × test-LLM matrix (p. 9).
    87	  - [V] **Random Forest split importance** per feature (p. 10).
    88	  - [V] **Likert means/medians** from the survey (p. 11).
    89	  - [I] Why these metrics were chosen is not justified.
    90	  - [I] Retries are triggered both by non-code answers and by flagged names (p. 4). The give-up rate is therefore a pipeline outcome, not a pure hallucination rate, and it also absorbs detector false positives (see §9).
    91	  - Not reported: detector precision/recall against a manually checked ground truth on the 300-prompt run.
    92	- Statistical testing:
    93	  - [V] Bootstrap CIs are reported for the F1 matrix only (p. 10).
    94	  - No CIs or tests for give-up, rescue or tier rates, and no significance testing.

    96	## 7. Key findings
    97	1. **Pipeline outcome.** [V] On `llama-3.1-8b`:
    98	   - 186/300 prompts (62%) produced code on the first try (p. 7).
    99	   - 114 triggered a retry, and 28 of those were fixed by the retry (24.6% intra-model rescue) (p. 7).
   100	   - 86/300 (28.7%) exhausted the budget (p. 7).
   101	   - The fallback ran on 85 of those 86 and recovered 14 (16.5%) (p. 7).
   102	   - End-to-end, 228/300 (76%) prompts finished clean. The remaining 72 would get a "do not pip install" warning (p. 7).
   103	2. **Most of the give-up reduction came from preprocessing fixes, not the classifier.** [V] Primary give-up was:
   104	   - v0: 79% (55/70), broken regex on the full text (p. 7);
   105	   - v1: 57% (33/58), AST + code-only regex (p. 7);
   106	   - v2: 30% (18/60) on 60 prompts and 28.7% (86/300) on 300 prompts, after adding the reconciler (p. 7).
   107	
   108	   The reconciler fired 29 times over 4 distinct alias pairs in the 300-prompt run (p. 7). [A] The extractor and reconciler fixes together "caused a 49-point drop"; "Changing the classifier itself did not help much" (p. 12).
   109	3. **Give-up rate rises with prompt tier.** [V] Rates by tier:
   110	   - Data Engineering 0% (n=20); Security & DevOps 5% (n=20); Level 1/Level 2 10% (n=10 each) (pp. 7–8).
   111	   - Hallucination Bait 55% (n=20); Adversarial (Realistic Hallucination Bait) 73.3% (n=30) (p. 8).
   112	   - Direct Slopsquatting Stress Tests 30% (n=30) (p. 8). This sits below the abstract's "40 to 73% on slopsquat baits" (p. 1).
   113	
   114	   [I] Table 2 is sorted by rate, not by any independent measure of how adversarial a prompt is. The "Level N" tiers are not monotone (Level 8 = 0%, Level 4 = 60%; pp. 7–8). The abstract's "scales almost linearly with prompt adversariality" (p. 1) is therefore an author claim with no defined adversariality scale.
   115	4. **"Already-registered lookalike" finding (the paper's headline).**
   116	   - [V] 385 runs produced 823 verdicts: 644 `real` (78.3%) and 179 `hallucinated` (21.7%) (p. 8).
   117	   - [V] Of the 179 flags, "Half were true 404s". The other half returned PyPI status 200 and were flagged by the classifier on suspicious metadata. The paper later gives 90 `status=200` flags (pp. 8–9).
   118	   - [V] Table 3, "Wild caught PyPI registered squats and lookalikes" (pp. 8–9):
   119	
   120	     | Name | Canonical project (per Table 3) | P(fake) | Flags |
   121	     |---|---|---|---|
   122	     | `pil` | Pillow | 0.89 | 36 |
   123	     | `faiss` | faiss-cpu/-gpu | 0.57 | 10 |
   124	     | `tabula` | tabula-py | 0.57 | 4 |
   125	     | `haystack` | now haystack-ai | 0.56 | 2 |
   126	     | `camelot` | camelot-py | 0.95 | 1 |
   127	     | `skimage` | scikit-image | 0.58 | 1 |
   128	     | `fastyaml` | none identified | 0.99 | 1 |
   129	     | `fastvector` | none identified | 0.82 | 1 |
   130	     | `graphbrain` | ambiguous | 0.92 | 2 |
   131	
   132	     Further rows include `aiworkflow`, `taskgraph`, `promptstudio`, `flowgraph-ai`, `embeddinghub`, and "22 more" names with one or more flags each.
   133	   - [A] "Approximately half of the hallucinated recommendations produced by the LLM were already present on PyPI as squats or low-quality lookalikes", so a deterministic-only check "would have caught only the other half" (p. 9).
   134	   - [V] Security invariant: for all 90 `status=200` flags, the reconciler was never called (p. 9).
   135	   - [A] The reconciler "correctly refused to help every single time" against an attacker suite. The attacker suite is not described (p. 6).
   136	   - [I] **This finding needs caution.** In Table 3, 36 + 10 = 46 of the 90 status-200 flags (≈51%) come from `pil` and `faiss`. Both are the normal *import* names of real projects (`import PIL` for Pillow, `import faiss` for faiss-cpu). Several other rows (`skimage`, `camelot`, `tabula`, `haystack`) are also import or legacy names of legitimate projects. A large share of the "already registered" half is therefore probably correct `import` statements whose import name happens to be a separate, low-quality PyPI project. That is a real install-time risk if a user types `pip install <import name>`, but it is not the LLM inventing a package. Because the reconciler deliberately does not run on 200 responses (p. 5), the design itself produces these flags. The authors also admit they have not audited the ≥30 registered names (pp. 13–14).
   137	5. **Classifier transfer.** [V]
   138	   - The first per-model row split leaked: 72.9% of off-diagonal test rows contained package names already in training (p. 9).
   139	   - On the corrected package-disjoint split, F1 ranges from 0.833 to 1.000 (pp. 9–10).
   140	   - Two test columns (llama-4-scout, qwen3-27b) have only 2 positives each, giving CIs of [0.00, 1.00]. The llama columns have 5 positives each (CI [0.67, 1.00]) (p. 10).
   141	   - [A] One classifier trained on `gpt-oss-120b` (~410 rows) "works well across all seven models", so matched-pair training "is not needed" (p. 10).
   142	6. **The classifier is in effect a two-feature metadata rule.** [V]
   143	   - `log_maintainers` provides 57.6% of the split importance and `github_url_present` another 24.5% (82% together) (p. 10).
   144	   - Rule C (OR over the two features) reaches mean F1 0.99 versus 0.98 for the Random Forest. Strict-AND rules reach 0.53–0.55 (p. 12).
   145	   - [A] "the 400-tree Random Forest does not really give us more help than the simple OR baseline" (p. 12).
   146	   - [I] The prose then states the rule as "zero PyPI maintainers AND no GitHub URL", which contradicts the table's finding that the OR rule wins (p. 12). The exact rule is ambiguous.
   147	7. **Same-family fallback mostly fails.** [V] 71 of 85 give-ups (83.5%) failed again on `llama-3.3-70b`. The same invented names recurred in both models' outputs (e.g. `pdfgenius`, `ultrarag`, `hyperfaiss`, `fastyaml`, `vectorcache`, `embedflow`, `taskgraph`) (p. 10). [A] A cross-family fallback should work better, but this was not tested (pp. 11, 13).
   148	8. **Bait refusal.** [V] Bonus Stress Test, 10 prompts that name fabricated packages (p. 11):
   149	   - 1 bait was used verbatim (`ultrarag`) and caught by the detector.
   150	   - 3 became nearby variants (`fastvector`, `fastyaml`, `faiss`).
   151	   - 6 were "refused outright", and real packages were substituted.
   152	   - The pipeline finished clean on 6/10.

   154	   [I] The paper reports this inconsistently. The abstract says the model "refused 6 of 10 direct baits unaided" (p. 1); §6.8 says "The LLM refused the bait name on 9 of 10 prompts" (p. 11).

   157	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
   158	- [A] Only one model pair was evaluated (llama-3.1-8b → llama-3.3-70b). A cross-family test was not affordable on the Groq budget (p. 13).
   159	- [A] The `pypi_maintainers_count` feature "is basically 0" because the PyPI JSON API only shows maintainers to admins. This "might cause false positives for small legitimate packages" (p. 13).
   160	- [A] Transferability cells rest on 2–12 hallucinated test examples, so two columns are uninformative. More runs or pooled cross-validation are needed (pp. 10, 13).
   161	- [A] About 82% of the classifier's signal comes from two metadata features, so attackers could evade it by registering squats with realistic-looking metadata. This was not tested (p. 13).
   162	- [A] The ≥30 registered names flagged as suspicious were not individually audited (pp. 13–14).
   163	- [A] The user study participants were the intern's friends (p. 14).
   164	- [A] Drift:
   165	  - brand-new legitimate packages will be mis-flagged (zero maintainers, no GitHub link, not in the 15k list);
   166	  - the reference list goes stale;
   167	  - packages can be renamed or taken over (`haystack` → `haystack-ai`).
   168	
   169	  None of the proposed mitigations (monthly snapshot refresh, quarterly retraining, 24 h metadata cache, false-positive monitoring) is implemented (p. 14).

   171	## 9. Limitations we identified
   172	- [I] **No ground truth for the 300-prompt run.** Detector precision and recall are never measured against manually labelled package names. "Hallucinated" means "flagged by the detector". The 179 flags, and the 50/50 split, therefore mix true hallucinations with false positives.
   173	- [I] **Construct problem in the "already registered" finding.** As shown in §7 finding 4, about half of the status-200 flags are `pil` and `faiss`, which are standard import names. The paper's own security rule (the reconciler runs only after a 404) turns correct imports into "hallucinations" whenever someone else has registered the import name. The headline "half of hallucinations are registered lookalikes" (pp. 1, 9, 15) probably overstates LLM invention and understates the import-name/install-name ambiguity.
   174	- [I] **Train/serve skew in the top feature.** If `log_maintainers` (57.6% of importance) is near zero for most packages at inference via the JSON API (p. 13), but training data were "pulled" by another route ("Sargam's dataset helps a little by pulling metadata", p. 13), the live classifier probably flags legitimate status-200 packages on that feature alone. This would inflate the registered-lookalike count.
   175	- [I] **Possibly circular training labels.** How training labels were assigned is not reported. If "hallucinated" was derived from PyPI non-existence, then features such as "no maintainers" and "no GitHub URL" are trivially true for 404 names. That would explain the near-perfect F1 and the dominance of metadata features.
   176	- [I] **Overstated baseline comparison.** The conclusion that the system "cuts the give-up rate from 79% (unmitigated) to 28.7%" (p. 15) compares against v0, a version with a broken extractor on a different 70-prompt set (p. 7). That is a bug-fix comparison, not an unmitigated baseline.
   177	- [I] **Internal inconsistencies:**
   178	  - bait refusal 6/10 vs 9/10 (pp. 1, 11);
   179	  - "40 to 73%" vs the 30% tier (pp. 1, 8);
   180	  - retry budget "up to 2 attempts" vs a three-step temperature schedule (pp. 3, 6);
   181	  - "AND" vs "OR" rule wording (p. 12).
   182	- [I] **Unverifiable model identifier.** `qwen3-27b` is given without provider or version (p. 2). We could not confirm the identifier from the paper.
   183	- [I] **Weak survey.** The user study tests the standalone UI, not the detector's accuracy. With a friends-and-peers sample, it says little about effectiveness.
   184	
   185	## 10. Threats to validity
   186	- Internal:
   187	  - The prompt set was written by the authors, and the tiers are defined post hoc.
   188	  - Detector false positives are counted as hallucinations.
   189	  - Same-family names recur across primary and fallback, so the two runs are not independent.
   190	  - Leakage in the first classifier split was found and fixed (p. 9). The labelling procedure is not reported.
   191	- External:
   192	  - One small model (llama-3.1-8b) through one API provider (Groq), Python/PyPI only.
   193	  - No genuinely local inference: hardware, quantization and runtime are not reported.
   194	  - Single-line prompts are not agentic multi-file tasks.
   195	- Construct:
   196	  - "Give-up" mixes non-code answers, true hallucinations and detector false positives.
   197	  - "Hallucination" is defined by the detector itself.
   198	  - "Squat or lookalike" status was not audited (pp. 13–14).
   199	- Statistical conclusion:
   200	  - Only F1 has CIs, and those are very wide (p. 10).
   201	  - Tier rates rest on n = 5–30 prompts each, with no CIs (pp. 7–8).
   202	  - Single run per prompt; nothing on seed variation.
   203	- Reproducibility:
   204	  - [A] Artefacts are said to be on GitHub (p. 15).
   205	  - Not reported: model versions, Groq dates, classifier threshold, training-data construction. Groq's hosted models change over time.

   207	## 11. Future research directions
   208	- Stated by authors [A]:
   209	  - cross-family fallback pairing, e.g. Llama → Qwen or GPT-OSS (pp. 11, 14);
   210	  - richer features (first-upload age, release cadence, owner-network overlap, README quality, repository activity), which must beat the two-feature rule (p. 14);
   211	  - about 3× more hallucinated examples per model, or pooled cross-validation (pp. 10, 14);
   212	  - drift handling: monthly top-N refresh and quarterly retraining (p. 14);
   213	  - adversarial squats with realistic metadata are named as untested (p. 13).
   214	- Suggested by us [I]:
   215	  1. Manually audit every flagged name, and keep three cases apart: (a) a correct import name whose PyPI namesake is a different project; (b) a hallucinated name that is registered; (c) a hallucinated name that is unregistered.
   216	  2. Evaluate the 404 + metadata rule against synthetic squats with realistic metadata (maintainers, GitHub URL, upload age).
   217	  3. Replace the unavailable maintainer feature with upload age and release history from the PyPI JSON/Simple API.
   218	  4. Run the models truly locally (e.g. quantized 7–8B models through a local runtime) to test whether quantization changes the rates.

   220	## 12. Relevance to our research
   221	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ3 (primary: tool-side defence), RQ2 (registered lookalikes, name recurrence across same-family models), RQ1 (rates by prompt tier for one small model), RQ4 (pitfalls: extractor scope, import-name reconciliation, split leakage), RQ5 (untested: cross-family fallback, realistic-metadata squats, local inference).
   222	- How it informs our work [I]:
   223	  - **Laptop-scale feasibility.** The defence is cheap: a PyPI JSON lookup plus a two-feature rule, which the authors say fits in "one line of Python" (p. 12). It needs no GPU and runs on any laptop. It is a natural baseline for our defence study. The authors' own evaluation was done on a free API tier, not locally, so a truly local replication (Ollama or llama.cpp with quantized models) would add something new.
   224	  - **What a measurement study should do better.** The paper lists the pitfalls a laptop-scale measurement must handle:
   225	    - extract only from code fences, with AST parsing;
   226	    - keep a separate import-name ↔ distribution-name map, and record PyPI status separately from "hallucinated";
   227	    - snapshot PyPI responses with timestamps;
   228	    - hand-label a sample to estimate precision.
   229	  - **Open question worth testing.** How many LLM-suggested names are already registered on PyPI, and by whom. With careful import/install handling, this is directly measurable on a laptop. This paper's estimate (~50%) is the number to check, and we have reason to think it is inflated by import-name collisions.
   230	  - **Weight.** Single preprint, one model pair, unaudited labels: treat as **weak** evidence. Use it for design ideas and pitfalls, not for effect sizes.

=== [PDF page 1] ===

 Names Can Hurt:
 Spotting Slopsquatting Risks Caused by Package Name Hallucinations
 in Local Coding LLMs

 Akash Raj Sargam Sahu
 M.Tech, School of Artificial Intelligence and Data B.Tech, CSE Department
 Science Jaypee University of Engineering and Technology,
 Indian Institute of Technology Jodhpur Guna
 m25ai1116@iitj.ac.in sargamsahu1606@gmail.com
 ORCID: 0009-0005-5666-3967


Version: v1, arXiv, August 2026



Abstract
When a code generating language model fabricates a Python package name, an adversary who has pre-
registered that name on PyPI can convert that hallucination into a supply chain compromise. This event
has been termed as ‘slopsquatting’.

We propose a two layer detector to counter this issue. The first layer performs a deterministic PyPI
existence check. The second is a Random Forest classifier trained on ten features derived from the
package name and its PyPI metadata. An import name reconciler bridges the two, resolving cases such
as `import cv2` versus `pip install opencv-python` without a security bypass. The detector is embedded
in a LangGraph state machine that retries at escalating temperatures and, on repeated failure, routes to
a stronger fallback model.

Across 300 curated prompts, the pipeline produces hallucination free code on 76% of runs. The primary
exhausts its retry budget on 28.7%; intra model retries recover roughly a quarter of those, and cross
model fallback recovers a further 16.5% of the remainder.

Four findings have been observed. First, half of the flagged hallucinations are packages already
registered on PyPI, as low quality lookalikes of well known projects, caught by the classifier rather than
the deterministic layer (e.g., pil, faiss, tabula, haystack). Second, hallucination rate scales almost linearly
with prompt adversariality, from 0 to 10% on routine coding to 40 to 73% on slopsquat baits. Third, the
weaker primary refused 6 of 10 direct baits unaided, suggesting recent instruction tuning provides a
baseline defense. Fourth, when primary and fallback share a model family, approximately 84% of
primary failures recur on the fallback, motivating cross family pairing.

A user study (n = 24) reports mean satisfaction 4.4 out of 5 and 21 of 24 stated adoption intent. The
second layer classifier is interchangeable: Section 6.10 shows a hand written two feature rule matches
the ML version on the current features.
The paper releases the code, the prompts, and the classifiers for each LLM with the complete run log.

=== [PDF page 2] ===

1. Introduction
A command such as `pip install pdfgenius` may simply return a 404, in which case nothing harmful
occurs. The same is true of `pip install cloudmindai`. But if an attacker has already claimed the name on
PyPI, an inexpensive and to our knowledge, weakly policed action, then a developer who trusts a coding
assistant may instead install attacker controlled software. Spracklen et al. (2024) termed this attack
pattern slopsquatting and showed that frontier LLMs hallucinate often enough to make the attack
economically plausible.

Subsequent work has focused largely on frontier proprietary models. We instead study a different part
of the model landscape: small, open-weight, locally runnable LLMs in the 7B to 70B range. This
population matters for three reasons.

First, these are the models that many developers actually run outside large companies. Second, they
tend to hallucinate more often than frontier systems. Third, local deployment removes the convenient
fallback of asking a stronger hosted model to verify the recommendation, so local defenses must
themselves operate locally.

This paper does five things.

 1. We construct a two-layer detector consisting of a deterministic PyPI check and a per-LLM
 Random Forest, trained across seven LLMs (`gpt-5`, `gpt-oss-120b`, `llama-3.1-8b`, `llama-3.3-
 70b`, `llama-4-scout`, `qwen3-27b`, and `qwen3-32b`). The agent evaluation uses two Groq-
 hosted models that fit into our free‑tier budget. The primary model is `llama-3.1-8b`. The
 fallback model is `llama-3.3-70b`.
 2. We add an import‑name reconciler for the common Python situation where the import name
 does not match the install name, such as `cv2` versus `opencv‑python` or `PIL` versus `Pillow`.
 The reconciler is intentionally narrow. It is triggered when PyPI returns a 404 for the extracted
 name. A broader rule could let attackers bypass the classifier by registering a squat under the
 alias. Section 4.4 explains this security argument in detail.
 3. We embed the detector in a LangGraph agent. The agent retries generations while raising the
 temperature and sends repeated failures to a fallback. Every attempt is saved to a JSONL log.
 4. We evaluate the system with 300 prompts that cover intermediate, difficult and adversarial
 settings. Section 6 shows the results.
 5. We also ran a controlled user acceptance study, on the standalone classifier UI using an
 evaluation protocol. The study design tasks and procedures but the participants were Sargam’s
 CS undergraduate peers. Therefore a small amount of desirability bias might still be present.

All artifacts are released.

2. Background and Related Work
Spracklen et al. (2024) provides the core reference point. They measured package hallucination rates for
frontier LLMs across coding benchmarks and showed that registering frequently hallucinated PyPI
names creates a credible attack surface. Follow-up studies have extended this observation to additional
models and languages, but have remained concentrated in the frontier-model setting.

=== [PDF page 3] ===

Existing mitigations fall into three broad categories.

Deterministic verification against a package index or lockfile is the cheapest option, because a 404
conclusively shows that a name does not resolve. However, it only addresses fabricated names. An
attacker who has already registered the hallucinated name trivially bypasses a pure 404 check.

LLM self-verification, in which the same model or a stronger sibling is asked to double-check the
recommendation, is inexpensive and can help in practice. However, it remains vulnerable to the same
hallucinations it is meant to detect. Homogeneity between the generator and verifier further limits its
effectiveness, a point we revisit in Section 6.7.

The third family uses ML classifiers over package metadata, training supervised models on features such
as maintainer count, download rank, and name similarity to known packages. Prior work typically trains
a single classifier and deploys it across models. We initially trained matched per-LLM classifiers before
finding that cross-model transferability is high enough for a single classifier to suffice, as discussed in
Section 6.6.

Our pipeline combines deterministic and ML checks and uses the reconciler as the connecting
mechanism. We treat LLM self-verification as a baseline rather than as the primary mitigation.

3. System Overview
The pipeline is conceptually simple. We send a user prompt to the main LLM. We then look in the
answer for import statements. Pip install commands that appear only inside code fences, not in regular
text. Every name we pull out goes through a two‑step detector. If any package comes out marked as
hallucinated we ask the system to try with a higher temperature (first 0.7, then 1.0 then 1.2) but only if
we still have retries left. When we run out of retries we hand the job over to a fallback LLM and start the
whole loop over. We record every try, in logs/agent_runs.jsonl. Figure 1 shows the pipeline.

=== [PDF page 4] ===

Figure 1: The process of the slopsquat-safe coding agent. First a user prompt goes to the LLM. If the LLM
gives non-code answers or makes up fake package names the system tries again. If it keeps failing it
sends the task to a fallback LLM. We only look for packages inside code blocks. After that we use a layer,
an import-name reconciler and a metadata classifier to decide if the response is safe.

=== [PDF page 5] ===

4. Detector Design
4.1 Extractor
The extractor uses AST parsing inside every code block. It only keeps the module name from each import
statement. For example `import numpy as np` gives us `numpy` not `np` or `as`. If the code block is
messy with text or uses a language the system uses regex instead. Even then the regex only looks inside
code blocks. The regex finds the name after `import` and stops at spaces, commas or the word ` as `. It
also ignores Python words and shell tokens.

We must keep the regex inside code blocks. In a version we ran the regex on the whole LLM response.
That caused problems because it pulled words like `github` `python` and `spacy-lg` out of English
sentences. Fixing this removed most of the alerts we saw early on.

A specific bug actually helped us improve. One person in our study typed `Install requests, flask and
pandas.` ; she noticed two bugs: The tool mistook ‘and’ as a hallucinated package; also, it took `pandas.`
(with a period) as different than `pandas`. She was right. We fixed that, and ended up rewriting the
system to handle over thirty similar issues.

4.2 Deterministic layer
For every name we find we check the PyPI JSON API. If we get a 404 error we know the package name is
fake. If we get a 200 response we send the package info to the classifier to check it closely.

4.3 Random Forest classifier
The classifier looks at ten features. Eight features come from the package name and two come from the
metadata.

The name features are the length of the name; how many parts it has; if it has numbers; if it repeats
letters three times; if it uses words like `super`, `pro`, `ai` or `magic`; if it uses generic words like `helper`
or `tools`; if it starts with `py-` or `python-`; and how close the name is to a real package in a list of
15,000 top PyPI names.

The metadata features are the number of maintainers and whether the package has a GitHub URL.

The Random Forest uses 400 trees. Sargam trained specific classifiers for each LLM during her
internship. Later we saw that a classifier trained on one LLM works well on others too. We think this is
because the features we chose work for any LLM not because the design was perfect.

4.4 Import name reconciliation
Some Python packages use different names for installing and importing. For example you install
`opencv-python`. Import `cv2`. You install `Pillow` but import `PIL`. A simple system would call these as
hallucinated packages. In our tests these mismatches caused most of our mistakes.

The reconciler is a list in a YAML file with 24 entries. It only runs if the deterministic layer gets a 404
error. If the name is in our list we look up the install name and check it again. The package is only
marked as `real` if it passes both the PyPI check and the classifier check.

This order is very important, for security. Imagine an attacker makes a package named `cv2`. PyPI would
say it exists with a 200 code. Because of this the deterministic layer does not stop it. The reconciler

=== [PDF page 6] ===

never even runs. The classifier then looks at the `cv2` package metadata. Since a fake package usually
has no maintainers or GitHub link the classifier should flag it as suspicious. This means the reconciler
cannot accidentally help an attacker. We tested this with attacker packages and the reconciler correctly
refused to help every single time.

5. Agent Design
We built the agent as a LangGraph state machine (Chase 2024) using six nodes: `generate`,
`classify_output` ,`extract_packages` ,`label_packages`, `decide_retry` and `finalize`. We also used three
edges to handle cases where the agent does not write code to manage retry loops, when the agent finds
flagged packages and to handle the finalization process.

The retry budget starts at 1 which means the agent gets up to 2 attempts on the model and we
increased the temperature from 0.7 to 1.0 to 1.2. If the agent still hallucinates after the retry budget is
gone the system moves to a fallback model. This fallback model uses its retry budget and its own
matched classifier. We make sure the output from the fallback model is logged as a lineage-tagged
record that points back to the primary run ID.

Every time the agent runs it adds a JSON line to `logs/agent_runs.jsonl`. This line includes the ID,
timestamp, model, prompt, retry counters, extracted packages, verdicts for each package the final
response text and the role tag (`primary` or `fallback`). We use this log to get all the data for the
analyses in Section 6.

6. Evaluation
6.1 Setup
We tested the agent using 300 prompts. We wrote these prompts by hand. Every prompt is a single-line
Python coding request. About 140 of these are coding tasks like Data Engineering, Security and DevOps
basic scripts and standard workflows. About 55 are tasks involving obscure dependencies and
uncommon libraries. The last 105 are adversarial. Some of these prompts name packages while others
use tricky wording to try and make the agent invent something like asking for 'the newest and most
capable library for X'.

The agent uses `llama-3.1-8b` as the model and `llama-3.3-70b` as the fallback model. We paired each
model with its classifier from Sargam’s catalog. The retry budget is 1, for each model.

All primary generations are logged; fallback runs are launched only when the primary gives up.

We report the primary give-up rate, fallback rescue rate (the fraction of primary give-up cases recovered
by the fallback), end-to-end clean rate (the fraction of prompts for which the pipeline terminates
without hallucinated recommendations), and per-tier and per-name breakdowns.

Cross-model transferability (Section 6.6) is computed offline from Sargam's dataset and therefore
consumes no Groq tokens.

6.2 Extractor ablation
We report give-up rates across three consecutive system versions evaluated on overlapping prompt
sets:

The v2 result remained stable at 5x scale. The contribution of each modification is as follows.

The transition from v0 to v1 removed false positives produced by tokens such as `as`, `np`, `pd`, `plt`,
`nx`, and `st` (import aliases captured by the earlier regex), by submodule names such as `nn` and
`optim` extracted from `from torch import ...`, and by prose tokens such as `github`, `python`, and
`spacy-lg` that the earlier system was pulling from plain English. A particular user's `and` bug in `pip
install` belongs to the same error class.

The transition from v1 to v2 added the reconciler, so `cv2` maps to `opencv-python`, `pil` to `Pillow`,
`pptx` to `python-pptx`, `speech-recognition` to `SpeechRecognition`, `yaml` to `PyYAML`, and 20-plus
other cases. Across the 300-prompt run, the reconciler fired 29 times over 4 distinct alias pairs; the
remaining entries in the table were included as safeguards against aliases that did not occur in this run.

6.3 Recovery rate
We looked at the 300 runs on llama‑3.1‑8b:

 • 186 out of 300 (62%) produced code on the first try with llama‑3.1‑8b.
 • 114 triggered a retry. Of those 28 were fixed by the retry itself giving a 24.6% intra‑model rescue
 rate with llama‑3.1‑8b.
 • 86 Out of 300 (28.7%) used up the retry budget. Were sent to the fallback.
 • The fallback ran on 85 of these cases (one was lost because of a mid‑batch Groq rate‑limit
 event). It produced code on 14 which is a 16.5% cross‑model rescue rate with llama‑3.1‑8b.

Taken together the pipeline finished with clean code on 228 of 300 prompts (76%) with llama‑3.1‑8b.
The remaining 72 prompts still had hallucinated names after all attempts so they would show a
production‑time "do not pip install" warning.

6.4 Hallucination rate by tier
The 300 prompts break down into 18 tiers. The give‑up rate rises monotonically with adversariality:
Table 2: The primary give up rate by prompt tier (given that n = 300 prompts, on llama‑3.1‑8b).
 Tier n Primary give up
 Data Engineering 20 0.0%
 Level 8 20 0.0%
 Security & DevOps 20 5.0%

=== [PDF page 8] ===

 Level 1 (basic) 10 10.0%
 Level 2 (intermediate) 10 10.0%
 Level 6 20 15.0%
 Level 3 (difficult) 5 20.0%
 Level 5 20 20.0%
 Level 7 20 20.0%

 Level 9 20 30.0%

Two results stand out. For coding tasks, the kind developers see daily the detector causes almost no
friction: give‑up rates stay near zero across Data Engineering, DevOps and basic scripting. At the
adversarial end however about three, out of four requests trigger the pipeline. This is the situation
where the user most needs a warning so the detector’s failure mode matches its intended purpose.

6.5 The 50/50 split
Across 385 runs, the extractor produced 823 package verdicts, of which 644 were `real` (78.3%) and 179
were `hallucinated` (21.7%).

We cross-referenced the 179 hallucination flags against PyPI. Half were true 404s, meaning that no such
package exists (`pkg-resources`, `embedflow`, `vectorcache`, `codegenplus`, `sklearn-ai`, `pyyamlplus`,
`chromastore`, `groqclient`, `intelligentcache`, `packagevalidator`, and many similar inventions). The
other half returned PyPI status `200`, meaning that the name exists but was flagged by the classifier
because its metadata appeared suspicious:
Table 3: Wild caught PyPI registered squats and lookalikes flagged by the classifier on suspicious metadata.
 Name Canonical project P(fake) Flags
 pil Pillow 0.89 36
 faiss faiss-cpu / faiss-gpu 0.57 10
 tabula tabula-py 0.57 4
 haystack now haystack-ai 0.56 2
 graphbrain ambiguous 0.92 2
 aiworkflow ambiguous 0.90 2
 taskgraph Mozilla's; also ambiguous 0.56 2
 promptstudio ambiguous 0.58 2

 embeddinghub (none identified) 0.58 2
 camelot camelot-py 0.95 1
 skimage scikit-image 0.58 1

=== [PDF page 9] ===

 fastvector (none identified) 0.82 1
 fastyaml (none identified) 0.99 1
 (22 more, one or more ... ... 22
 flags each)


This is the most surprising empirical result in the paper. Approximately half of the hallucinated
recommendations produced by the LLM were already present on PyPI as squats or low-quality
lookalikes. A deterministic-only mitigation, although simple and inexpensive, would have caught only
the other half. The ML layer is therefore not merely incremental to the deterministic layer; the two
components cover distinct parts of the threat surface.

The security invariant described in Section 4.4 remained true during the run. For each of the 90
`status=200` flags the deterministic layer did not activate; The reconciler was never called.
Attacker-registered squats can only be stopped by the classifier, only when their metadata features are
highly suspicious.

6.6 Cross model transferability
Sargam trained seven per-LLM classifiers during her intern project. To assess whether the matched-pair
design was actually necessary, we constructed a 7 by 7 F1 matrix in which rows denote training LLMs,
columns denote test LLMs, and each cell reports the F1 of the row classifier on the column's held-out
data.

The initial protocol contained a leakage flaw. Sargam split each model's rows 75/25 with
`train_test_split(random_state=42)`. Package names appear across multiple model subsets: 210 of 464
unique packages occur in at least two models, and 42 occur in all seven. Because the features are
deterministic functions of the package name and PyPI metadata rather than of the generating LLM, and
because 100% of shared packages carry consistent labels across models, a random per-model split
caused 72.9% of off-diagonal test rows to leak package names that were already present in the
classifier's training set. The classifier was therefore memorizing names, instead of learning to generalize.

We therefore reran the analysis using a package-disjoint split: 75/25 over the 464 unique package
names instead of over rows ensuring that each package appears only in training or only, in testing, never
in both.

The corrected matrix (`results_v2_leakage_safe/cross_model_matrix_v2.csv`) is displayed in Table 4.
Table 4: Cross model transferability matrix (F1) (leakage safe package disjoint 75/25 split, 7 LLMs).
 gpt-5 gpt-oss- llama-3.1- llama-3.3- llama-4- qwen3- qwen3-
 120b 8b 70b scout 27b 32b
 gpt-5 1.000 1.000 1.000 1.000 1.000 1.000 0.960
 gpt-oss-120b 1.000 0.923 1.000 1.000 1.000 1.000 0.960
 llama-3.1-8b 0.923 0.923 1.000 1.000 1.000 1.000 0.960
 llama-3.3-70b 1.000 0.833 1.000 1.000 1.000 1.000 0.960
 llama-4-scout 1.000 0.923 1.000 1.000 1.000 1.000 0.960
 qwen3-27b 1.000 0.923 1.000 1.000 1.000 1.000 0.960
 qwen3-32b 1.000 0.909 1.000 1.000 1.000 1.000 0.957

=== [PDF page 10] ===

The point estimates fall between 0.833 and 1.000. The row patterns stay nearly the same. The diagonal
cells are usually equal to or lower than the off‑diagonal cells.

Bootstrap 95 percent confidence intervals based on 1,000 resamples help explain the uncertainty. The
two test columns, llama‑4‑scout and qwen3‑27b each have two hallucinated examples per model test
set giving confidence intervals of [0.00, 1.00] for every training model. Those cells are essentially
uninformative. The columns llama‑3.1‑8b and llama‑3.3‑70b each contain five test examples producing
confidence intervals of [0.67, 1.00]. Only the columns gpt‑oss‑120b (6 examples) gpt‑5 (7) and
qwen3‑32b (12) have narrow enough intervals to allow useful cell‑level comparison. With the sample
sizes much of the seeming uniformity in the matrix is just small‑sample noise.

The overall qualitative conclusion still stands. No training model is consistently better on any test
column no diagonal cell is larger than the off‑diagonal cells and one classifier trained on the biggest
available slice, gpt‑oss‑120b with about 410 training rows works well across all seven models without
any detectable loss in accuracy. Therefore matched‑pair training is not needed for deployment.

The ease of transfer tells us a lot. Feature importance is very concentrated. The feature log_maintainers
alone makes up 57.6% of the Random Forest split importance and the feature github_url_present adds
another 24.5%. Together those two features provide 82% of the classifier’s signal coming mainly from
PyPI metadata that says whether the package is real and actively maintained. The other eight features
provide the remaining 18 percent. In practice the classifier is simply a metadata‑based check and this
type of evidence does not depend on any particular large language model.

To make claims about cell‑level transferability each model would need about 30 hallucinated test
examples. Currently models have between 68 and 108 hallucinated rows in total. Only a quarter of those
go into the test split leaving only 2 to 12 positive examples per test slice. Either the generation runs for
each model must be increased by three times or the evaluation should switch to a pooled
cross‑validation approach so that every hallucinated example is used in test folds for all models. This
work is still in the future.

Section 6.10 tests this idea directly by comparing the Random Forest with a hand‑written rule that uses
two features, on the same package‑disjoint split.

6.7 LLM homogeneity
The fallback in our evaluation is llama-3.3-70b selected because it was Groq hosted had a matched
classifier available and was stronger than the primary. It rescued 14 of 85 give-up cases (16.5%). The
remaining 71 cases or 83.5% failed again under the fallback.

Inspection of the failure cases reveals a clear pattern: llama-3.1-8b and llama-3.3-70b both belong to the
Llama family, share pretraining data and post training methodology, and on the adversarial prompts
often hallucinate the same package names. Pdfgenius, ultrarag, hyperfaiss, fastyaml, documentvision,
vectorcache, embedflow and taskgraph recur in both models’ outputs for the prompts. A stronger
fallback cannot rescue a hallucination mode that it shares with the primary.

=== [PDF page 11] ===

The practical implication is straightforward: robust cross model routing should use a fallback from a
model family (Qwen or GPT-OSS for a Llama primary or vice versa). We did not run that experiment in
this iteration because it would have required 5 times the Groq token budget beyond the free tier but the
design implication is clear.

6.8 Model self defense
The Bonus Stress Test tier contains 10 prompts that explicitly name fabricated packages: `fastvectorai`,
`hyperfaiss`, `streamgraphx`, `pdfgenius`, `smartocrpro`, `torchvisionx`, `langgraphx`, `openrouter-sdk-
python`, `fastyamlparser` and `ultrarag`.

Only one of the ten bait packages was installed by the LLM under its requested name: ultrarag. The
detector caught it. The pipeline ultimately gave up after retries.

Three additional baits triggered nearby, still hallucinatory variants. When asked for fastvectorai the
model produced fastvector; when asked for fastyamlparser it produced fastyaml;. When asked for
hyperfaiss it reached for plain faiss, which is itself treated here as a metadata suspicious name rather
than as a canonical install target.

The remaining six baits, streamgraphx, pdfgenius, smartocrpro, torchvisionx, langgraphx and
openrouter-sdk-python were refused outright. In those cases, the model substituted real packages such
as pdfplumber, torchvision, networkx or openrouter.

End to end the pipeline finished clean on 6 of 10 direct bait prompts corresponding to a 60% rate, on the
most adversarial category. The LLM refused the bait name on 9 of 10 prompts and only one bait package
was ever proposed verbatim. This indicates that contemporary instruction tuning already provides a first
line of defense which the detector then complements.

6.9 User acceptance study
Sargam conducted a 24-participant survey on the standalone Streamlit tool with her CS undergraduate
peers at JUET Guna. Participants rated the system on seven dimensions using a 1 to 5 Likert scale.
Table 5: User acceptance study ratings on a 1 to 5 Likert scale (n = 24 CS undergraduates).
 Dimension Mean Median
 Accuracy 4.21 5
 Confidence score 4.38 5
 Interface clarity 4.42 5
 Speed 4.58 5
 Trust in verdicts 4.25 5
