=== [PDF page 12] ===

be used a lot in life. Also the study gave comments: one person’s bad experience showed a problem, in
the extractor that led to the rewrite in Section 4.1.

6.10 Rule-based baseline
Because the important features were `log_maintainers` and `github_url_present` (Section 6.6) we tested
a simple rule system on the same package-disjoint split that was used in Section 6.6. We looked at three
versions: a strict rule that required both features, a strict rule plus `lev<=3` and a more relaxed rule that
used OR.
Table 6: Rule based baselines versus Random Forest on the leakage safe package disjoint split. Rule C (looser OR)
matches or beats the RF on all 7 test slices.
 Model Rule A: strict Rule B: strict Rule C: looser RF F1
 AND (2 feat) AND + lev<=3 OR (2 feat)
 gpt-5 0.70 0.70 1.00 1.00
 gpt-oss-120b 0.52 0.52 1.00 0.92
 llama-3.1-8b 0.45 0.43 1.00 1.00
 llama-3.3-70b 0.59 0.56 1.00 1.00
 llama-4-scout 0.31 0.29 1.00 1.00
 qwen3-27b 0.57 0.50 1.00 1.00
 qwen3-32b 0.71 0.71 0.96 0.96
 Mean 0.55 0.53 0.99 0.98


When we use the strict versions, the F1 values drop to about 0.53 or 0.55. This happens because asking
for both signals makes it much harder to find packages. For example a real package might be missing a
GitHub URL in its PyPI metadata. A real package might also be brand new, have very little history. These
real packages end up looking like hallucinations.

To put it simply the classifier basically becomes one rule: if a package has zero PyPI maintainers AND no
GitHub URL it is probably a hallucination. Everything else is probably real. You can write that rule in one
line of Python. Because of this the 400-tree Random Forest does not really give us more help than the
simple OR baseline using our current features.

This does not mean the two-layer architecture is a bad idea. We still need a layer whether it uses ML or
simple rules to catch the 50% of hallucinations that use names already taken by squatters on PyPI
(Section 6.5). A simple 404 check alone cannot find those hallucinations.



7. Discussion


 1. The way we clean the data matters most for the precision of the classifier. The two big changes
 that helped us stop giving up much, rewriting the extractor and adding the reconciler, are both
 preprocessing steps. Together these two changes caused a 49-point drop. Changing the classifier
 itself did not help much. This is not a new idea in ML research but it is worth saying again, in
 real-world text pipelines the extractor is often where most errors come from.

=== [PDF page 13] ===

 2. The security rule works. We checked the reconciler design, which only allows a rescue after a
 PyPI 404 against an attacker suite. We also tested it across 300 prompts (90 `status=200` flags,
 with zero rescues). The design is easy to understand. Any future updates to the mapping file
 must follow this strict rule.
 3. The two-layer detector makes sense based on our data. The current ML version is not the only
 way to do it. About half of what a local LLM hallucinates are names that someone has already
 registered on PyPI. This means a simple 404 check leaves a lot of threats open. However, Section
 6.10 shows that with our features a simple rule-based layer works just as well as or even better
 than the Random Forest.
 4. The fact that LLMs are so similar makes it hard to switch between models. Using a fallback from
 the same model family only rescues about one out of six failures. Using a fallback from different
 model family should work better and testing that idea is our next big experiment.
 5. It was good to see that the models can defend themselves. The weaker primary model in our
 pair refused 60% of tricks without any help from the detector. If this keeps happening with
 future models we should view the detector as something that works alongside instruction
 tuning rather than something that replaces it.
 6. Regarding the choice of classifier, rules and Random Forests are basically the same in this setup.
 The Random Forest still has three benefits even though the OR rule matches the Random
 Forest’s F1 (Section 6.10). First the Random Forest gives the classifier probability scores instead
 of just hard labels and this helps when the classifier shows results in a user interface or sets
 thresholds. Second it is easier for the classifier to add features later if we find better features.
 Third the Random Forest can handle connections between features without the classifier having
 to redesign everything.


7.1 Limitations

 1. Our evaluation uses one pair of models `llama-3.1-8b` and `llama-3.3-70b`. Testing pairs
 from families, such as Llama to Qwen or Llama to GPT-OSS would prove the model
 similarity claim but we did not have enough Groq token budget to do it.
 2. The `pypi_maintainers_count` feature in the classifier is basically 0 for projects because
 the PyPI JSON API only shows maintainers if you are an admin. Sargam’s dataset helps a
 little by pulling metadata. So this feature might cause false positives for small legitimate
 packages. In the future the classifier should use signals such as the upload date or how
 often a package is updated.
 3. The cross-model transferability matrix still looks good. The numbers for each cell are
 limited because each model had between 2 and 12 hallucinated tests. This means two of
 the test columns do not really tell us much. We need model runs or pooled cross-
 validation to be more certain.
 4. The classifier relies heavily, around 82%, on `log_maintainers` and `github_url_present`.
 This means the classifier is basically a soft version of a deterministic check on PyPI
 metadata. This might make it easy for attackers to trick the classifier by registering
 squats with metadata that looks real. We did not test for this kind of attack
 5. Our finding about squats, in Section 6.5 shows at least 30 names registered on PyPI that
 the classifier thinks are suspicious. We have not checked every one to see if they are

=== [PDF page 14] ===

 actually low‑quality lookalikes or niche legitimate projects. A PyPI audit would make this
 claim stronger.
 6. The user acceptance study used a group of people, from the intern’s friends so the
 results might be biased.

7.1.1 Drift and freshness
The evaluation is a snapshot in time. The paper does not currently address data drift. The evaluation
shows that three concrete failure modes stand out. First brand new legitimate packages are
systematically mis‑flagged because their maintainer count is zero their GitHub link may not yet appear
in PyPI metadata. Their name will not be in the fixed 15,000 name reference list so every one of our
three dominant features reads them as suspicious for months after publication. Second as popularity
shifts, packages that emerge and become popular after the snapshot register as far from any top
package until the reference list is refreshed so Levenshtein distance loses meaning at the tail. Third,
packages that are abandoned silently taken over or renamed after training can flip category without the
classifier noticing on names it still trusts; haystack becoming haystack‑ai is an example already present
in our data. None of the following mitigations are implemented in the system but each would be
reasonable before any long‑lived production use: refreshing the top N PyPI snapshot on a monthly
schedule; retraining the classifier on a rolling quarterly window using a newer raw_master_dataset.csv;
adding a per‑package cache with a 24 hour TTL so PyPI metadata is always reasonably fresh at inference
time; and monitoring the live false‑positive rate on production runs so that a drift threshold can
automatically trigger retraining. We treat each of these as future work and would prioritize at least the
first two.

7.2 Future work
The most natural extensions of this work fall into three groups.

For the classifier, the next question is whether richer features are worth their complexity. We
intentionally limited the paper to 10 hand-crafted metadata and name signals, because Section 6.10
establishes the baseline that richer features would need to beat; a study that simply added more
features without that comparison would be less informative. Candidate extensions include release
cadence, first-upload age, owner-network overlap, README quality signals, and repository activity
features.

For the agent, the most important extension is cross-family fallback pairing. The current same-family
pairing (`llama-3.1-8b` to `llama-3.3-70b`) rescues only 16.5% of primary give-up cases because both
models share hallucination patterns (Section 6.7). Pairing Llama with Qwen or GPT-OSS is the obvious
next step for evaluation.

To keep evaluation the main need is tighter transferability confidence intervals. We must scale
per‑model hallucinated‑example generation about three times to obtain at least thirty positive test
examples for each model or we should shift to pooled cross‑validation where every hallucinated
example counts across all folds.

For deployment robustness, drift handling and refresh policies matter most. As discussed in Section
7.1.1 the monthly refresh of the top‑N PyPI snapshot and the quarterly retraining are the two
mitigations we would prioritize before any production deployment.

=== [PDF page 15] ===

8. Conclusion
The two‑layer detector, with retry and fallback routing solves 76% of the 300 prompts with clean
hallucination‑free code. It also cuts the give‑up rate from 79% (unmitigated) to 28.7%. Half of the
hallucinations that small local LLMs produce already exist on PyPI as low‑quality squats or lookalikes.
This fact shows that a second layer, beyond existence checks is needed. Hallucination rates follow
adversariality closely so the detector stays quiet on routine tasks and only activates when warnings are
most needed. The weaker of the two models refuses 60% of direct bait prompts on its own. Same‑family
fallback routing saves 16.5% of the remaining failures so pairing models from different families becomes
the most natural next step.

All release artifacts, such as the code, mapping table, three‑hundred prompts, seven classifiers, 385
record run log and retrained leakage‑safe transferability matrix are available at:
“https://github.com/sargamsahu1011/package-hallucination-detector ”.

Acknowledgments
Sargam Sahu, a summer intern at Kruman Corporations and a student at JUET‑Guna, built the per‑LLM
Random Forest classifier catalog, curated the fifteen‑thousand‑package PyPI reference list for
name‑similarity features developed the Streamlit tool and coordinated the twenty‑four‑participant user
acceptance study. One user’s survey response revealed an extractor preprocessing bug that led to the
rework of Section 4.1. The primary author added the two‑layer detector integration, the pipeline, the
reconciler and its security design and the three‑hundred prompt evaluation.

References
Breiman, L. (2001). Random Forests. Machine Learning, 45(1), 5-32.

Chase, H. and the LangChain team (2024). LangGraph documentation. https://langchain-
ai.github.io/langgraph.

Spracklen, J., Wijewickrama, R., Sakib, A. H. M. N., Maiti, A., Viswanath, B., and Jadliwala, M. (2024). We
Have a Package for You! A Comprehensive Analysis of Package Hallucinations by Code Generating LLMs.
arXiv:2406.10279.

Appendix A. Curated Import Alias Mapping
The complete mapping is released as `data/import_to_pypi.yaml`. It contains 24 entries. Each entry
corresponds to a used Python project. The import name for each project is different from its PyPI install
name. The file header states the security invariants explicitly. The file forbids speculative additions.

Appendix B. Extractor Test Suite
Twelve regression tests in `tests/test_extractor.py` cover import-alias handling. The tests also cover
submodule imports. The tests include comma-separated imports. The tests check `pip install` with
version specifiers and flags. The tests include comments, in bash blocks. The tests cover prose outside
code fences. The tests handle prose-and-code responses. The tests capture slopsquat baits. The tests
capture import-alias reconciliation candidates. All 12 tests pass on the extractor.

=== [PDF page 16] ===

Appendix C. Evaluation Prompt Set
The 300 prompts are listed in `data/eval_prompts.txt`. One prompt appears on each line. Blank lines are
skipped by the batch runner. Comment lines that start with `#` are skipped. Tier boundaries are marked
with comment headers.

Real-but-uninstalled packages and invented packages are therefore merged. The paper says nothing about whether names exist on PyPI or about squatting.

   120	- [I] **Abstract ranges are not traceable.** The abstract's "8.1-40%", "16-70%" and "14-85%" do not match the table ranges directly.
   121	- [I] **Unspecified model versions and mixed temperatures.** Model versions are not given, and temperatures differ between closed (1.0) and open (0.4) models, which confounds model comparisons.
   122	- [I] **Inconsistent annotation share.** The double-annotated share is "One third" (p. 7) but "25%" in the Table 8 caption (p. 18).
   123	- [I] **Thin reproducibility and statistics.** No CIs, a single Pass@1 sample, and no code release reported.
   124	
   125	## 10. Threats to validity
   126	- Internal: o3-mini is both a detector baseline and the repair model. Granite outputs come from different sources across experiments (p. 10). RIF is a relative metric.
   127	- External: Python, three benchmarks, older closed models (Claude-3, GPT-3.5/4) and small open models; no agentic setting.
   128	- Construct: "hallucination" is operationalised through runtime error types against an installed environment. Benchmark underspecification inflates counts, which the authors partly correct (pp. 9, 12).
   129	- Statistical conclusion: no tests or CIs. Kappa is substantial (0.79) (p. 7).
   130	- Reproducibility: hardware and benchmarks are reported; model versions, code and outputs are not.
   131	
   132	## 11. Future research directions
   133	- Stated by authors [A]:
   134	  - use the model's internal states for detection (p. 12);
   135	  - extend static tools with data-flow and control-flow tracking (pp. 7–8);
   136	  - build benchmarks that accept multiple valid solutions and specify input/output types (p. 9);
   137	  - study where hallucinations originate (p. 12);
   138	  - extend to other languages (p. 4).

   140	  - add a registry-existence layer (PyPI/npm) to the static pipeline, so that "not installed" is separated from "does not exist" and from "exists but is a squat";
   141	  - report package-level results separately.

   144	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ3 (static analysis and constrained decoding as cheap defences; cost and effectiveness), RQ4 (environment-based ground truth, benchmark-noise pitfalls, annotation reliability), RQ1 (hallucination shares across small and large models, partially), RQ5 (laptop feasibility).
   145	- How it informs our work [I]:
   146	  - **Proof of laptop feasibility.** The whole study, including constrained decoding of 2–8B models, ran on an M2 machine with 24 GB RAM (p. 17).
   147	  - **Cheap import-level screening.** Mypy/Pyright with stubs run in about 1–2.5 s per sample (p. 19), a cheap pre-execution layer for import-level hallucinations. However, they check the *installed environment*, not the registry, so they cannot tell a slopsquatted package (which installs fine) from a legitimate one. A registry-aware check is still needed.
   148	  - **Constrained decoding is not worth it here.** It costs about +12 s per request for small, inconsistent gains (p. 11).
   149	  - **Measurement lesson.** Separate benchmark noise from model hallucination, and validate a subset by hand.
   150	  - Evidence strength: **moderate** (claimed peer-reviewed, sound manual analysis, but the package-level relevance is indirect).

Annotation reliability and validation One third of the annotations were labeled by two domain anno-
tators for two purposes: a) to validate reliability and b) to establish guidelines and a systematic rubric for
annotation, which can be found as a supplemental material of this work. This resulted in an average Cohen’s
kappa of 0.79 across the eight annotated labels. All open-closed labels exceeded 0.8 agreement, while the
categorical labels ranged from 0.69 to 0.77. These results demonstrated sufficient annotator reliability to
proceed with a single annotation for the remaining dataset. More details on inter-annotation agreement can
be found in the Appendix D.1.
We consider four metrics: Caught is the percentage of cases that were flagged. TP (True Positives) is
the percentage of cases where the hallucination was correctly identified for the right reason. Overlap is the
percentage of cases identified by one tool that were also identified by the other tool. Capable is the percentage
of cases we believe the method could potentially catch (and for the correct reason rather than by chance).
In Table 2, for Caught and TP columns, we observe a high rate of False Positives (FP) when manually
examining why the hallucination was generated. Due to the FP, we observe variability in the Overlap
column between the detected samples. However, in Odex, this is when the grammar is far from static. This
is particularly evident in the datetime library, where the way it is imported collides with the built-in and
module definitions, resulting in higher TN for the grammar that translates into high precision and recall,
whereas for Static it is a FP.

represent a concrete, addressable gap; resolving them would meaningfully increase detection in data science
benchmarks like DS-1000, which is a standard for data science libraries using dataframes.
In Table 2, we see that on Odex, static tools are capable of detecting 70.5% of hallucinations; this also
translates into higher recall observed in Table 1. This is because many cases of Odex do not return anything
in the function, resulting in returning None being an easy true positive for the Static tools to identify.
However, this is not the case for BigCode, with a more diverse source of hallucinations.

Type annotations remain a challenge for static analysis Manual inspection reveals the limits of
type annotations in static analysis tools for detecting errors. One key issue with the grammar approach is
the limited information in docstrings. For example, docstrings do not define namespaces, and so int32 in
result = tf.random.uniform(..., dtype=tf.int32) is marked as an error. However, this also occurs
with more robust methods, such as Pyright and Mypy, where we observe instances in which function calls
are resolved using type stubs that contain undefined parameter types in their annotations, for example, on
result = np.random.choice(a=[(3,3),(3,4)], samples, p=prob), static analysis tools are unable to
detect a as an imaginary feature, as its definition requires a 1D np.array. With inaccurate and unspecified
data types and dimensions in data structures, those hallucinations will become false negatives.
Another false negative for that grammar happens when it is unable to link an attribute to the library
name or alias. To see the issue this causes, consider cv = CountVectorizer(stop_words=’english’,
punctuation_pattern=r’\\W’). punctuation_pattern is a hallucination, but the grammar does not iden-
tify it because this code doesn’t use the library name or alias in the call, instead importing the object using
from ... import CountVectorizer. We could modify the grammar to avoid requiring the explicit use of
the library name or alias, but that would introduce additional false positives. Tracking import statements
would require features beyond those supported by llama.cpp.

5.1.2 Causes of Hallucinations and Identifying False Positives

For each hallucination in the sample, we also annotated the cause and whether it occurred during the LLM’s
code or while processing the test. These results yield allows us to distinguish between hallucinations that
static methods could in principle resolve, and those that require fundamentally different approaches. Table 9
in the Appendix describes examples of root cause failures and why these could be detected based on the
capability of each detection tool.
There were three hallucination categories that fall outside the scope of static analysis by nature, not by
limitation of current tools, these relate to prompt underspecification rather than code analysis. (1) When

5.2 Repair

In this section, we turn from detecting errors to repairing them. We evaluate on the examples that contained
an error when executed: 2210 samples in DS-1000, 2001 in BigCode, and 1291 in Odex (across all six
generation models). To repair the error, we prompt an LLM with the code, the error, and a request to
resolve the issue. We try o3-mini combined with static analysis tools, or no tool at all.
Table 4 shows that our approach consistently improved all metrics, particularly execution rate (ER). Mean-
while, Table 5 shows Repair on Imaginary Features (RIF ), which addresses when repair fails, how often it
is due to an imaginary feature? In most cases, there is no improvement in fixing hallucinations; moreover,
in Odex, the hallucination rate increased; o3-mini performs better without static analysis on DS-1000 and
BigCodeBench, but not on Odex. While repair consistently improves executability, imaginary features prove
resistant. This reveals detection and repair as fundamentally decoupled challenges.

    18	# Library Hallucinations in LLM-Generated Code: A Risk Analysis Grounded in Developer Queries
    19	
    20	- Authors: Twist, Lukas; Harman, Mark; Yannakoudakis, Helen; Zhang, Jie M.
    21	- Year / venue: 2026, Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (published)
    22	- DOI: 10.18653/2026.emnlp-main.78 · URL: https://doi.org/10.18653/2026.emnlp-main.78
    23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
    24	
    25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
    26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
    27	
    28	**Source tier:** EMNLP 2026 main conference, pp. 1785–1812 (p. 1). Tier 1, peer-reviewed.
    29	
    30	## 1. Research objective
    31	- [A] The authors present "the first systematic study of how user-level prompt variations influence library hallucinations". They cover library *name* hallucinations (invalid imports) and *member* hallucinations (invalid calls from valid libraries) (p. 1).
    32	- [A] They also want to provide a reproducible benchmark (LibHalluBench) built from the highest-risk conditions (pp. 1–2).
    33	
    34	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
    35	- No numbered RQs. The paper runs two main experiments (pp. 3–4):
    36	  - **Exp. 1, user language.** Do realistic library descriptions mined from StackExchange (e.g. "fast", "modern", "from 2025") change hallucination rates?
    37	  - **Exp. 2, user mistakes.** Do one-character typos, multi-character typos, or fake names/members cause hallucinations?
    38	- Additional studies (pp. 7–8): prompt engineering, ecosystem generalisability, rarity-seeking language, PyPI-tool access, and ablations/controls.
    39	
    40	## 3. Methodology
    41	- Research design: [V] Controlled experiments that vary one prompt slot (`{library directive}`) in a fixed template, measured across seven LLMs with three responses per prompt (pp. 3–4, 15).
    42	- Approach / model / intervention:
    43	  - [V] **Extraction.** Code blocks are extracted by regex. Python `ast` reads Import/ImportFrom (handling aliases and namespace packages) and Call/Attribute nodes (p. 4).
    44	  - [V] **Name check.** Names are compared with PyPI using PyPA name normalisation (p. 4).
    45	  - [V] **Member check.** Members are compared with scraped official documentation (latest version) (pp. 4–5).
    46	  - [V] **Version exclusion.** Responses that state a valid explicit version are excluded (p. 5).
    47	  - [V] **Generated mistakes.** Typos and fake names are generated by o4-mini. Edit distance is checked (1, or 2–8), and every name is verified to be non-existent (pp. 4, 17).
    48	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] "No description" (Exp. 1) and "None, valid library/member" (Exp. 2) conditions; un-prompted vs prompt-engineered vs tool-augmented runs (pp. 5–6, 18, 21).
    49	
    50	## 4. Dataset and sample
    51	- Data source(s):
    52	  - [V] BigCodeBench (1,140 tasks), filtered to tasks that do not name the ground-truth library and whose libraries have accessible documentation. This gives 356 tasks using 30 libraries; 10% are held out for preliminary experiments (p. 3). LibHalluBench is built from 321 seed tasks (p. 8).
    53	  - [V] Software Recommendations StackExchange: over 20,000 questions, filtered to 3,917 library-related questions and clustered into nine descriptors. 23 question titles contain a year (pp. 4, 16).
    54	  - [V] CodeInsight test split (1,860 records). The longest 50% were kept, 500 were sampled, and an LLM rewrote them to be library- and language-agnostic (p. 19).
    55	- Sample size (N) and unit:
    56	  - [V] Three responses per prompt (p. 4).
    57	  - [V] Two instances of each error type per task (p. 4).
    58	  - [V] Ecosystem study: one response per task, with 140 Python, 161 JavaScript and 184 Rust libraries (pp. 7, 20).
    59	- Sampling / selection method:
    60	  - [V] The SRSE filter was validated on 200 hand-labelled questions (precision and recall 0.95) (p. 15).
    61	  - [V] Clusters were retained if they linked to at least 20 questions (p. 16).
    62	- Data availability:
    63	  - [V] Code and full model outputs are on GitHub (p. 2).
    64	  - [V] LibHalluBench is on Hugging Face (gated access) and on PyPI (`libhallubench`), with a canary string (pp. 8, 23).
    65	
    66	## 5. Experimental setup
    67	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
    68	  - [V] **Models, with exact versions** (p. 15):
    69	
    70	    | Model | Version | Temperature | top_p |
    71	    |---|---|---|---|
    72	    | GPT-4o-mini | gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18 | 1.0 | 1.0 |
    73	    | GPT-5-mini | gpt-5-mini-2025-08-07 | 1.0 | 1.0 |
    74	    | Ministral-8B | ministral-2410 | 0.3 | 1.0 |
    75	    | Qwen-2.5-Coder | qwen2.5-coder-32b-instruct | 0.7 | 0.8 |
    76	    | Llama-3.3 | llama-3.3-70b-instruct-turbo | 0.6 | 0.9 |
    77	    | DeepSeek-V3.1 | deepseek-chat-v3.1 | 0.6 | 0.5 |
    78	    | Claude-4.5-Haiku | claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 | 1.0 | 1.0 |
    79	
    80	  - [V] All models are accessed via provider APIs (OpenAI, Mistral, Together, DeepSeek, Anthropic). Each call is a fresh session with no system prompt. Study date: January 2026 (pp. 3, 15).
    81	  - [V] DeepSeek-V3.1 was replaced by V3.2 for the ecosystem and ablation runs (p. 14).
    82	  - Hardware: not reported (API-only).
    83	- Code availability: [V] GitHub repository (pp. 2, 23).
    84	
    85	## 6. Evaluation metrics
    86	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
    87	  - [V] **RHR:** share of responses containing a hallucination.
    88	  - [V] **THR:** share of tasks with at least one hallucinating response out of three (p. 5).
    89	  - [V] **Tool study:** hallucination rate, share of responses using the tool, tool calls per response, and share of no-code responses (p. 21).
    90	  - [V] **Detector validation:** precision and recall on 200 high-risk responses (pp. 5, 15).
    91	  - [V] In Exp. 2 with valid names, the rate shown is how often the requested valid library was *not* used (p. 6).
    92	- Statistical testing: none reported (no tests, CIs or effect sizes). "Significantly" is used descriptively (pp. 6, 8).
    93	
    94	## 7. Key findings
    95	1. [V] **Normal prompts rarely produce invented library names.** With "No description" and adjective prompts, library-name RHR is ≤0.31% for all models (p. 5).
    96	2. [V] **Year-based prompts drive library-name hallucination.** "From 2025" THR (p. 5):
    97	   - GPT-4o-mini 84.74%
    98	   - GPT-5-mini 63.86%
    99	   - Qwen-2.5-Coder 61.68%
   100	   - DeepSeek-V3.1 38.01%
   101	   - Ministral-8B 32.40%
   102	   - Llama-3.3 1.87%
   103	   - Claude-4.5-Haiku 0.62%
   104	
   105	   [V] A year control shows "from 2022" stays <1.1% RHR, while "from 2026" gives DeepSeek-V3.2 59.81% vs Claude 0.73% (p. 28). [A] Knowledge cut-off contributes but does not fully explain the effect (p. 28).
   106	3. [V] **User mistakes are accepted** (library-name THR, p. 6):
   107	   - one-character typos: up to 25.86% (GPT-5-mini);
   108	   - multi-character typos: up to 79.44%;
   109	   - fake library names: 90.50–99.22% for GPT-4o-mini, GPT-5-mini and Ministral-8B, vs 20.72% for Qwen-2.5-Coder.
   110	
   111	   [V] Average usage of fake members is 31% vs 69% for fake names (p. 7). [A] The authors link this to sycophancy and say LLMs "may amplify typosquatting risks" (pp. 2, 6).
   112	4. [V] **Rarity-seeking language.** "Hidden gem" raises the average library-name THR to 5.35%, the highest of the adjective prompts (p. 8).
   113	5. [V] **Prompt engineering is inconsistent.** Self-analysis reduces hallucinations in 29/36 settings and explicit-check in 30/36. Chain-of-thought and step-back are inconsistent, e.g. Qwen-2.5-Coder fake-name RHR rises by 28.66 points under chain-of-thought (pp. 18–19).
   114	6. [V] **A PyPI-existence tool helps but does not remove the problem** (pp. 8, 21):
   115	   - GPT-4o-mini calls it on 98.65% of "from 2025" responses, with 2.49% hallucination.
   116	   - GPT-5-mini calls it on only 7.89% and returns no code 90.76% of the time.
   117	   - Under user mistakes, invalid libraries are still accepted in up to 38.79% of cases.
   118	7. [V] **Other ecosystems** (CodeInsight, RHR; p. 20):
   119	   - JavaScript fake names 27.2–88.8%;
   120	   - Rust fake names 41.30–96.76%;
   121	   - Rust "from 2025" up to 57.40% (Qwen).
   122	8. [V] **Detector validation.** 24 responses were auto-flagged and 23 were true hallucinations (95.8% precision). No false negatives were found in the 200-response sample. The one false positive was `pywintypes` (pp. 5, 15).
   123	9. [V] **LibHalluBench baselines** (overall task-level rate across the Describe and Specify splits): Llama-3.3 10.4% lowest; GPT-4o-mini 39.0% and GPT-5-mini 39.8% highest (p. 23).
   124	10. [V] **Robustness.** Greedy decoding and Qwen3-235B-generated mistakes leave the qualitative patterns unchanged (pp. 26–27).
   125	
   126	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
   127	- [A] Generalisability: a finite set of tasks, ecosystems and model versions. Behaviour may differ for other languages, domain frameworks, low-resource ecosystems or future models (p. 9).
   128	- [A] Internal validity: automatic extraction and prompt construction are mitigated with unit tests and manual validation (pp. 9–10).
   129	- [A] External validity: dataset bias and LLM nondeterminism and updates. Leakage would make the results conservative (p. 10).
   130	- [A] Evolving models and package ecosystems may affect reproducibility (p. 10).
   131	- [A] The prompt-engineering study is not exhaustive, and the tool study is a "small case study" on the GPT models only (pp. 7–8).
   132	
   133	## 9. Limitations we identified
   134	- [I] **Exp. 2 measures compliance, not spontaneous invention.** The invalid name comes from the user prompt, so the attacker cannot predict it from the model. This is a *typosquatting-amplification* threat model, not classic slopsquatting of model-invented names.
   135	- [I] **Registered names count as valid.** Generated mistakes were filtered to be *unregistered* (pp. 4, 17), and any name present on PyPI counts as valid (p. 4). Hallucinations that collide with already-registered or squatted names are therefore invisible by design, which undercounts the real security risk.
   136	- [I] **Registry snapshot undated.** The main check's PyPI snapshot date is not reported. The tool used a "cached PyPI package list" (p. 22) and the study ran in January 2026 (p. 15).
   137	- [I] **Persistence not reported.** Whether the same invented names repeat across runs or models is not reported. This is a central question for slopsquatting (RQ2).
   138	- [I] **Small validation sample.** Detector precision rests on 24 flagged responses. Recall is inferred from 200 responses drawn from only two high-risk conditions (p. 15).
   139	- [I] **Mixed temperatures.** Default temperatures differ across models (0.3–1.0) (p. 15), which confounds model comparisons. The greedy ablation (p. 26) partly addresses this.
   140	- [I] **No uncertainty reporting.** Differences such as 0.10% vs 0.31% equal one response or task.
   141	- [I] **API models only.** No local or quantized models were tested.
   142	
   143	## 10. Threats to validity
   144	- Internal:
   145	  - Year prompts are partly confounded with knowledge cut-off; the control is small (p. 28).
   146	  - Typos generated by an LLM may not match real human typos; the provider ablation mitigates this (p. 27).
   147	- External:
   148	  - The main results rest on one benchmark (BigCodeBench, 30 libraries) and single-turn, single-function prompts; there is no agentic setting.
   149	  - The ecosystem study extends to JS and Rust (p. 20).
   150	- Construct:
   151	  - "Hallucination" means "not on the registry or in the docs". Already-registered hallucinations are counted as correct.
   152	  - Exp. 2 compliance is labelled as hallucination.
   153	- Statistical conclusion: no tests or CIs. Three responses per prompt give limited per-task resolution.
   154	- Reproducibility: strong. Versions, parameters, prompts, code, outputs and the benchmark are all released (pp. 2, 15–17, 23). The DeepSeek version had to be swapped (p. 14).
   155	
   156	## 11. Future research directions
   157	- Stated by authors [A]:
   158	  - cut-off-aware behaviour and anti-sycophancy behaviour;
   159	  - lightweight pre-decision existence checks;
   160	  - reporting hallucination, refusal, tool-use and calibration metrics (p. 9);
   161	  - more robust approaches (grounding, fine-tuning, architecture) (p. 19);
   162	  - agentic coding workflows (p. 9).
   163	- Suggested by us [I]:
   164	  - measure name repetition and how many invented names are already registered;
   165	  - run LibHalluBench on local quantized models;
   166	  - test a *forced*, non-optional client-side existence check versus model-invoked tools.
   167	
   168	## 12. Relevance to our research
   169	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (drivers: prompt type, model, ecosystem), RQ3 (prompt-engineering and tool-use defences), RQ4 (PyPI normalisation, version exclusion, detector validation, benchmark), RQ2 (typosquat amplification, indirectly), RQ5 (untested: local/quantized models, agents, registered-name collisions).
   170	- How it informs our work [I]:
   171	  - **A ready-made trigger set.** LibHalluBench (4,173 prompts) and the `libhallubench` package give a laptop-runnable trigger set. Year-based and typo/fake-name prompts are the highest-yield conditions for a small measurement study.
   172	  - **Untested setting.** Running the benchmark against local quantized open models (none tested here) is an obvious, cheap extension.
   173	  - **Why a forced check matters.** The tool study shows a model-invoked existence check depends on the model choosing to call it (GPT-5-mini rarely did). A *forced*, client-side check, as in raj2026names, avoids that dependency. The comparison is a well-defined defence experiment.
   174	  - **Inherit the methods.** Adopt the PyPI name normalisation and the version-exclusion rule. Add a status for "registered but suspicious", which this paper by design does not measure.
   175	  - Evidence strength: **moderate–strong** (peer-reviewed, 7 models, repeated sampling, ablations), but there is no inferential statistics and the main results rest on one benchmark.

   177	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
   178	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
   179	|---|---|---|---|---|
   180	| RQ1 | Under ordinary or adjective prompts, library-name hallucination is near 0% (≤0.31% RHR) across 7 LLMs | 5 | V | moderate |
   181	| RQ1 | "From 2025" prompts cause library-name hallucinations in up to 84.74% of tasks (GPT-4o-mini), with strong model dependence (Claude-4.5-Haiku 0.62%) | 5 | V | strong |
   182	| RQ1 | Fake library names in prompts are used in up to 99.22% of tasks; one-character typos in up to 25.86% | 6 | V | strong |
   183	| RQ1 | Patterns persist in JavaScript and Rust (fake-name RHR up to 88.8% JS, 96.76% Rust) | 20 | V | moderate |
   184	| RQ3 | Self-analysis and explicit-check prompts reduce hallucinations in 29/36 and 30/36 settings; chain-of-thought and step-back are unreliable | 18, 19 | V | moderate |

LLM responses are returned either as raw code or
    in Markdown format. We extract code blocks using
    regex matching of triple-backtick segments fol-
    lowed by a language identifier (Cone, 2025). For
    each Python block, we construct an abstract syn-
    tax tree using Python’s ast module (PSF, 2025).
    We traverse Import and ImportFrom nodes to
    identify imported libraries, accounting for aliased
    imports and namespace packages, and Call and
    Attribute nodes to detect library members.
       Following previous work, we consider any error
    in the generated code to be a hallucination (Lee
    et al., 2025), and operationalise the detection of
    two specific types. To detect library name halluci-
    nations, we compare imported libraries against the
    Python Package Index (PyPI) (PyPI, 2025), fol-
    lowing prior methodology (Krishna et al., 2025;
    Spracklen et al., 2025). To address mismatches be-
    tween import names and the registered PyPI name,
    we apply package name normalisation (PyPA,
    2025b).
       To detect library member hallucinations, we
    scrape the official documentation for each ground-
    truth library and check against it. We use docu-
    mentation from the latest version of each library,

    5.2   Ecosystem Generalisability

    To examine whether our observations extend be-
    yond the primary dataset, we conduct an additional
    experiment using CodeInsight, a separate corpus
    of code-generation tasks also sourced from Stack-
    Exchange. We sample 500 tasks and use an LLM to
    rewrite them to be language- and library-agnostic,

    subsequently generating Python, JavaScript, and
    Rust candidate libraries (yielding 140, 161, and
    184 distinct libraries, respectively). These lan-
    guages provide coverage across distinct package
    ecosystems and programming paradigms: Python
    and JavaScript are widely used dynamic lan-
    guages with large package ecosystems, while Rust
    is statically typed, compiled, and has been shown
    to be underutilised by LLMs compared with more
    established default choices (Twist et al., 2026). We
,   then follow the same experimental setup used pre-
    viously to evaluate library name hallucination be-
    haviour under year-based prompts and user mis-
    takes, for all LLMs in the study.

       The results show hallucination patterns broadly
    consistent with earlier findings. Python shows
    higher hallucination rates under user mistakes for
    this more diverse set of libraries, suggesting that
s   naming errors are more readily accepted for less
    widely known packages. For JavaScript, halluci-

    LLMs; despite the ecosystem’s well-known dy-

    12	---
    13	<!-- Frontmatter: single-line values; they feed literature-matrix.md via `rlab index`.
    14	     status: draft (in progress) -> ready (analyst self-check passed) -> complete (critical review passed).

    17	
    18	# Backstabber’s Knife Collection: A Review of Open Source Software Supply Chain Attacks
    19	
    20	- Authors: Ohm, Marc; Plate, Henrik; Sykosch, Arnold; Meier, Michael
    21	- Year / venue: 2020, Lecture Notes in Computer Science (book)
    22	- DOI: 10.1007/978-3-030-52683-2_2 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-52683-2_2
    23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
    24	
    25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
    26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
    27	
    28	**Source tier:** LNCS book chapter (per metadata), 2020. The analysed text is the arXiv v1 version (arXiv:2005.09535v1, 19 May 2020; p. 1) and may differ slightly from the published chapter. It is used as **background only**: pre-LLM, seminal (241 citations per metadata).
    29	
    30	## 1. Research objective
    31	- [A] Give a structured overview of how attackers inject malicious code into open-source dependency trees and trigger it. The aim is to support preventive and detective safeguards (p. 1).
    32	- [A] Provide a manually curated dataset of malicious packages used in real-world attacks (pp. 1–2).
    33	
    34	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
    35	- No formal RQs. There are two contributions (p. 2):
    36	  1. manual analysis and categorisation of 174 real malicious packages (2015–2019);
    37	  2. two attack trees, one for *injection* and one for *execution*.
    38	
    39	## 3. Methodology
    40	- Research design: [V] Qualitative and descriptive (pp. 4–5).
    41	  - Attack trees were built iteratively. Each malicious package or information source was mapped to a node, and a new node was added when none fitted.
    42	  - Packages were analysed and categorised by hand.
    43	- Approach — the attack trees (read from Fig. 2, p. 7, and Fig. 3, p. 9):
    44	  - [V] **Injection tree.** Root: "Injection of Malicious Code (into dependency tree)" (p. 7).
    45	    - **Create New Package**: {Trojan Horse; Typosquatting; Use After Free} (p. 7).
    46	    - **Infect Existing Package** (p. 7):
    47	      - Inject into Source: Pull Request as contributor; Commit as maintainer, via weak/compromised credentials or API tokens, or via social engineering to become maintainer.
    48	      - Inject during the Build: Compromise Build System, by manipulating the package download or running a malicious build on shared systems.
    49	      - Inject into Repository System: weak/compromised credentials or API tokens; exploit vulnerabilities; deploy in an alternative repository or mirror.
    50	  - [V] **Execution tree** (p. 9). Root: "Execute Malicious Behavior".
    51	    - During Different Life Cycle Phases: {Install Scripts; Test Case; Runtime}.
    52	    - Conditional Execution: {Application State; Dependency Tree; Operating System}.
    53	  - [A] **New packages.** Creating a new package "using a name that is not used by anybody else avoids interference with other legitimate project maintainers. However, such a package has to be discovered and referenced by downstream users", for example via typosquatting or by promoting a trojan horse (p. 7).
    54	  - [A] **Install-time execution.** "Such install scripts exist for Python and Node.js" and run automatically during installation (p. 8).
    55	  - [A] **Import-time execution.** In Python, runtime triggering can be achieved through code in `__init__.py`, which runs on `import` (p. 9).
    56	- Baselines or comparison conditions: not applicable (descriptive study).
    57	
    58	## 4. Dataset and sample
    59	- Data source(s):
    60	  - [V] The Snyk vulnerability database, language-specific security advisories and research blogs were reviewed between 2 July and 2 August 2019, with an update on 27 January 2020 (p. 4).
    61	  - [V] Malicious code was retrieved from deprecated mirrors, internet archives and research repositories, because the registries had removed it (p. 4).
    62	  - [V] Publication dates come from Libraries.io (p. 5).
    63	- Sample size (N) and unit:
    64	  - [V] 469 malicious packages identified; 59 proof-of-concept packages excluded; at least one malicious version obtained for 174 (p. 9).
    65	  - [V] Download success by registry (pp. 9–10): npm 109/374 (29.14%), PyPI 28/44 (63.64%), RubyGems 37/41 (90.24%), Maven Central 0/10.
    66	  - [V] Composition: npm 62.6%, PyPI 16.1%, RubyGems 21.3% (p. 10).
    67	- Sampling / selection method: [V] Every malicious package found in the sources whose code could be obtained (pp. 4, 9). This is a convenience sample of *disclosed* and *retrievable* attacks.
    68	- Data availability: [V] On GitHub, "access will be granted on justified request only due to ethical reasons" (p. 10).
    69	
    70	## 5. Experimental setup
    71	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Manual code analysis to confirm maliciousness and classify trigger, conditions, injection, objective, targeted OS and obfuscation. Clusters were found through code reuse and dependency relations (pp. 4–5, 11–16). The number of coders and their agreement are not reported.
    72	- Code availability: not applicable / not reported.
    73	
    74	## 6. Evaluation metrics
    75	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
    76	  - [V] Category shares per registry and overall (Figs. 6–11).
    77	  - [V] Days between publication and disclosure.
    78	  - [V] Levenshtein distance from a typosquat to its target.
    79	  - [V] Cluster size and timing (pp. 10–16).
    80	- Statistical testing: descriptive statistics only (mean, min, max, standard deviation, median) (pp. 11–12, 15). No tests.
    81	
    82	## 7. Key findings
    83	1. [V] **Exposure time.** On average a malicious package was available for 209 days before public reporting (median 67, max 1,216). PyPI had the highest average (p. 11).
    84	2. [V] **Install-time execution dominates.** 56% of packages trigger at install time, 43% at runtime and 1% in tests (p. 11).
    85	   - By registry (Fig. 6): npm 64% install / 34% runtime / 2% test; PyPI 96% install; RubyGems 100% runtime, because Ruby has no install hooks (p. 11).
    86	   - [I] The remaining 4% for PyPI appears to be runtime, based on the bar shading and arithmetic consistency with the overall 43%.
    87	3. [V] **Conditional execution.** 41% of packages check a condition (application state, dependency tree or OS) before running. This is an evasion technique against sandboxes (p. 12). PyPI and RubyGems packages mostly run unconditionally (p. 12).
    88	4. [V] **Typosquatting dominates injection.** 61% of packages mimic existing names. The mean Levenshtein distance to the target is 2.3 (median 1, max 11, e.g. `pythonkafka` → `kafka-python`). Common techniques: adding or removing hyphens, dropping letters, swapping commonly mistyped letters (p. 12).
    89	   - From Fig. 8: PyPI is 75% typosquatting and 25% trojan horse; overall trojan horse is 11% (p. 13).
    90	   - [V] Trojan horses are "a new package which consist of nothing but the malicious package", with "No meaningful typo-squatting targets" (p. 13).
    91	5. [V] **Objectives.** Most packages aim at data exfiltration (e.g. `~/.ssh/*`, `~/.npmrc`, environment variables). 34% are droppers, 5% backdoors, 3% denial-of-service and 3% financial gain (p. 13).
    92	   - 53% are OS-agnostic (p. 14) and 49% use obfuscation, mostly Base64/hex (pp. 14–15).
    93	6. [V] **Clusters.** 21 clusters cover 157 of the 174 packages (90%). The largest (crossenv) has 36 packages published in two waves. One cluster spans npm and RubyGems (pp. 15–16).
    94	7. [A] **Countermeasures.** These include multi-factor authentication for maintainers, "version pinning and disablement of install scripts for open source users", and build isolation. They should be "enforced by default" (p. 16).
    95	
    96	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
    97	- [A] The dataset is biased toward npm. No malicious packages could be obtained for Java (Maven) or PHP (p. 18).
    98	- [A] About 34% are droppers whose second-stage payload may be unavailable (p. 18).
    99	- [A] Most packages were downloaded from mirrors or archives (an injection vector listed in the tree). The authors argue they are still valid, since maliciousness was confirmed by hand (p. 18).
   100	- [A] The attack trees are not complete: they omit vectors not yet observed or described (p. 4).
   101	- [A] Selection of infection targets cannot yet be validated from the data (p. 7).
   102	
   103	## 9. Limitations we identified
   104	- [I] **Small PyPI sample.** Only 28 PyPI packages; the PyPI percentages rest on very few cases.
   105	- [I] **Sample biased toward detected attacks.** Only disclosed and retrievable attacks are included. Undetected or quickly deleted packages are missing, so the shares describe *detected* attacks.
   106	- [I] **Unknown reliability of the hand coding.** Single-pass manual categorisation with no reported inter-rater agreement.
   107	- [I] **Pre-LLM.** The attack tree has no node for discovery through automated recommendation, which is exactly the channel slopsquatting uses. Registry defences may have changed since 2019; the paper does not cover this.
   108	- [I] **Bar-chart readings.** Per-registry shares are read from bar charts (Figs. 6–11), whose text extraction is garbled. We checked Figs. 6 and 8 against the PDF images.
   109	
   110	## 10. Threats to validity
   111	- Internal: the classification is subjective, done by hand, with no agreement measure.
   112	- External: mostly npm; 2015–2019 only; registries and attacker tactics have evolved since.
   113	- Construct: "typosquatting" is decided by judgement of name similarity. "Trojan horse" is a residual category.
   114	- Statistical conclusion: descriptive only; the PyPI subset is small.
   115	- Reproducibility: the dataset is available on request (p. 10). The attack trees are fully shown (pp. 7, 9).
   116	
   117	## 11. Future research directions
   118	- Stated by authors [A]:
   119	  - collect existing safeguards and run a gap analysis against the attack vectors (p. 18);
   120	  - repository-wide scanning that exploits code reuse across campaigns (p. 18);
   121	  - supervised learning on the labelled dataset (p. 18);
   122	  - use the dataset as a benchmark, and continue curating it (p. 18).
   123	- Suggested by us [I]:
   124	  - extend the injection tree with an "AI-recommended name" discovery node (slopsquatting) under Create New Package;
   125	  - measure whether slopsquatted packages follow the same install-time and conditional-execution patterns.
   126	
   127	## 12. Relevance to our research
   128	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ2 (attack model: how a registered name becomes malicious execution on the victim), RQ3 (baseline countermeasures: disabling install scripts, pinning), RQ5 (background for designing a safe study).
   129	- How it informs our work [I]:
   130	  - **Placing slopsquatting in the tree.** It is a *Create New Package* attack, close to "trojan horse": a fresh name with no lookalike target. It differs from typosquatting in how victims find the package. Here the LLM supplies the "discovery and referencing" step that the authors identify as the obstacle for new packages (p. 7).
   131	  - **Installing is enough to be compromised.** Install-time execution is the main trigger on PyPI (96%) (p. 11), and import-time `__init__.py` execution is also possible (p. 9). An agent or user that runs `pip install` / `npm install` on a hallucinated name can be compromised immediately. A defence must act **before** installation.
   132	  - **Implication for a measurement study.** Use read-only registry metadata (no installs). Any dynamic analysis must run in a sandbox, since 41% of malicious packages run only under certain conditions (p. 12) and may evade sandboxes.
   133	  - **Implication for a lightweight defence.** Combine a pre-install existence/metadata check with the authors' user-side countermeasures: version pinning and disabled install scripts (p. 16). The edit-distance profile of typosquats (mean 2.3, median 1; p. 12) helps design a lookalike check for hallucinated names.
   134	  - Evidence strength: **moderate** as background (real-world data, but descriptive, pre-2020, small PyPI subset).
   135	
   136	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
   137	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
   138	|---|---|---|---|---|
   139	| RQ2 | Attack tree: new malicious packages enter via Create New Package (trojan horse, typosquatting, use-after-free) but must be "discovered and referenced" by downstream users | 7 | A | moderate |
   140	| RQ2 | 56% of 174 real malicious packages execute at install time (PyPI 96%, npm 64%); Python and Node.js support install scripts, and Python `__init__.py` runs on import | 8, 9, 11 | V | moderate |
   141	| RQ2 | 61% of malicious packages used typosquatting (PyPI 75%); mean edit distance to target 2.3, median 1 | 12, 13 | V | moderate |
   142	| RQ2 | Trojan-horse packages with no lookalike target are 11% overall and 25% on PyPI, the closest pre-LLM analogue to slopsquatted names | 13 | V (shares) / I (analogy) | weak |
   143	| RQ2 | Malicious packages stayed available for 209 days on average (median 67) before disclosure | 11 | V | moderate |
   144	| RQ4 | 41% of malicious packages execute only under conditions (app state, dependency tree, OS), which hinders sandbox-based dynamic detection | 12 | V | moderate |
   145	| RQ3 | Recommended user-side countermeasures: version pinning and disabling install scripts, enforced by default | 16 | A | weak |
   146	
   147	## 14. Key quotes
   148	> "such a package has to be discovered and referenced by downstream users in order to end up in the dependency trees of victim packages" (p. 7)
   149	
   150	> "Such install scripts exist for Python and Node.js, and may be used to perform pre- or post-installation activities." (p. 8)
   151	
   152	> "most malicious packages (56%) start their routines on installation" (p. 11)

dependency tree (e.g. npm/load-from-cwd-or-npm/3.0.2 ) or whether the package
is executed on a certain operating system (e.g. PyPI/libpeshka/0.6 ).
    The majority of packages published on PyPI and RubyGems execute uncon-
ditionally. For npm the ratio of conditional and unconditional execution is nearly
equal.

5.5     Injection of Malicious Package
In Figure 8 it is apparent that most (61%) malicious packages mimic
existing packages’ names via typosquatting. A deeper analysis of that
phenomenon revealed that the Levenshtein distance of an average typosquatting
package to its target is 2.3 (min = 0, max = 11, ρ = 2.05, x̃ = 1.0). In some cases
the typosquatting target is available from another package repository, e.g. the
Linux package repository apt under the exact same name. This is for instance
the case for python-sqlite. The maximum distance of 11 is reached in the case
of pythonkafka which targeted kafka-python. Common techniques are adding or
removing hyphens, leaving out single letters, or exchange of letters that are often
mistyped. An word that is targeted exceptionally often is ,,color” or, respectively,
its British English counterpart: ,,colour”.
    The second most common injection method was the infection of an existing
package. This may often be achieved with compromised credentials for the
repository system (e.g. npm/eslint-scope/3.7.2 ). In most cases, the exact infection
technique could not be determined in retrospect. This is because the related
source is often removed from the version control system or no further details
about the injection are made public. Hence, these packages are listed as infect
existing package.

## Critical review: 2026-11-12-package-hallucination-and-slopsquatting (8 analyses, all `status: ready`)

The harness blocks file writes, so I did not save a report file. If you want one on disk, the next free name is `/Users/makky/Downloads/AI-Research-Lab-main/research/2026-11-12-package-hallucination-and-slopsquatting/reports/critical-review-2026-11-12.md`. The `reports/` folder is currently empty.

**Result: 0 pass, 7 pass-with-minor-fixes, 1 fail (mirandapena2026empirical).**

- `rlab cite-check` passes for all 8 analyses.
- None of the 8 papers is retracted.
- `rlab validate` returns MISMATCH for 2 papers (liu2026packmonitor, raj2026names). The other 6 are verified.
- I checked every number in Key findings and the evidence tables against `fulltext.txt`. Unless a finding below says otherwise, the numbers and page refs match the paper.

---

### 1. liu2026packmonitor — pass-with-minor-fixes

1. **Analyst notes / Source tier: validation flag not recorded.**
   - Current: nothing is said about validation.
   - Actual: `rlab validate` gives `MISMATCH`. Crossref and OpenAlex match exactly, but the arXiv title similarity is only 0.854. The PDF itself is arXiv v2, which prints the ACM DOI and "Proc. ACM Softw. Eng. 3, ISSTA, Article ISSTA027" (p. 1).
   - Add: "rlab validate: MISMATCH caused only by the arXiv listing title differing from the published title (similarity 0.854). Crossref and OpenAlex verified; DOI printed in PDF (p. 1)."
2. **§3 Baselines: quote is not verbatim.**
   - Current: `SR and RAG "follow prior work [41]" (p. 11)`.
   - p. 11 actually says: "Following prior work on mitigating package hallucinations [41], we include three representative baselines".
   - Fix: replace with that verbatim wording, or remove the quotation marks.
3. **§5 Hallucination decision: wrong page for the definition.**
   - Current: "[V] a recommended package counts as hallucinated if it is not a valid PyPI name … (p. 12)".
   - p. 12 only defines the metrics. The definition is on p. 2 ("non-existent packages") and p. 6 (membership in an "official registry snapshot or a curated allowlist").
   - Fix: cite p. 2 and p. 6. Add [I]: the paper's own motivating example is an import-path vs install-name confusion ("google.protobuf" is a legitimate import path, "google-protobuf" is not a listed package; p. 6). The mask only guarantees that *some* listed name is produced.
4. **§12 Laptop feasibility: unsupported claim.**
   - Current: "It needs logits but no GPU".
   - The paper never says this. All runs were on 8×A100 (p. 12). The paper names "GPU or CPU specifications" only as a timing threat (p. 19).
   - Fix: "[I] Needs a locally decoded open-weight model exposing logits and its tokenizer. CPU-only operation is untested; all timings come from an A100 server (p. 12, p. 19). DFA loading of ≤0.25 s (p. 17) is a host-side cost and does not show the 7–8B decoding itself is laptop-feasible."
5. **§7 finding 1: fair comparison context missing.**
   - The "best baseline" RAG+SR on CodeLlama (1.30% PHR) comes with only 231 recommended packages, against 1,004 for vanilla (p. 13).
   - Add this clause here as well as in §9, so the evidence matrix does not cite 1.30% as a like-for-like rate.

### 2. djire2026evaluating — pass-with-minor-fixes

1. **§9 Internal inconsistencies, third bullet: wrong accusation.**
   - Current: "The conclusion says CD 'reduced hallucination in 19 of 32' … The results say CD is never lowest".
   - These two statements measure different things, and both are true:
     - From Table 4 (p. 7), CD is below Vanilla in exactly 19/32 cells: gemma-1b 4, gemma-4b 2, llama-8b 4, mistral 2, qwen-1.5b 4, qwen-3b 3, deepseek 0.
     - CD is the lowest strategy in no cell (p. 6).
   - The Nudging point is also misquoted. The conclusion gives Nudging the best trade-off "among the guided decoding strategies", and in the same paragraph says "Greedy decoding provides the strongest average trade-off, followed by Self-Refine and Nudging" (p. 11).
   - Corrected text: "[I] The conclusion calls Nudging the best trade-off 'among the guided decoding strategies' (p. 11), although the paper itself counts Greedy as a guided strategy (p. 2) and Greedy has the best trade-off (p. 8)."
   - Remove the CD claim.
2. **§9 first bullet: "18 of 32" mis-framed.**
   - The abstract says RAG "reduces the PHR in 18 of 32". In Table 4, RAG is below Vanilla in **24/32** cells and lowest in 19/32 (p. 7).
   - Corrected: "Abstract '18 of 32' (p. 1) matches neither the 24/32 reductions nor the 19/32 'lowest' count derivable from Table 4 (p. 7)."
3. **New §9 item: author claim contradicted by the paper's own table.**
   - p. 6 says RAG lowers PHR in Python, Ruby and Rust "without increasing PHR for any model in these languages".
   - Table 4 shows mistral-7b Rust going from 18.6 to 20.8 under RAG (p. 7).
   - Add as [I], citing p. 6 vs p. 7.
4. **§3 Nudging: unexplained surrogate design.**
   - Current: "[V] Nudging: the surrogate is the largest model in the family".
   - Add [I]: llama-8b and mistral-7b are single-model families, and gemma-4b, deepseek-6.7b and qwen-3b are the largest of their families (p. 3). For 5 of 8 models the surrogate would be the model itself. The paper does not explain this (p. 5).
5. **§4 Sample: wrong unit.**
   - Current: "Generated packages per configuration range from 1,470 to 32,337 (Table 3, p. 6)".
   - Table 3 covers vanilla decoding only, per model × language.
   - Fix: "…per model–language cell under vanilla decoding".
6. **§13 Evidence table, RQ3 "Guided decoding … needs internal access" row: labels mixed.**
   - The row is labelled V but mixes our [I] about access with [V] results.
   - Fix: split it into a V row (DoLa 38.0% average; syntax errors) and an I row (white-box access needed).
   - The RQ5 row "Latency/overhead … not reported" is labelled A, but it is our observation. Relabel it I.
7. **§5: import→distribution mapping consequence missing.**
   - The analysis notes that the code-generation mapping (`cv2` → `opencv-python`) is not reported.
   - Add [I]: in the code-generation extension, imports are "validated against the same registry snapshots" (p. 6). Unregistered import names such as `cv2` therefore probably count as hallucinations, which inflates the code-generation counts in Fig. 1.

### 3. liu2026mitigating — pass-with-minor-fixes

1. **Frontmatter `main_finding`: wrong about Valid-Rate.**
   - Current: "…keeping Valid-Rate and HumanEval within ±2%".
   - Table II (p. 7): Valid-Rate rises +6.4% on edit prompts. On unseen prompts Qwen3 falls 0.7990 → 0.7434 (−7.0%) and DeepSeekCoder rises 0.7978 → 0.8909. Only HumanEval stays within ±2% (Table VI, p. 9).
   - Corrected: "…Valid-Rate rises on average (+6.4% edit) but falls 7% for Qwen3 on unseen prompts; HumanEval within ±2%."
2. **§13 cost row: unit not supported.**
   - Current: "editing ~83 s + localization ~24 s per model".
   - Table V gives averages "across models" and does not define the unit (per fold of 50 edit cases is likely) (p. 9).
   - Fix: "…per edit run (unit undefined), averaged across models".
3. **§5 cost table: cheaper baselines omitted.**
   - DINM has a lower edit time (11.97 s) and localization time (0.92 s) than BOUND, and ROME has a lower test time (10.86 s) (Table V, p. 9).
   - So the paper's statement that BOUND's editing "is lower than ROME, MEMIT, and Full-FT" is true only because DINM is left out.
   - Add these rows, or a note.
4. **§7: Full-FT result omitted.**
   - On DeepSeekCoder Edit50, Full-FT beats BOUND: Package-HR 0.0188 vs 0.0745, Valid-Rate 0.9500 vs 0.9480 (Table II, p. 7).
   - Add this. It qualifies "best overall balance".
5. **§9: missing threat (hallucinated-name overlap).**
   - Edit cases use the model's own hallucinated names (p. 5). The unseen prompts come from the same per-model pool and may contain the same recurring fake names.
   - Add [I]: "unseen" generalisation may partly be suppression of memorised names. Name overlap between folds is not reported.

### 4. spracklen2026llm — pass-with-minor-fixes

1. **§9 "Surgical" is overstated: the gradient-ascent (GA) evidence is missing.**
   - DeepSeek-7B: GA reaches 7.2% HR with unchanged utility (Avg 66.95 vs 66.98) and code KL 0.0031, against 0.0796 for AU (Table 1, p. 10).
   - DeepSeek-16B: GA keeps Avg 77.35, against 73.17 for AU.
   - Add [I]: AU wins on HR, but GA dominates on drift and utility. The result is a trade-off, not dominance.
2. **New §9 item: tuning and checkpoint selection favour AU.**
   - Learning rates: AU 5×10⁻⁵ (7B) and 2×10⁻⁵ (16B); GA and NPO 1×10⁻⁵.
   - Epochs: GA uses 1 outer / 10 inner epochs.
   - Checkpoints: GA and NPO report the "final" checkpoint, while AU, CE-only and NPO-only report a selected one (60, or "50 restarted") (Table 3, p. 19).
   - Add as [I], comparison fairness.
3. **§9 Internal inconsistencies: one more to add.**
   - Appendix D says the 16B AU result is "a restart from a similar configured run at checkpoint 60" (p. 18). Table 3 lists the checkpoint as "50 restarted" (p. 19).
   - §5 currently repeats "checkpoint 60" as fact. Mark it as inconsistent.
4. **§7 finding 3: missing contrast.**
   - Add that HumanEval on 16B drops 81.1 → 73.2, while GA keeps 79.9 (p. 10).

### 5. raj2026names — pass-with-minor-fixes

1. **Source tier / Analyst notes: verification status misstated.**
   - Current: "`metadata.json` verification is 'single-source (openalex)'" and "Verification is single-source".
   - `metadata.json` actually shows: `status: MISMATCH`; arXiv ok (1.0); OpenAlex ok (1.0); Crossref "not found". Crossref cannot find it because the DOI is a Zenodo (DataCite) DOI. PDF identity is only "probable": no arXiv ID is printed, only "Version: v1, arXiv, August 2026" (p. 1).
   - Corrected: "rlab validate: MISMATCH (arXiv and OpenAlex agree; the Zenodo DOI is not in Crossref); PDF identity probable."
2. **§5 / §9: standard-library (stdlib) handling not reported.**
   - The extractor keeps every top-level import module from the AST (p. 5), and any PyPI 404 is "fake" (p. 5). Without a stdlib filter, `import os`/`json`/`sys` would trigger retries.
   - The paper never says how stdlib modules are excluded. A grep finds no "stdlib", "standard library" or "built-in".
   - Add "Stdlib handling: not reported", plus [I] that this directly affects give-up rates.
3. **§7 finding 4 [I]: stronger evidence available from the paper itself.**
   - The reconciler table maps "`pil` to `Pillow`" (p. 7). But `pil` returns 200, so by design the reconciler can never fire for it (p. 5). Instead it is flagged 36 times as a "squat" (Table 3, p. 8).
   - The 404 half also contains import-name errors: `pkg-resources` (the module `pkg_resources` ships with setuptools) is listed as an invention (p. 8). The paper also counts `faiss` as a "hallucinatory variant" in the bait test (p. 11).
   - Add these page-referenced points. Doing so moves the import-name argument partly from general knowledge to paper evidence.
4. **§13 RQ4 row "fixing extraction … cut give-up from 79% to ~29%": strength too high.**
   - Currently V / moderate. The versions were run on different, overlapping prompt sets (70, 58, 60 and 300 prompts; Table 1, p. 7) with no fixed comparison set.
   - Change strength to weak, and add "different prompt sets".
5. **§9 (optional): factual error in the paper's related work.**
   - Add [I]: the paper attributes the term "slopsquatting" to Spracklen et al. (2024) (p. 2). The paper gives no evidence for this attribution.
   - Its 3-item reference list (p. 15) supports the weak-grounding point.

### 6. mirandapena2026empirical — fail (the repair claim in the evidence table contradicts the paper's own Table 5)

1. **§7 finding 6, §13 RQ3 row 3, frontmatter `main_finding`, §12: wrong RIF claim.**
   - Current: "The RIF does not fall and increases on Odex" / "does not reduce the hallucination share (RIF)" / "LLM repair improves execution, not hallucinations".
   - Table 5 (p. 10) shows RIF falls sharply on DS-1000 for every model and every repair method, e.g. claude-3 9.1 → 2.7, Gemma2 22.3 → 8.1, Qwen3 25.4 → 6.1. It rises on Odex for the small models, and is roughly flat on BigCode.
   - The analysis repeats the authors' "In most cases, there is no improvement in fixing hallucinations" (p. 10) as [V], but their own table contradicts it.
   - Corrected: "[V] RIF falls on DS-1000 for all models (e.g. 9.1 → 2.7), is roughly flat on BigCode, and rises on Odex for the small models (e.g. Qwen3 31.3 → 55.6) (p. 10). [A] The authors summarise this as 'no improvement in most cases' (p. 10), which overstates the table." Update the main_finding and the evidence row to match.
2. **§9 "Abstract ranges are not traceable" and §7 finding 1: partly wrong.**
   - The abstract's "14-85% of library hallucinations" is exactly Pyright's IFR range in Table 10 (0.14–0.85, p. 20).
   - Correct the bullet: "14–85% = Pyright IFR range (p. 20). '16–70%' and '8.1–40%' could not be matched (Pyright all-error recall is 0.16–0.82, p. 6; no-repair RIF is 8.1–44.9, p. 10)."
3. **§13 RQ4 row "Over 30% … in Odex/BigCode": overgeneralised.**
   - "Ambiguous output" is 30.3% on Odex but 26.6% on BigCode (Table 3, p. 8).
   - Fix: "≈27–30% (Odex 30.3%, BigCode 26.6%) of sampled hallucinations; authors say 'over 30%' (p. 9)."
4. **§7 finding 2/3 and §13 row 1: detection vs correct-reason detection.**
   - The "3–85%" detection range is recall. In manual analysis, static tools were right "for the right reason" (TP) in only 37.6% (DS-1000), 4.0% (Odex) and 10.0% (BigCode) of sampled cases (Table 2, p. 8).
   - Add this to the evidence row so the matrix does not overstate detection.
5. **§9 "Package-level results are not separated out": inaccurate.**
   - Table 3 has a "Library" cause category: 14.7 / 6.6 / 6.0% (p. 8).
   - Corrected: "Package-level causes are a small share (Library category 6–15%, p. 8); the detection metrics are not broken down by it."
6. **Source tier: open decision.**
   - The analysis handles the TMLR claim honestly. It still needs the orchestrator to decide: re-resolve the metadata, or keep the preprint tier until the OpenReview acceptance is checked.
   - Do not hand-edit `metadata.json`.

### 7. twist2026library — pass-with-minor-fixes

1. **§3 Name check and §12 "Inherit the methods": the method does not solve import names.**
   - Current: "[V] Names are compared with PyPI using PyPA name normalisation (p. 4)" and "Adopt the PyPI name normalisation".
   - p. 4 claims normalisation addresses "mismatches between import names and the registered PyPI name". PyPA normalisation only folds case and `-_.` characters; it cannot map `dateutil` → `python-dateutil` or `cv2` → `opencv-python`. The paper's own evidence shows this: the dateutil case had to be corrected manually (p. 15), and the one false positive is `pywintypes` (provided by pywin32) (p. 15).
   - Add [I]: the check effectively tests whether the import name exists on PyPI. Import names registered by third parties therefore count as valid.
   - Replace "Adopt the PyPI name normalisation" with "adopt normalisation plus an explicit import→distribution map".
2. **§4 Sample size: unsupported.**
   - Current: "Ecosystem study: one response per task … (pp. 7, 20)".
   - p. 7 says "we then follow the same experimental setup used previously", which implies three responses. I found no statement of one response.
   - Fix: remove "one response per task", or mark it "not stated".
3. **§5: registry lists for the other ecosystems missing.**
   - Add: JavaScript names are validated against `all-the-package-names` (jsDelivr, 2026) and Rust against the Cargo registry (p. 20). Neither snapshot is dated precisely.
   - A "January 2026 snapshot" is cited only for the top-PyPI list in the rarity study (p. 19). It does not cover the main check.
4. **Frontmatter `main_finding`: imprecise.**
   - "user typos/fake names (up to 26%/99%)" refers to one-character typos only. Multi-character typos reach 79.44% (p. 6).
   - Fix: "one-char typos up to 26%, multi-char up to 79%, fake names up to 99%".

### 8. ohm2020backstabbers — pass-with-minor-fixes

1. **Source tier: wording conflicts with §3 of the standards.**
   - Current: "LNCS book chapter … used as **background only**".
   - "Background only" is the tier-4 wording. Metadata gives a peer-reviewed proceedings chapter (`book-chapter`, Springer LNCS), which is tier 2 or better.
   - Corrected: "Tier 2 (LNCS proceedings chapter per metadata); used as background because it predates LLMs, not because of source quality."
2. **§7 finding 5: number missing.**
   - "Most packages aim at data exfiltration" should carry the number the paper gives: 55% (p. 16–17, "(55%)" on p. 18).
3. **§12 RQ2 placement: useful context missing.**
   - Add [V]: some typosquats have Levenshtein distance 0 because they reuse a name that exists in another repository (e.g. `python-sqlite` from apt) (p. 12).
   - This is the pre-LLM analogue of the cross-ecosystem and import-name confusions in raj2026names, twist2026library and liu2026packmonitor.

---

## Cross-paper notes for the evidence matrix

**A. How each paper decides that a name is hallucinated. The definitions are not comparable, so do not pool rates.**

| Key | Ground truth | Snapshot date | Stdlib | Names checked | Registered-but-malicious names |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| liu2026packmonitor | PyPI list, 706,618 names via official API (p. 12, 19) | not reported | n/a (only `pip install` args) | install args after `pip install` | count as valid |
| djire2026evaluating | registry ∪ stdlib manifests (p. 3–4) | 2026-03-04 | Python and Ruby corrected; JS/Rust unclear (p. 5) | recommended names; code-gen imports, mapping unstated | valid |
| liu2026mitigating | on PyPI **and** ≥1 release before model cutoff (p. 5) | ~2026-06-14 (ref., p. 11); cutoffs unreported | not reported | recommendations; code-gen imports mapped by the base LLM (p. 7) | post-cutoff registrations count as hallucinated (the only paper that does this) |
| spracklen2026llm | static PyPI snapshot (p. 20) | not reported | not reported | `pip install` lines + model answers to "required"/"useful" (p. 8) | valid; authors flag oracle poisoning (p. 12) |
| raj2026names | live PyPI JSON API; 404 = fake, 200 → classifier (p. 5) | live, undated | not reported | import names (AST) + `pip install` in fences | **flagged** if the metadata looks suspicious |
| mirandapena2026empirical | installed benchmark environment + builtins (p. 4, 18) | n/a | builtins allowed | imports/members at runtime | not addressed |
| twist2026library | PyPI + PyPA normalisation (p. 4); npm list; crates (p. 20) | not reported (study Jan 2026) | not reported | import names (AST) | valid |

- **Import vs install names.** raj2026names and twist2026library treat the same strings oppositely:
  - Twist counts any registered import name as valid.
  - Raj flags registered import names (`pil`, `faiss`, `skimage`) as hallucinated "squats".
  - Djire's code-generation mode and Twist probably count unregistered import names (`cv2`) as hallucinations.
  - For RQ4, record this as a contradiction caused by method, not by data.
- **Stdlib.** Only djire2026evaluating quantifies the stdlib error (+7.6 to +9.4 pp for Python, p. 5). For the other five Python papers, base rates may carry that inflation. This is a matrix-level caveat.
- **Release-date cutoff.** Only liu2026mitigating uses one. Every other paper scores names registered after the model's training (including attacker squats) as correct, which undercounts exploitable names. That bears directly on RQ2.

**B. Hardware and access needed by each defence (RQ3/RQ5).**

| Defence | Access | Hardware actually used |
|---|---|---|
| PackMonitor (logit masking) | white-box logits + tokenizer; no training | 8×A100 (p. 12); CPU untested |
| Greedy / RAG / Self-Refine (djire2026evaluating) | black-box (RAG needs an index) | "single GPU", type unreported; no latency data |
| CD / DoLa / ALCD / Nudging (djire2026evaluating) | logits or hidden states, sometimes two models | same as above |
| BOUND (liu2026mitigating) | weights + gradients, LoRA training; adapter only at inference | 8×A100 (p. 6) |
| Adaptive unlearning (spracklen2026llm) | full-parameter fine-tuning | MI210/MI300, 12–24 h runs (p. 8, 19) |
| raj2026names | black-box; network calls to the PyPI JSON API + small RF/rule | API models (Groq); no local inference |
| Static tools + grammar (mirandapena2026empirical) | CPU static analysis; grammar decoding needs local llama.cpp | M2, 24 GB RAM (p. 17); +12 s per request (p. 11) |
| Prompting / PyPI tool (twist2026library) | black-box; the model must choose to call the tool | API only |
| ohm2020backstabbers | user-side: pin versions, disable install scripts (p. 16) | n/a |

- Only mirandapena2026empirical actually ran on a laptop-class machine.
- "Local" in raj2026names is the model class, not the deployment.

**C. Contradictions and duplicated data.**

- **SFT numbers are not independent.** PackMonitor's Package4U vanilla and SFT figures (16.14 / 26.28 → 2.66 / 10.27%) and the HumanEval drops (−26.9 / −14.0) are quoted from Spracklen et al. [41] (liu2026packmonitor p. 4, 14, 16). In the matrix, cite them to spracklen2024we, not as a replication.
- **HFuzzer link.** liu2026mitigating shares authors with zhao2025hfuzzer, and PackMonitor uses HFuzzer as its main benchmark. These three are not independent groups.
- **RAG is unstable in both studies that test it.** It slightly raises hallucination in PackMonitor (p. 12–13), and raises JavaScript PHR by 12.7 pp in djire2026evaluating (p. 6). The direction is consistent; the size differs by ecosystem.
- **Self-refine with and without registry feedback.** In liu2026mitigating the loop gets validity feedback (p. 5); in djire2026evaluating that is unreported. Their results are not comparable.
- **Fake names supplied by the user.** djire2026evaluating (adversarial vanilla 46.6–92.5%, p. 9), twist2026library (fake-name THR 20.7–99.2%, p. 6) and raj2026names (bait refusal 6/10 or 9/10, p. 1 vs p. 11) all measure compliance with names supplied by the user. That is a typosquat-amplification threat, not spontaneous invention, and the metrics differ.
- **Relative vs absolute reductions.** liu2026mitigating (−65.4%) and spracklen2026llm (−88%) report relative reductions on deliberately hallucination-heavy prompt sets (selected for Sample-HR > 0.5, or hand-picked). twist2026library shows near-0% under ordinary prompts (p. 5). Report absolute residual rates and the selection method next to any reduction figure.
- **Utility evidence is weak everywhere.**
  - PackMonitor's HumanEval check cannot trigger the intervention (no `pip install` in HumanEval).
  - liu2026mitigating's Qwen3 baseline of 23.29% pass@1 looks off.
  - spracklen2026llm 16B loses 7.9 pp on HumanEval.
  - Mark all utility claims as weak.
- **Persistence evidence for RQ2 is thin in this batch.** Only raj2026names reports names recurring across two same-family models (p. 10; small n, labels unaudited). Twist and Djire do not report it.
